title: Brazil protects 1.6 million acres, creates 4 Amazon reserves, and expands Caatinga park
content:
More than 1.6 million acres of Brazilian ecosystems have been placed under protection, expanding conservation efforts in a country considered one of the most ecologically important on Earth.
The newly protected area spans parts of the Amazon and the Caatinga. The measures aim to preserve biodiversity while supporting local communities and Indigenous territories.
Here's what to know
According to an Instagram post from actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announced on September 8 that four Sustainable Development Reserves would be established in the Amazon and that Sete Cidades National Park in the Caatinga would be enlarged.
All four reserves are in the region around the BR-319 highway, and they are meant to safeguard biodiversity while helping defend Indigenous Peoples' ancestral territories.
In Piauí, Sete Cidades National Park is being expanded by more than 17,000 acres (6,900 hectares). DiCaprio said the added protection benefits threatened species, including the endemic Cerrado Little Brown Bat.
Altogether, these new protections total more than 1.6 million acres (676,000 hectares).
More background
This step follows Brazil's establishment of the Rio Tanaru Indigenous Peoples National Park in June 2026.
Protecting intact ecosystems can preserve wildlife habitat, store planet-cooling carbon, and ease pressure from destructive land use.
Sustainable Development Reserves are designed to both conserve nature and to support the people who live in and depend on these landscapes. That can help traditional and local communities maintain livelihoods tied to standing forests, rather than seeing those areas cleared or degraded.
Healthier forests help regulate rainfall, stabilize regional climates, and protect freshwater systems that millions of people rely on directly or indirectly. Stronger protection for Indigenous territories also aligns with long-standing evidence that Indigenous stewardship is among the most effective forms of conservation.
What's being done?
The designations also come with major funding commitments. DiCaprio said more than $47 million is tied to sustainable forest management, along with more than $46 million for restoration and territorial initiatives.
The money is expected to help pay for territorial protection, restoration work, community-led projects, and forest management.
DiCaprio also said the designations received support from @andesamazonfund, Re:wild, @artintoacres, @bezosearthfund, @moorefound, and the Wyss Foundation.
He wrote that these are "important efforts to protect critical ecosystems while supporting the communities who live in and depend on them."
Where can I learn more?
Brazil's new reserves are part of an effort to slow deforestation, repair damaged landscapes, and rebuild the country's environmental vigor. The stories below look at how policy shifts, better monitoring, and reforestation work are affecting the Amazon and other ecosystems across Brazil.
• Across the Amazon, surging deforestation spurred the Brazilian government into stronger conservation action.
• Brazil's native seed networks face obstacles even as its 30-million-acre reforestation plan moves forward.
• In Brazil, improved monitoring helped the Atlantic Forest reach its lowest deforestation in 40 years.
Protected areas tend to have the biggest impact when enforcement, restoration, and tangible political support back them.

title: Partnership with Qatar a key pillar in addressing global humanitarian crises, says UNHCR official
content:
Representative of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to Qatar Ahmed Lotfy Mohsen has affirmed that the strategic partnership with Qatar serves as a pivotal pillar in addressing global humanitarian crises.
Speaking to the Qatar News Agency (QNA), he stated that Qatar – represented by government bodies and charitable institutions – has, through its close co-operation with the UN agency, provided financial contributions totaling $440mn since 2010.
These funds, Mohsen said, have supported protection programmes and provided life-saving assistance to forcibly displaced persons worldwide.
He added that Qatar’s support extends beyond the financial realm to include logistical and in-kind assistance.
This includes, the official said, facilitating the transport of relief supplies to acute crisis zones – such as Afghanistan and Lebanon – as well as playing a prominent diplomatic role in fostering the stability and dialogue necessary for implementing voluntary return and local integration programmes.
On the actual impact on the ground, Mohsen noted that the support included $40mn provided through the Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD) since 2019 in the form of flexible, unearmarked funding.
This, he said, granted the UNHCR exceptional flexibility to respond rapidly to emergencies and direct resources toward the most underfunded operations, thereby ensuring the continuity of essential services such as healthcare, education, and shelter.
Regarding innovative financing tools and Islamic philanthropy, Mohsen noted that total contributions from Qatar – comprising Zakat and voluntary charity – since 2018 have amounted to nearly $145mn.
This includes a strategic agreement signed by Qatar Charity (QC) last June to contribute $10mn to the Global Islamic Fund for Refugees (GIFR).
The UN official stated that the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) – convening under the theme Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All and coinciding with the 75th anniversary of the 1951 Refugee Convention – marks a pivotal moment to reflect on the legacy of international protection and to reaffirm the commitment to upholding the dignity and rights of the forcibly displaced.
He added that escalating global humanitarian challenges and the unprecedented number of displaced persons necessitate active international solidarity and the building of effective partnerships.
Mohsen pointed out that the strategic partnership between the UNHCR and Qatar serves as a successful, real-world model of constructive co-operation between governments and international organisations in addressing complex humanitarian crises.

title: Morocco plans nearly MAD 4 billion investment in mental health by 2030
content:
The Ministry of Health and Social Protection launched the “Mental Health 2030” Plan Thursday in Rabat, a national framework aimed at expanding access to mental health services, improving the quality of care and promoting mental health services.
The plan marks a new phase in Morocco’s public health policy. Its goal is to promote mental health and prevent mental disorders, while supporting rehabilitation and social reintegration.
By 2030, the plan aims to significantly expand mental health care capacity. The number of beds is expected to rise from 2,466 to about 4,728. The number of psychiatric hospitals will increase from 10 to 17. Intermediate-care facilities will rise from four to 24. The expansion is intended to ensure the availability of mental health services across all regions of the Kingdom.
Nearly MAD 4 billion in funding
The implementation of the “Mental Health 2030” Plan will receive nearly MAD 4 billion in funding to support the various measures and actions planned. The plan also seeks to bring services closer to citizens by strengthening the role of primary health care and intermediate-care facilities, improving coordination with hospital and specialized facilities, and establishing a territorial organization adapted to the needs of local populations.
The plan places particular emphasis on strengthening human resources. The number of psychologists in the public sector is expected to increase from 32 to 786. Annual psychiatrist training capacity will rise from 36 to 124. Annual training capacity for nurses specializing in mental health will increase from 490 to 750. A legal framework governing the profession of psychologist will also be established.
Abderrazak Ouanas, chairman of the Lalla Oumkeltoum Foundation for Mental Health, praised the Royal Solicitude extended to people experiencing mental health vulnerabilities. He said the foundation’s presidency by Princess Lalla Oumkeltoum reflects an enlightened royal vision that places mental health among the national priorities of the health sector.
Read also : Health Ministry launches Mental Health Plan 2030
The implementation of the plan represents a structured and ambitious response to a human and societal imperative. It requires the mobilization and coordination of efforts by all stakeholders. Mental health is an essential determinant of public health and social cohesion.
Ouanas reaffirmed the foundation’s commitment to this national effort and its determination to make its full institutional contribution to the success of the plan, which marks a new era in the promotion of mental health in line with the Royal Solicitude.
Awatef Belakhel of the World Health Organization (WHO) office in Morocco said the plan reflects a human-centered vision focused on strengthening human rights, combating social stigma and ensuring adequate support and assistance. Mental health is a fundamental right, an essential condition for individual and collective development, and an indispensable pillar of universal health coverage.
Fadoua Rahhaoui of the Ministry of Health and Social Protection’s Noncommunicable Diseases Division reviewed the plan’s main strategic priorities and the initiatives that could deliver results in the short and medium term. She said these initiatives include building and upgrading mental health infrastructure, strengthening initial and continuing training, developing new skills and modernizing the legal framework.

title: Mali: One Man's Quest to End Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) in Mali
content:
United Nations — After years of defending FGM as a cultural practice, Sidi Haidara came to a realization: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.
In Mali, an estimated nine out of ten women and girls have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM). And for years, Sidi Haidara, a father and recognized leader in his community, believed the practice was simply part of life.
Like many people in his community in central Mali, he saw it as a tradition passed down through generations - one that should be preserved.
Today, he walks from village to village with a very different message: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
His story goes beyond one man's personal transformation. Across parts of West and Central Africa, FGM remains deeply rooted - with Mali having one of the highest rates in the region and no laws that specifically criminalize the practice. Even recently, some men in Mali have launched an all-male pro-FGM campaign on the grounds of protecting tradition.
In places where social norms are deeply entrenched, change often begins with trusted voices from within the community - voices like Haidara's.
After spending years defending female genital mutilation, Sidi Haidara now leads community dialogues in Mopti, Mali, encouraging families to protect girls' rights and abandon the practice. Credit: UN Women/Dieneba Deme
How UN Women and partners are shifting mindsets and empowering new anti-FGM advocates in Mali
"I used to believe that this practice was part of our traditions and needed to be preserved", says Haidara.
Nothing suggested that he would one day become one of the people advocating for its abandonment.
His perspective began to change after taking part in training sessions, workshops, and community dialogues organized through the Men and Boys as Agents of Change project, implemented by UN Women with financial support from the Government of Germany.
As he listened to different experiences and learned about the consequences of FGM, he began questioning his beliefs - beliefs he had never challenged before. He also came to understand that lasting change cannot simply be imposed - it grows through dialogue, trust, and community ownership.
"UN Women's trainings - with the support of Germany - transformed my understanding of female genital mutilation. I learned about the physical, psychological, and social consequences that this practice imposes on girls."
How to end FGM in Mali: Begin with listening, questioning, and conversing
"Today, I regularly organize awareness-raising sessions with families, religious leaders, young people, and women", he explains.
Rather than telling people what to think, he encourages conversations about what it means to protect girls and challenges long-held beliefs through dialogue.
Little by little, those conversations are making a difference. "I can see change: more parents are asking questions, several families are abandoning female genital mutilation, and discussions about protecting girls have become more open."
"I am convinced that protecting girls today means investing in the future of our entire community."
People can change - and so can social norms
Haidara's journey is part of a broader movement taking place across the regions of Mopti and Gao in Mali.
With support from the Government of Germany, UN Women works alongside religious and traditional leaders, women, young people, and men like Haidara who are committed to community-driven initiatives that prevent violence against women and girls and challenge harmful social norms.
To date, 50 community initiatives have been implemented across the two regions, while eight community-dialogue platforms provide spaces for people to discuss girls' rights, their protection, and ways to prevent gender-based violence.
For Haidara, abandoning a harmful practice is about more than leaving a tradition behind. It is about giving girls the opportunity to grow up safely, stay in school, and shape their own futures.
His journey shows that some of the most meaningful changes happen when those who once upheld harmful social norms become the people helping to transform them.
Haidara knows traditions do not change overnight. But every conversation creates an opportunity for reflection. Every family that chooses to protect its daughters helps write a different future from the one that generations before them inherited.
In Mopti and Gao, these conversations are showing that lasting change does not necessarily begin with a new law or policy. More often, it begins when communities themselves decide to imagine a different future for their girls.
Source: UNFPA
IPS UN Bureau

title: 'We will sow' — Odesa farmers defiant in face of relentless Russian assaults
content:
'We will sow' — Odesa farmers defiant in face of relentless Russian assaults
Volodymyr Varbanets, 76, a farmer, stands in the grain warehouse in Odesa Oblast, Ukraine, in August 2026. (Karina Piliuhina / The Kyiv Independent)
ODESA OBLAST — Volodymyr Varbanets sinks his hands into a mound of wheat, letting the golden kernels slip between his fingers.
This year brought an unusually good harvest, the best since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion, he says. Behind him, hundreds of metric tons of wheat, barley, lentils, and peas fill the farm's warehouses.
"But we cannot sell it," he sighs.
For more than 20 years, Varbanets has worked this land, sowing and harvesting crops across 206 hectares. At 76, he still climbs behind the wheel of his tractor or combine. Three of the men who once worked on the farm have been mobilized, leaving him, his son, and another worker to tend the fields.
Normally, by late August, trucks would already be carrying his harvest from the farm to the three deep-water ports of the Greater Odesa logistics hub about 50 kilometers south. From there, it would be loaded onto commercial cargo vessels and shipped across the Black Sea to markets worldwide.
"We cannot sell it."
But this year, the harvest remains in the warehouse.
Since mid-July, Russia has intensified its attacks on Odesa's ports and adjacent infrastructure. Although the ports remain technically open, fewer ships now dare to enter this new maritime kill zone.
"The ports are almost blocked," says Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association Ukrport.
'Ship Hunting' Campaign
On July 13, a Russian strike on a Togolese-flagged cargo vessel killed five people and injured 10 as it unloaded mineral fertilizers at the port of Odesa.
Six days later, three Russian cruise missiles struck the Golden Leo, a civilian bulk carrier loaded with corn, shortly after it left Chornomorsk. The attack killed 10 people, including nine crew members from India and Syria, and a Ukrainian maritime pilot. The damaged vessel sank a week later in the Black Sea.
"The corridor is not working, the ports are standing still, nobody is taking grain."
Both ships were traveling the maritime corridor used by merchant ships to reach Greater Odesa's three deep-water ports: Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi. Ukraine established the maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia did not renew the agreement that Turkey and the United Nations had brokered separately with each side to allow for the export of grain from Ukrainian ports. Ukrainian strikes on Russian naval facilities and warships opened up the corridor for commercial shipping.
Barinov describes the increase in Russian attacks on civilian commercial vessels in the Black Sea this summer as a systematic targeting campaign rather than sporadic hits.
"It's ship hunting," says Barinov.
In July, 169 vessels entered the ports of Greater Odesa. By late August, only one or two ships a day were arriving, according to Barinov.
Container lines were among the first to suspend calls, he says. Their ships run on fixed schedules and cannot afford to wait indefinitely for safe passage. Bulk carriers transporting grain or iron ore have more flexible schedules, but Barinov says even those operators are increasingly reluctant to enter Odesa.
Some shipowners have offered crews substantially higher pay to make the journey, he adds. But at some point the problem is no longer one of schedules, freight rates, or insurance premiums.
"They are afraid for their lives," Barinov says. "It's not a matter of money."
Working at a loss
The drop in traffic has come at the height of Ukraine's harvest season.
Between Aug. 1 and Aug. 26, Ukraine exported around 1.42 million metric tons of agricultural products, around one-third of the possible export volume with full logistics access, the Agriculture Ministry estimates. Grain was hit hardest, with exports at 822,000 metric tons, around one-fifth of the potential volume.
"The corridor is not working, the ports are standing still, nobody is taking grain," says Varbanets, looking at his harvest. "And if somebody does take grain, then it is for next to nothing."
Last year, he says, even the cheapest wheat sold for around Hr 11,000 ($265) a ton. Today, buyers are offering him roughly Hr 3,500 to 4,000 ($84 to $96). Lentils that previously sold for around Hr 25,000 ($602) a ton now fetch about Hr 15,000 ($361).
At the same time, the farm's costs for diesel, fertilizer, and spare parts have risen.
"We are not even working for zero," he says. "We are working at a loss."
Varbanets still needs to pay his workers and taxes, and settle with the owners of the land he leases. In a few weeks, he has to sow again.
read also
The grain can be kept in his warehouse for about a year, Varbanets adds. But it has to be moved regularly to preserve its quality; at his farm, he uses a loader to shift it from one part of the warehouse to another.
"Grain has to be constantly in motion," he explains.
The grain elevators have little room for new deliveries. Until enough ships arrive to carry the stored grain away, they cannot empty, leaving farmers with fewer places to send their harvest.
No Good Alternative
Ukraine has other routes for moving its exports, but none match the capacity of the deep-water ports around Odesa.
Ukraine’s Danube ports of Izmail and Reni became crucial after Russia's 2022 blockade and, as ships retreat from Greater Odesa, have taken on more traffic. For farmers like Varbanets, rerouting grain to the Danube means a much longer and more expensive journey.
Izmail is roughly 400 kilometers away from his farm, and Varbanets estimates that the cost of transporting grain there can amount to 30-35% of the grain's sale value, before accounting for delays.
The Danube ports are smaller and constrained by the Sulina Canal, which limits the size of vessels that can reach them. Barinov says ships carrying around 5,000 to 7,000 metric tons can use the route, a fraction of the capacity available at Greater Odesa's deep-water terminals.
"Nobody is taking grain."
Moving the cargo of a single 100,000-metric ton capacity ship overland would require roughly 5,000 trucks, each requiring a driver, documents, fuel, and a border crossing, Barinov adds.
The Danube route offers no escape from Russian attacks either. Russia has repeatedly targeted ports and logistics infrastructure there, leaving Ukraine's backup route slower, smaller, and exposed to many of the same dangers as Odesa.
By the end of August, around 70 vessels were waiting to enter the Sulina Canal en route to Ukraine's Danube ports. The shift has kept some exports moving, but it has also shown how quickly alternative routes become congested when traffic is diverted from Greater Odesa.
Romania's port of Constanta is another option. Ukrainian cargo can reach it by rail or road. While Constanta already handles Romanian and other European exports, border capacity, railway links, and cargo transfers all create additional bottlenecks for Ukrainian cargo.
read also
Defending the corridor
What keeps the corridor open at all is a force of Ukrainian Navy patrol boats that work around the clock, serving as mobile air-defense groups along the coast. Each vessel covers an assigned sector, monitoring the waters, detecting and neutralizing explosive devices, watching for unmanned boats, and shooting down low-flying Russian attack drones.
When an incoming aerial threat is detected, Yevhen, a 32-year-old serviceman of the Ukrainian Navy identified by first name only for security reasons, puts on his body armor and helmet, climbs into the turret, and takes his position at the machine gun.
Shahed drones have chased their boat more than once while they were out at sea, he says.
"We fired back," says Yevhen, who served in the airborne forces before joining the Navy. He never expected to end up at sea.
"I can't swim," he adds with a smile.
But the boats' machine guns offer little protection against missiles launched from occupied Crimea and Russia. Crews increasingly face jet-powered Shahed variants and Banderols, which travel faster than conventional Shaheds and are harder to intercept.
Russia sends alternating types of drones and missiles at intervals of 30-minutes to an hour, says Oleh Zasyadvovk, a captain 2nd rank and communications officer with the Ukrainian Navy.
"There is no period of more than an hour without an alert," he says. "The tactics change almost every day."
During particularly demanding shifts, Yevhen says, he spends more than 24 hours at sea and goes for as long as two days without sleep.
The next harvest
For Varbanets, the lack of viable alternative routes is becoming more pressing as storage space dwindles. His wheat, barley, lentils, and peas already fill most of the warehouse space, while the next harvest approaches.
"There will be nowhere to pour the sunflower," he says.
On his way to the sunflower fields, Varbanets passes the village cemetery where four Ukrainian flags mark the graves of local men killed fighting in the war. One of them grew up with his grandson, who worked on the farm as an agronomist and is now serving in the military.
Further along the road, the war has cut through the farmland. The soil is charred where a Russian drone shot down nearby crashed and burned. The crash sparked a fire that burned around 600 hectares of land and damaged the tree lines that protect the soil from wind and snow in winter, Varbanets says.
Asked whether he will replant the burned fields, he answers: "What else can we do? We will sow."

title: Van Akkrum naar Amerika en terug: het bijzondere verhaal van bejaardenhuis Coopersburg – alleen deze zaterdag te bezoeken
content:
Van Akkrum naar Amerika en terug: het bijzondere verhaal van bejaardenhuis Coopersburg – alleen deze zaterdag te bezoeken
Een verslag door een auteur ter plaatse
Open Monumentendag Aan de rand van het Friese Akkrum staat het rijksmonumentale Coopersburg, in 1901 geopend als bejaardenhuis. Een bijzonder gebouw, maar het verhaal erachter is minstens zo fascinerend. Stichter Frank Cooper werd geboren in Akkrum, vertrok naar de VS en maakte daar fortuin. Alleen deze zaterdag, tijdens Open Monumentendag, is Coopersburg geopend voor publiek.
Een groepje keurig geklede ouderen kijkt ontspannen in de camera. Het is 1901, het jaar waarin bejaardenhuis Coopersburg in Akkrum (een Fries dorpje nabij Sneek en Heerenveen) zijn eerste bewoners verwelkomt. Achter hen strekt zich een langgerekt gebouw uit van bruine bakstenen, afgewerkt met witte sierbanden en zwarte dakpannen.
Architectuurhistorisch valt het onder de zogeheten overgangsarchitectuur: een weinig sexy, maar toch veelzeggend hokje tussen de neostijlen en modernere stromingen als jugendstil en art deco. In het midden trekt een statig middendeel met zuilen en torentjes de aandacht. Aan weerszijden daarvan staan tien kleine woningen, elk met een eigen voordeur, erker en gevel. Los van elkaar zouden het haast huisjes kunnen zijn, maar samen vormen ze een imposant en opvallend symmetrisch geheel.
Nieuw leven in Amerika
Coopersburg is het levenswerk van de Friese Folkert Kuipers, die in 1866 via Harlingen in het Engelse Hull op een boot stapte om voorgoed zijn geluk in de Verenigde Staten te beproeven. Het was op z’n zachtst gezegd een roerige tijd toen hij de overtocht maakte: het bloed van de Amerikaanse Burgeroorlog was nog maar net opgedroogd, de toenmalige president Abraham Lincoln was even daarvoor doodgeschoten en in het ‘Wilde Westen’ waren gewapende conflicten tussen het Amerikaanse leger, kolonisten en verschillende inheemse naties nog aan de orde van de dag. Niet zo gek dus dat de ouders van de toen 22-jarige Folkert zijn vertrek met lede ogen aanzagen en hem alvast geld toestopten voor de terugreis. „Maar niets of niemand kon hem tegenhouden”, vertelt Anne Dijkstra, oud-voorzitter van de historische vereniging Akkrum Ald en Nij, lachend. „Hij was een ondernemende jongen, sprak goed Engels en was vastbesloten het te maken in Amerika.”
In New York City werd Folkert opgevangen en gecontroleerd bij Castle Garden op het zuidelijkste puntje van Manhattan – Ellis Island werd pas geopend in 1892 – en verwelkomd door Friezen die al eerder de overtocht hadden gemaakt. De extreme armoede in het 19de-eeuwse New York dwong hem om naar Buffalo te vertrekken, waar hij al snel werk én een vrouw vond. Een Nederlandse zelfs, de in Middelburg geboren Antonetta Gerrardina de Graaff. „Ze trouwden en verdienden een beetje geld met de verkoop van herenvesten die Nettie maakte, waardoor een paar jaar later een grote droom in vervulling ging: een eigen winkel”, gaat Dijkstra verder. „Folkert heeft veel aan zijn eerste vrouw te danken.”
Toch leefde Nettie niet lang genoeg om het grote succes mee te maken; in 1879 stierf ze aan de complicaties van een buitenbaarmoederlijke zwangerschap, nadat ze eerder vijf gezonde kinderen had gekregen. Afleiding voor zijn verdriet vond Frank – Folkert Harmen Kuipers bekt niet zo lekker in de VS, dus logischerwijs had hij zijn naam laten wijzigen in Frank Harmon Cooper – in doorwerken. Samen met mantelhandelaar Henry Siegel opende hij in 1887 zijn eerste grote warenhuis in Chicago. Een grote brand leidde in 1891 tot de opening van een nieuwe vestiging in een gigantisch pand aan een van de hoofdstraten van de stad. En dat succes leidde weer tot een ‘Big Store’ op de plek waar Frank het eigenlijk in 1866 al wilde maken: New York City.
Meet me at the fountain
Met die zaken schreven Siegel & Cooper warenhuisgeschiedenis. Pier van der Heide, bestuurslid van de historische vereniging: „In Chicago verkochten ruim tweeduizend medewerkers meubilair, kleding, kruidenierswaren en boeken. Verder zaten er in het gebouw een bank, arbeidsbureau, telegraafkantoor, dokter, tandarts en kappers – een slimme manier om van een bezoeker ook een klant te maken.” In New York had het warenhuis zelfs een kinderopvang en restaurants. Beide panden waren voorzien van de modernste voorzieningen: draaideuren, roltrappen, liften, elektrisch licht en zelfs airconditioning. Ook trof je in allebei de winkels bij binnenkomst meteen een sierlijke fontein aan. Een herkenbaar ontmoetingspunt voor klanten, waaruit in New York de bekende uitspraak ‘Meet me at the fountain’ voortkwam.
Frank had niet alleen oog voor zijn klanten, maar ook voor zijn personeel. Zo zorgde hij voor een ziekenfonds, sportfaciliteiten, woonruimte voor vrouwelijke medewerkers en zelfs vakantiehuisjes. „Frank H. Cooper is een naam in Chicago die gedurende minstens tien jaar gestaan heeft voor alles wat in de handelswereld modern en up-to-date is. (…) Zijn personeel treedt hij opgeruimd tegemoet en zijn persoonlijke aantrekkingskracht valt op waar hij gaat”, schreef de Chicago Tribune lovend in 1901.
Terug naar Akkrum
Franks groeiende fortuin zorgde ervoor dat hij regelmatig kon terugkeren naar Akkrum. Tijdens een van die bezoeken werd hij getroffen door de zichtbare armoede in zijn geboorteplaats, vooral onder ouderen, en besloot hij dat daar iets aan moest gebeuren.
Tijdens een van de bezoeken aan Akkrum werd hij getroffen door de zichtbare armoede in zijn geboorteplaats, vooral onder ouderen
In 1899 richtte hij de stichting Coopersburg op en vroeg hij gemeentearchitect Folkert Hoekstra om een tehuis te ontwerpen. Vervolgens ging het zeker voor die tijd erg rap: nog geen twee jaar later stond het gebouw er. Op 8 mei 1901 werd Coopersburg officieel geopend, een moment waarvoor Frank met een hele delegatie de oceaan overstak: zijn vijf kinderen en hun aanhang, een handjevol kleinkinderen en zelfs twee kindermeisjes.
Frank bleef ook na de bouw financieel verantwoordelijk voor zijn plan. Om de ouderen te onderhouden stortte hij een flink bedrag in de stichting, die werd bestuurd door regenten die hij zelf aanwees. Dat bestuur kwam samen in de regentenkamer, die zich in het middengebouw bevindt en nog grotendeels in originele staat is. Boven de haard prijken de namen van alle bestuursleden die Coopersburg door de jaren heen heeft gehad.
Uniek is ook het gastenboek dat sinds 1901 prominent op tafel ligt. Alle bezoekers van Coopersburg staan erin vermeld, van bloemisten, bakkers en koopmannen tot een journalist van het Algemeen Handelsblad. Ook aan Frank zelf herinnert de kamer. Aan de muur hangt een schilderij van zijn beroemde Big Store, dat hij liet maken voor zijn vader. Wie goed kijkt, ziet dat de raampjes van het warenhuis zijn ingelegd met parelmoer.
In elke woning – tweeëntwintig in totaal, waarvan twee in het middengebouw – was plek voor twee bewoners. Man of vrouw maakte daarbij niet uit, en ook geloof speelde geen rol. Dat was opvallend voor die tijd. „Hoe de bewoners zelf met die gemengde bewoning omgingen, weten we niet”, vertelt Jan Eijzenga, secretaris bij de historische vereniging. „Maar je kunt je voorstellen dat het niet altijd eenvoudig was om een woning met iemand te delen die je niet zelf had uitgekozen. In het archief hebben we aandoenlijke briefjes gevonden van bewoners die de regenten smeekten om niet bij een bepaalde alleenwonende persoon te worden geplaatst.”
Mausoleum in de tuin
De woningen zijn inmiddels eigendom van een woningstichting en niet te bezichtigen – ook niet tijdens Open Monumentendag. Wel toegankelijk is de weelderige tuin voor en achter Coopersburg, met slingerpaadjes, bruggetjes, een fontein en kruisvormige zonnewijzer. Maar de echte blikvanger staat verderop in de tuin: het mausoleum – ook een rijksmonument – van Frank en zijn eerste vrouw Nettie.
Een opvallende parel tussen het groen, maar bovenal het laatste eerbetoon van hun kinderen aan hun ouders. Het werd door een lokale architect ontworpen in een ingetogen art-nouveaustijl. Boven de zware houten entree zijn de portretten van Frank en Nettie gebeeldhouwd en aan weerszijden staan twee vrouwenfiguren, die rouw en de overwinning op de dood symboliseren. Daarachter liggen de twee grote tombes, uitgevoerd in wit marmer. In die van Frank werd zijn gebalsemde lichaam bijgezet. Nettie, die al in 1879 was overleden, werd uiteindelijk alleen nog met haar botten te ruste gelegd. Normaal blijft het mausoleum gesloten, maar deze zaterdag kunnen bezoekers ook de binnenkant bekijken.
Frank kwam van niks en werd groot in Amerika. Hij heeft daar een enorm leven en imperium opgebouwd, maar is altijd een van ons gebleven
Open Monumentendag op Coopersburg is dit jaar extra speciaal, want het rijksmonument bestaat 125 jaar. In de tuin is daarom een fototentoonstelling te zien met oude beelden van Coopersburg en Akkrum. Ook worden twee splinternieuwe bronzen beeltenissen onthuld van Frank en Nettie, gemaakt door de Friese beeldhouwer Ben van der Geest. Maar waarom is er juist nu zoveel aandacht voor het echtpaar? „We zijn ontzettend trots op deze geschiedenis”, zegt Dijkstra. „Frank kwam van niks en werd groot in Amerika. Hij heeft daar een enorm leven en imperium opgebouwd, maar is altijd een van ons gebleven.”
Misschien is dat wel precies wat Coopersburg zo bijzonder maakt: het gebouw vertelt het verhaal van een man die de wereld introk en er fortuin maakte, maar zijn grootste blijvende stempel juist in zijn kleine geboortedorp achterliet.

title: After nearly 50 years, this master craftsman is hanging up his tools
content:
After nearly 50 years, this master craftsman is hanging up his tools
Craftsmen of Tasmania's heritage construction trade have had a busy month inside a 146-year-old church in Campbell Town.
A solid plasterer, a stained glass worker, and a heritage building specialist have been working together to help restore the former Brickhill memorial church.
Gavin Merrington, 64, expects it will be his last major restoration project.
After nearly 50 years spent repairing stained glass in buildings across Tasmania, he's preparing to hang up the tools — for the big jobs at least.
Original stained glass restored
The Campbell Town project, in Tasmania's midlands, hasn't been a small task.
The church's original High Street-facing main window had never been replaced, and after nearly 150 years, the soft lead holding the glass together was well and truly breaking down.
"The putty under the lead starts to wash out and then the water gets in, and they just degenerate," Mr Merrington said.
"You could see a few broken [pieces], but when you pull them out they start to separate and there were heaps broken."
Mr Merrington was able to track down the exact type of glass used in the original windows.
Intricate pieces were then hand-painted and fired in a kiln, with the process repeated many times until the desired colour and effect were reached.
That was done for "maybe 90 pieces", he said.
Based out of his studio in South Hobart, the work on the main windows at Brickhill took 10 weeks.
The glass was then carefully transported to Campbell Town, placed in a wooden crate and secured with screws before being levered 5 metres off the ground to where it needed to be fitted.
"If you touch it on the scaffold you're likely to break something, and they're very heavy too, so it's a matter of being careful and having lots of hands on the windows to get them up," he said.
Leadlighting around the world
It was a newspaper ad that inspired Mr Merrington to pick up the trade of leadlighting at the age of 16.
He has spent much of his career working on church windows, a passion that has taken him around the world.
After being awarded a Churchill Fellowship in 2014, Mr Merrington travelled to Europe to learn from global experts in glazing and glass preservation — skills he brought home to Tasmania.
"Coming back it was just sort of reiterated, we're on the right path and we're looking good as far as the skills that are being disseminated around Australia,"he said.
"Australia is quite up with world trends as far as conservation."
Mr Merrington lists Launceston's Holy trinity church and Hobart churches St Mary's cathedral and All Saints as some of his favourite projects he has worked on.
Heritage trades 'quite a community'
Heritage building specialist Peter Evans, who has also been working on the Brickhill project, first met Mr Merrington 20 years ago on a different church restoration.
He said that was typical of Tasmania's heritage trades, with many of the people working on these buildings having known each other for decades.
"It's quite a community; we all rely heavily on each other," he said.
"All the people I work with, a lot of our relationships go back 35 to 38 years."
A fifth-generation Campbell Town local, Mr Evans said the region was dotted with Victorian farmhouses and churches that kept him and his team of six busy.
"[There was] such a flurry of buildings [built] in the 1830s, so this area here through to Hobart, but particularly the Midlands," he said.
"It's good to be able to take our part in preserving these buildings, and we'll hand over to the next generation, mainly just keeping them watertight and sound."
An unlikely owner
Ohio-born Matt Collins always wanted to buy a church.
After moving to Australia in 2017, he set his sights on Brickhill.
Built in 1880 with money left by former convict-turned-merchant Joseph Brickhill, the church was deconsecrated in 1964.
Since then, it has been a wool museum, a co-working space and now operates as short-stay accommodation.
"I think there is a duty and responsibility when you own or steward a building like this one to preserve it because it has such a rich history, relevance and significance to the local community,"Mr Collins said.
"I'm really, really honoured that I've had Gavin and his team come and work on this building, with all the years of experience and knowledge that they have."
Future of heritage crafts
After Brickhill, Mr Merrington is stepping back from major restoration work, but he is not walking away from the craft entirely.
He will continue working on smaller jobs and consultancy work.
Mr Merrington said he was confident his heritage trade was in safe hands.
"I've got an employee who will keep going after me hopefully, and he's got all the skills so that's really good,"he said.
Mr Merrington said while it was a "shame so many churches are being sold", having people such as Matt committed to restoring them was "better than it could have ever been expected", even compared to remaining in the church's hands.
He said after nearly 50 years of travelling the state, he was looking forward to a break.
"A few holidays, spend some time with the wife and the grandkids, that kind of thing," he said.

title: Triplets carry on father's FDNY legacy after 9/11
content:
Brothers pursue firefighting careers inspired by late FDNY father who died from 9/11-related illnesses
A firefighter father's 9/11 sacrifice is inspiring his triplet sons to serve.
NEW YORK -- The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks are not identical, but they share a common past and will soon share a common future.
They're three of the thousands of children who lost a parent 25 years ago on Sept. 11 or in the years after due to 9/11-related illnesses.
William Gormley's sons - Raymond, Billy and Kevin - were just 3 years old when their father rushed to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001. While many children lost parents that day, the brothers grew up with their father, only later learning the toll his work at Ground Zero had taken on his health.
"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways," Raymond said while sitting on a couch between his two brothers. "The same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything. No one understands me like these two understand me."
But for Kevin, Raymond and Billy didn't learn about what happened from the history books, they lived it and they always had each other to rely on.
"This is a huge point my father always made, he said, 'These are your people. You were born with them, and this is what you got til the end,'" Kevin said.
They don't remember what happened on Sept. 11, since they were so young.
"Now, 25 years later, we're understanding the full grasp of what happened that day," Raymond said.
William Gormley rushed to the twin towers after they were struck. Unlike many children, they didn't lose their dad that day. The reality of the work he did hit later in life.
Firefighter Gormley worked on the pile for months, looking for survivors and later, for the remains of victims.
"It makes you feel some pride knowing your father went in there selflessly to help others and do the best he could," Kevin said.
The family said the long-term effects of his work became apparent over time. Growing up, the brothers accompanied their father to numerous doctor appointments but did not fully understand the severity of his health problems.
"They never really told us anything really," Billy said. "But as kids we'd go to hospital waiting rooms in summer for doctors' appointments. But not knowing the severity."
Raymond added, "Growing up he had skin cancer, sinus issues. So growing up as a kid, I personally never really understood what that came from. It wasn't until he was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2016 that we put two together and realized it was from his time spent at Ground Zero."
William Gormley died of bladder and lung cancer in 2017. According to a report, he was one of more than 400 fire and EMS workers who have died from 9/11-related illnesses.
Asked whether his father would have made the same decision knowing what is now known about the dangers faced at Ground Zero, Raymond said there was no doubt.
"One hundred percent, without hesitation," he said. "Not only him, but every single person he went down with that day would go down to the pile again, without a doubt."
Today, a street in Brooklyn bears William Gormley's name, near the firehouse where he worked.
Despite their father's advice to seek work outside the fire service, the brothers found themselves drawn to the profession.
"My father would always say, 'When you get older, get a job where you sit behind a desk and write checks for people,'" Kyle said.
"He'd always say, 'Work with your brain, not your hands,'" Raymond added.
He went on to say, "So I'm a firefighter right now, an FDNY firefighter working at the same house he worked at, Ladder 174. So it's full circle really, it's crazy from him telling me to work with your brain, not your hands, and it's crazy I'm sleeping in the same bed he did 20 years ago."
Billy hopes to join the fire service soon.
"So I'm an EMT with the fire department at the moment," he said. "Waiting to join fire as well."
Kevin has also applied to become a firefighter.
"You hope one day, you can fill those shoes," he said.
The report said Billy and Kevin could join the fire academy as soon as this month.
The brothers said they were inspired not only by their father, but also by the support they received from firefighters after his death.
"Once I saw the camaraderie, everyone coming together, people driving us around, his old coworkers taking care of us, the laughs, the tears," Raymond said. "After that in my mind, it was something I would really like to do."
"Yeah, what they did was incredible how they took care of us, made sure everything was in order," another brother added.
And this didn't just have an impact on the three brothers, it impacted the entire family, including their big sister, Bridget.
"I think there's a beauty in that it was never forced down their throats," said Bridget. "My dad was never like, 'You're going to be a fireman!' Our dad was like, 'You're NOT going to be a fireman!'"
Bridget has also dedicated her work to preserving the stories of those affected by Sept. 11. She works with 9/11 survivors and produced a documentary about the dangers of toxic dust exposure. It's called, "Dust: Lingering Legacy of 9/11."
"Along the way, I got to know my father's friends better," she said. "I mean, I lost my dad, but I've got [sic] thousands of uncles now."
For the Gormley siblings, the events of Sept. 11 continue to shape their lives and careers. They say their shared experiences and bond have helped them navigate a loss that has defined much of their lives.
"Just being there for someone on their worst day, being their hope when there's no hope is really something special, something we take a lot of pride in," Raymond said.
"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways, the same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything, no one understands me like these two understand me," one of the brothers said.
As they continue their careers in public service, the brothers say they are carrying forward the values their father exemplified, together.

title: Rebelião da 3ª idade: a geração que revolucionou os costumes hoje luta por direitos e inclusão
content:
Um em cada cinco habitantes do Rio Grande do Sul tem 60 anos ou mais. Estamos falando de mais de 2 milhões de pessoas. E Porto Alegre é a capital brasileira com maior número de sexagenários e de homens e mulheres além dessa idade. Justamente aqui acaba de surgir uma iniciativa voltada à defesa da justiça, da dignidade, da autonomia e da vida mais plena possível para os velhos e velhas.
É o MOVER, o Movimento da Velharada Rebelde. O grupo lançou um manifesto afirmando que palavras como “velho” e velha” não os assusta. Adiante, afirma: “Somos os velhos e velhas do século 21, integrantes de uma geração que sonhou em mudar o mundo e que revolucionou os costumes”. Com convicção, acentua: “Fomos jovens rebeldes e não abrimos mão da nossa rebeldia”.
Amplo, o manifesto do MOVER trata desde a luta por aposentadorias decentes e do reajuste regular do salário-mínimo até a qualificação das casas de repouso, passando pela discussão do chamado “testamento vital” quando o idoso ou idosa decide o destino do seu corpo.
São inúmeras bandeiras onde não falta aquelas que acenam ao “mundo além de nós”, ou seja, às grandes questões que convulsionam a vida em sociedade e o futuro do planeta.
Nesta semana, De Fato recebe as jornalistas Rosina Duarte e Cristina Pozzobon, duas das fundadoras do MOVER, onde elas também questionam o uso de eufemismos para designar os mais velhos como “Melhor Idade”.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.
Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.

title: Assentamento Terra Vista recebe primeira turma de Filosofia na história do Pronera
content:
A cerimônia de abertura do curso de Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra foi realizada no dia 24 de agosto, no Assentamento Terra Vista, no município de Arataca, sul da Bahia. Esta é a primeira turma de graduação em Filosofia promovida pelo Programa Nacional de Educação na Reforma Agrária (Pronera) e conta com 50 estudantes, reunindo educadores populares, lideranças comunitárias e jovens originários de assentamentos, comunidades quilombolas e aldeias indígenas.
A formação é fruto de uma articulação construída desde o período pré-pandemia e reúne o Instituto Nacional de Colonização e Reforma Agrária (Incra), a Universidade Estadual de Santa Cruz (UESC), a Teia dos Povos e movimentos sociais do campo, como MST, CETA, CPT e MLT. Ao longo de quatro anos, as aulas e atividades de pesquisa serão desenvolvidas integralmente dentro do próprio assentamento.
A proposta pedagógica da Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra parte da Pedagogia da Alternância e da práxis agroecológica, colocando no centro as cosmovisões dos povos originários e das comunidades tradicionais.
Cris Ayie, do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) no território Claudemiro Dias Lima, integra a turma e destaca que uma das missões do grupo é poder ocupar esse lugar de disputa de ideias. “É um espaço de debates, de trazer realidades e se aprimorar no conhecimento que a gente já vem praticando ao longo dos tempos em cada território. É um espaço de confluência e de partilha de saberes. Essa turma é muito diversa e traz um acúmulo grande de experiências”, afirma.
Para o vice-reitor da UESC, Maurício Santana Moreau, a presença da academia no território estabelece uma relação horizontal de aprendizado mútuo. “A expectativa é que a gente trabalhe os saberes deles junto com o conhecimento acadêmico dos professores da universidade, e que quem saia ganhando seja toda a comunidade. Estamos muito felizes com esse momento importante e histórico”, observa.
O coordenador do curso e docente da UESC, professor Josué Cândido, explica o recorte específico da matriz curricular. “Esse curso tem um diferencial porque é uma filosofia da terra, voltada para pensar a questão agroecológica, o planeta e fazer com que nossos alunos se tornem seres críticos e reflexivos para levar essa contribuição para a educação na região”, relata.
Retomada do Pronera e soberania territorial
O início das aulas formaliza também a reorganização das instâncias regionais do programa. De acordo com Paulo Coqueiro, membro do Colegiado Estadual do Pronera na Bahia, o curso carrega duplo valor. “Esse curso inaugura a nova composição do Colegiado Estadual do Pronera na Bahia. É de uma grande importância histórica, quer seja por estar sediado dentro de um assentamento, quer seja por ser o primeiro curso dessa retomada”.
Fabrício Dias, chefe da Divisão de Educação do Campo do Incra Nacional, setor que gere o Pronera em âmbito federal, aponta o pioneirismo do debate filosófico na modalidade. “Depois de 28 anos de execução dessa política pública, realizamos a aula inaugural do primeiro curso de Filosofia do Pronera no Brasil todo. Foi um momento muito emocionante de retomada do programa na Bahia, principalmente com a inovação de trazer a filosofia para dentro do debate da educação do campo. Nossa expectativa é que esses alunos construam um outro pensar filosófico, aliado às populações tradicionais de todo o país”, ressalta.
No Terra Vista, a chegada da graduação é celebrada como consolidação de uma trajetória de luta pela terra e pelo conhecimento. Joelson Ferreira, liderança do assentamento e da Teia dos Povos, reforça o papel estratégico da formação. “Acredito que vai ser um marco para restabelecer um programa de formação capaz de ser instrumento de transformação da juventude e do povo que está nas áreas de reforma agrária, quilombolas e indígenas, para que a gente possa evoluir esse pensamento e construir uma militância capaz de entender e transformar a realidade. Essa parceria entre Incra, Pronera e UESC é fundamental para nos fortalecer”, observa Joelson.
Para Solange Brito, assentada no Terra Vista e integrante da Rede de Mulheres da Teia dos Povos, o impacto atinge diretamente o cotidiano da comunidade. “É de fundamental importância avançar na perspectiva política. Os estudantes pesquisando e se formando geram avanço na consciência da educação, da produção, da cultura e do fortalecimento dessa região tão rica, que é o bioma Mata Atlântica. Para nós, receber todos aqui representa um acúmulo de muita força”.
Com o calendário acadêmico em andamento no assentamento, a Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra projeta consolidar, até a conclusão da turma, uma rede de educadores e pesquisadores preparados para atuar tanto nas salas de aula quanto nas organizações comunitárias, articulando soberania alimentar, preservação ambiental e pensamento crítico no campo.

title: In Paash’s village, a fight over the space that keeps his memory alive
content:
Stay updated with the latest - Click here to follow us on Instagram
The words of Avtar Singh Sandhu, better known as Paash, have travelled far beyond Talwandi Salem, his birthplace in Jalandhar district. Nearly four decades after he was killed, his poetry continues to surface wherever people gather around democratic rights and resistance — at farmers’ protests, workers’ meetings, student gatherings and literary forums.
For generations of readers, Paash was not merely a poet who wrote about struggle; he was a poet who participated in it.
Ahead of his birth anniversary on September 9, however, his legacy has become the centre of a dispute in his native village. Tension erupted after the village panchayat allegedly tried to stop members of the Paash-Hans Raj Memorial Committee from erecting a pandal at an eponymous complex for the celebrations. Allegations of manhandling prompted the local administration to deploy police to prevent a confrontation.
The dispute centres around two kanals of land at the entrance of Talwandi Salem, where the Pash-Hans Raj Memorial has stood for 26 years. The committee says the land was allotted to it in 2000 through a written panchayat resolution. The panchayat, however, maintains that the land belongs to it.
The confrontation dates back to early August, when the Paash Memorial International Trust, the Paash-Hans Raj Shaheedi Yaadgar Committee and several unions approached the Nakodar SDM and local MLA with allegations of vandalism. According to their complaint, panchayat representatives broke the locks of the memorial gate. When the committee replaced them, one side of the gate was allegedly removed and panchayat representatives entered the premises and installed swings, pipes and open-gym equipment.
Local administrative officials initially maintained that the land belonged to the panchayat, while indicating that the matter was close to resolution. The dispute flared again when committee members arrived to prepare for Paash’s September 9 birth anniversary. A group led by sarpanch Pardeep Singh allegedly confronted them, including veteran activist Jhanda Singh Jethuke. Committee members alleged that some activists were pushed and that mobile phones were confiscated.
For villagers and Paash’s admirers, the confrontation has taken on a larger meaning. “It is a great disrespect to a great poet, and that too by the people and the panchayat of his own village,” said a local resident.
The memorial complex was initially undeveloped land. According to trust members, it was transformed over the years through voluntary contributions from admirers in Punjab and abroad, including supporters in the US, Canada and the UK. Today, the site includes an open-air theatre, green rooms and a library housing Paash’s writings, besides basic utilities. It has hosted memorial programmes, theatre performances and literary gatherings.
Paash and his close friend Hans Raj were assassinated by militants on March 23, 1988. Paash was 37. The committee says it has no objection to recreational facilities for villagers but argues that a cultural institution built over decades should not be altered without consultation.
“The issue is not about opposing swings or an open gym,” said Amolak Singh, trustee and committee member. “The question is why these facilities must be installed inside a memorial when the village has other public parks. There is no reason to disturb its character.”
He also questioned the circumstances in which the locks and part of the gate were allegedly removed and recreational equipment installed in the complex.
This year’s birth anniversary celebrations are planned both at the memorial and at the site where Paash and Hans Raj were killed, in the fields near a tubewell in the village.
Born on September 9, 1950, Paash emerged as one of modern Punjabi literature’s most distinctive voices. His poetry placed workers, farmers and the disenfranchised at the centre of literary expression. Sab Ton Khatarnak (The Most Dangerous), his best-known poem, remains a powerful warning against apathy and the loss of conscience.
Dr Kuldeep Singh, a Punjabi literature scholar and former professor at Punjabi University, Patiala, said Paash’s enduring influence could be compared with that of Faiz Ahmed Faiz and Pablo Neruda.
“Paash belongs to the people. Whenever resistance emerges, his poetry returns. His legacy should be expanded through a meaningful memorial, not reduced to a petty land dispute,” he said.
“His poems questioned oppression, communalism and the silencing of dissent, and his own life reflected that spirit of resistance. During the turbulent years of militancy in Punjab, he openly opposed Khalistani extremism and used his writing to challenge communal politics’,” he added.
His family is now working to preserve another part of that history. His wife and daughter, based in the US, have dedicated two acres of ancestral land — including the site near the tubewell where Paash and Hans Raj were killed — to the Avtar Singh Paash Memorial Trust for a second memorial.
For Sucha Singh, convenor of the committee and Paash’s cousin, the issue is also one of village identity. “People across the world know Talwandi Salem because Paash was born here,” he said.
The dispute has also raised a broader question about who should protect literary heritage.
Amolak Singh said political figures are often commemorated through government-backed memorials, while the preservation of literary legacies is frequently left to writers, admirers and civil society groups. Farmer, student and labour unions have since launched awareness campaigns in villages to build support for the memorial.
Nakodar SDM Simranjeet Singh said the administration was aware of the confrontation and that police had been deployed to maintain peace during the September 9 programme.
AAP chief spokesperson Neel Garg said the local administration should provide greater clarity on the dispute, while acknowledging that the controversy should not have arisen.
“What is happening in Talwandi Salem should not happen. Paash is an international poet whose work instills the spirit to fight for rights,” Garg said. He added that the matter would be brought to the notice of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.

title: WATCH: Anastasia Fourie shines at Zulu Reed Dance as 30 000 maidens gather in KZN
content:
The uMkhosi Womhlanga is a centuries‑old Zulu custom, revived in the late 20th century, aimed at promoting self‑respect.
Anastasia Fourie, a young debutant from Eshowe, KwaZulu‑Natal (KZN) drew national attention after participating in the 2026 uMkhosi Womhlanga (Zulu Reed Dance) at the Emashobeni Royal Palace near oPhongola, alongside fellow debutant Kelly Kleinbooi from Greytown.
Fourie and Kleinbooi joined around 30 000 maidens at the annual cultural festival, which has become a focal point of public curiosity and debate.
Maidens
From Msunduzi to Richmond, maidens were sent off with prayers, cultural teachings and messages of encouragement from municipal, traditional and community leaders before embarking on the journey to eMashobeni Royal Palace near uPhongolo.
The uMkhosi Womhlanga is a centuries‑old Zulu custom, revived in the late 20th century, aimed at promoting self‑respect, community solidarity, and delaying sexual activity among young unmarried women.
During the ceremony, maidens gather reeds from riverbanks and present them to King MisuZulu kaZwelithini as a pledge of purity.
Zulu culture
Speaking to broadcasters on site, Fourie expressed joy at her initiation into the custom.
“I enjoy really much. It’s an honour to be here with everyone, and it’s a new experience. I like the Zulu culture and how they celebrate it and just the way how everything is done into the culture. Yeah, I like how everything is done here. It’s not bad, but it’s good. They must just celebrate their virginity, happy that they still have it.”
She and Kleinbooi vowed to return to the ceremony every year, describing the journey and its cultural requirements as meaningful to their participation.
Traditional attire
Fourie’s choice to wear traditional attire tailored to her comfort prompted mild debate over dress codes, but attendees and spectators largely welcomed her presence.
The event created a hive of activity in oPhongola, KwaZulu‑Natal, as maidens from across the country paraded before the Amazulu king.
[WATCH] A debutant at the uMkhosi Womhlanga (reed dance), Anastasia Fourie, speaks to #Newzroom405‘s @Lethu_Nxumalo about her experience with the maidens attending the celebration at Emashobeni Royal Palace. pic.twitter.com/BCVJqucIL4
– Newzroom Afrika (@Newzroom405) September 12, 2026
Caution
Mpiyakhe Buthelezi, spokesperson for the king, cautioned against the misuse of photographs taken during the ceremony, warning that images of maidens should not be exploited to degrade participants or misrepresent the event.
“People are not coming here to be embarrassed. They are here to honour culture. We ask that photos not be taken in ways that disrespect the maidens or distort the meaning of the ceremony,” the spokesperson said.
Ubuntu
The annual gathering promotes values including dignity, Ubuntu, respect and abstinence and forms part of broader efforts to encourage social cohesion and the positive development of young women.
The event is supported by the KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) Department of Sport, Arts and Culture on behalf of the provincial government.

title: Ethiopia Writes a New Chapter in Global Environmental History With 56.8 Billion Planted Tree Seedlings
content:
Ethiopia Writes a New Chapter in Global Environmental History With 56.8 Billion Planted Tree Seedlings
Addis Ababa, September 10, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia has planted 56.8 billion tree seedlings over eight years through its Green Legacy Initiative, surpassing its initial 50-billion-seedling target and marking what the country describes as a new chapter in global environmental history.
Launched in 2019 at the initiative of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Green Legacy was conceived as a national response to land degradation, deforestation, biodiversity loss and the degradation of water resources, while linking environmental restoration with sustainable development.
The scale of the undertaking has grown far beyond a conventional tree-planting campaign. More than 3 billion seedlings have been planted in a single day during the initiative’s years of implementation, while more than 25 million citizens have been mobilized annually to take part in the nationwide effort.
The initiative has also been designed around the productive value of trees. About 60 percent of the seedlings planted are agroforestry species, including fruit trees, coffee and fodder varieties, while the remainder consists of forest trees.
The approach connects landscape restoration with food production, household livelihoods and the strengthening of rural economic security.
According to the reported outcomes of the initiative, annual deforestation has declined from 92,000 hectares to 27,000 hectares, while soil erosion on agricultural land has fallen from 130 tonnes per hectare annually to 54 tonnes.
The amount of sediment entering water bodies has likewise declined from 1.9 billion tonnes to 208 million tonnes annually.
The environmental campaign has also generated an economic and social dividend, with nearly 2.6 million jobs created for young people and women.
Fruit and forest clusters emerging across different parts of the country are further creating new opportunities for farmers while strengthening the productive value of restored landscapes.
At the heart of Green Legacy has been mass public participation, coordinated through government structures from the federal level to local communities.
The initiative has consequently developed into a nationwide movement in which environmental restoration is tied to civic participation, youth engagement and a broader sense of collective responsibility for the country’s natural resources.
For Ethiopia, the transformation represents more than the number of seedlings planted. It demonstrates an effort to confront environmental degradation at national scale while using restoration to advance livelihoods, food security, climate resilience and sustainable development.
The achievement was highlighted as Ethiopia concluded its 2026 Green Legacy tree-planting campaign on Thursday under the theme “Let Us Plant Hope.”
The completion of this year’s campaign gives added significance to the cumulative 56.8-billion figure, placing the latest milestone within an eight-year national environmental journey.
Through Green Legacy, Ethiopia is also presenting a different position in the global climate conversation: not only as a country confronting the consequences of climate change and desertification, but as one seeking to contribute actively to their solution through large-scale restoration and collective action.

title: This group has given domestic violence survivors cash with no strings attached for 10 years. It's working
content:
Sonya Passi founded her nonprofit, FreeFrom, in 2016, with a mission to “end gender-based violence by building economic freedom and safety with survivors.”
One of the main efforts of the organization is to give direct cash transfers to survivors of GBV — often no more than $1,500 — in an effort to prove that economic support could transform the lives of survivors. According to FreeFrom, one in two women and one in two transgender individuals will be subjected to GBV in their lifetimes.
At first, the organization started by helping survivors start their own businesses. While it still offers entrepreneurship support, when COVID-19 hit, the nonprofit answered the call from their community to provide support in cold, hard cash, too.
“I founded FreeFrom on a conviction that felt radical at the time: that gender-based violence is an economic problem, and that survivors — given unrestricted cash — already know how to solve it,” Passi told Good Good Good.
“This type of financial support was once dismissed as impractical. Over the last decade, FreeFrom has built the evidence that it works.”
On August 29, Passi represented the organization at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival, where FreeFrom was awarded $2 million, along with nine other nonprofits with missions to uplift women and girls.
And FreeFrom is celebrating its tenth anniversary with a major impact report — the evidence, Passi supplied, that these cash transfers are working.
“Since 2016, we've put $10 million directly into survivors' hands,” Passi summarized. “To understand the impact of this work, we surveyed survivors who had participated in our programs.”
According to the 10-year report, all survivors surveyed had participated in at least one FreeFrom cash assistance program, receiving up to $1,500, with many engaged across multiple programs over as many as five years.
The findings showed that 94% of those surveyed strengthened their sense of social well-being, and 93% strengthened their physical and psychological safety after engaging with the organization’s cash assistance program.
More than 90% of survivors also made meaningful progress in securing employment, stable housing, healthcare, and education. And 88% had strengthened their financial security. Among the survey pool, over half of respondents — 56% — improved across all domains measured.
“Gender-based violence is so painful, prevalent, and complex that we make the mistake of thinking we have to solve every single piece of the problem for survivors. We don’t,” Passi said.
“Survivors are incredibly resilient, resourceful, and know what they need. With a little bit of financial support, they are healing and getting to thriving.”
This belief stems from an organizational ethos to “trust survivors.” In the years following the surge of the #MeToo movement, phrases like this, and “believe women,” became a rallying cry to provide more credence to the stories and lived experiences of GBV survivors.
But beyond an “I believe you,” FreeFrom practices trust in a more generous and unrestricted way: Trusting that survivors know what they need to heal.
“Survivors never have to justify their situation to get support from us. No receipts, no explaining themselves,” Passi said. “They just get cash and decide for themselves what happens next. That's how our programs are designed, and it's why they work.”
That trust doesn’t seem to concern itself with how exactly survivors spend their money — rather, it cares about results.
“Before FreeFrom, half the survivors we surveyed were in financial crisis. Today, that's 10%. More than half were in immediate physical danger. Today, that's 13%. But what surprised us most was what survivors accomplished in areas we weren't even targeting,” Passi said.
“95% made progress finding employment and accessing healthcare. 93% pursued education. 91% secured housing. We don't help survivors with job applications or housing searches. We give them cash, trust them to decide what they need, and they do the rest themselves.”
There is programming beyond the initial “Safety Fund.”
FreeFrom also offers a savings matching program that helps survivors match dollar-to-dollar up to $55 per month to build up to $1,440 in emergency savings over the course of a year.
Community financial coaching, webinars, and a “next-step” program are also available.
“The money I'd obtained through the savings match program went directly to me putting a down payment on an apartment when my safety was at the most risk, and my abuser was threatening violence against me and my father,” one survivor shares anonymously in the 10-year report. “It came in handy during an unexpected time when I had to leave my home.”
Beyond those handful of support structures, the power is put directly back into the survivors’ hands.
“You helped me understand that financial instability wasn't a curse or something that just happens like I've been told,” one survivor also shared anonymously.
“I have learned to have my own agency with money, and for the first time in my life, I feel safe and trust myself with financial choices.”
Advancing systemic solutions
While FreeFrom has reached thousands through its programming, Passi knows that the world needs systemic change; one nonprofit can’t reach all the survivors in a given area, let alone the entire country.
“Lasting change means a world where survivor safety is built into the systems survivors depend on, so they can continue to thrive,” Passi said. “FreeFrom has helped introduce more than 1,200 bills and pass over 220 pieces of legislation across the U.S. in support of survivor financial security.”
In 2023, the organization's data helped Chicago build one of the largest municipally-funded cash assistance programs for survivors in the U.S. The hope is to reach more large cities in the coming years.
“FreeFrom’s goals now are about scale. We want cash assistance to become a population-level solution to ending GBV — backed by philanthropic investment and adopted by local, state, and federal governments,” Passi said. “We want survivor-centered policies to be a permanent fixture in political agendas.”
And she makes a compelling case: Cash transfers are more cost-effective than the existing GBV frameworks in most states.
“In New York City, it costs $9,000 for a survivor and one child to stay in a shelter for one month. In North Carolina, every single time the police are called to an incident of domestic violence, it costs the state $5,500,” she said.
“FreeFrom is giving survivors $1,500 or less. Cash is not just what survivors are consistently saying is their number one need. It’s also the most cost-effective and lasting solution there is.”
Other interventions, like providing employees with survivor-supportive protections or giving credit union members access to survivor-informed banking services, have also been rolled out in FreeFrom’s first decade of advocacy.
“Ten years ago, economic security wasn’t seen as a factor in survivor safety,” Passi said. “Today it is — and we're proud of the role FreeFrom played in that shift.”
The economic shift is not just about dollars and cents, but the potential of financial support to set survivors free.
“Every survivor who gets to safety breaks a cycle that would have otherwise repeated. Give a survivor the financial floor, and she builds a safer family and a safer community,” Passi said.
“That's the whole point of this work: Prove, one survivor at a time, that the cycle can break.”
