पुस्तकको भाषा नेपाली भए पनि नाचसित जोडिएका धेरै शब्दहरू नेवार चलनचल्तीका शब्दमै राख्नु जरुरी थियो। केही नाचमा ठाउँ अनुसार एउटै कुराका लागि प्रयोग गरिने शब्द फरक फरक पनि पाइयो। नेपालीकरण गरिएका केही नाम नेवार भाषामा लेख्दा फरक हुँदो रहेछ। म मधेसकी नेवार, साधारण नेवार भाषा बोल्न र बुझ्न त सक्छु तर स्तरीकृत नेवार भाषा मेरो वशको कुरा रहेन। यो समस्या समाधानको सिङ्गो जिम्मेवारी लिने कार्तिकनाचकी शोधार्थी एवं नेपाल भाषाकी प्राध्यापक सुनिता राजभण्डारीको पूर्ण सहयोगप्रति आभारी छु।
म ‘कम्प्युटर लिटरेट’ हुन सकिनँ। त्यसैले सुरुदेखि किरण श्रेष्ठ र मीन महर्जनले निकै सहयोग गर्नुभयो। तर, धेरै वर्षपछि पुनः लेख्न थालेपछि सुन्दा शाक्य, सुनिल शाक्य, उर्गेन डङ्गोल, अनिता डङ्गोल अक्षर विन्यासमा निरन्तर खट्नुभयो। यथार्थमा सुन्दा शाक्य र कमल सुवेदी पुस्तकका निमित्त सबैभन्दा नजिकका आफन्त बन्नुभयो। पुस्तक अन्तिम तयारीको क्रममा समग्र पाण्डुलिपि सम्पादन, पृष्ठविन्यास, भाषिक-व्याकरणगत शुद्धीकरण र स्रोत विश्लेषणमा होम भट्टराईको मेहनत उदाहरणीय छ।
विगतको कोरोना महामारीका बेला कोही न कोही मरेको सुनेर होला, त्यतिखेर सात वर्ष मात्र भएको नाति आयान जोशीले “मा ! चाँडै किताब छापिहाल्नुस्, तपाईं मरिहाल्यो भने तपाईंले लेखेको सबै डस्टबिनमा जान्छ” भनेका शब्दले सधैँ घचघच्याइरहे पनि पाँच-छ वर्ष बितेपछि मात्र प्रकाशन गर्न भ्याइयो। तर जे होस्, मेरो नातिका ती शब्दले मलाई पुनः प्रेरित गरेका हुन्। नातिनी मेधावी श्रेष्ठले पनि विभिन्न अभिलेखहरूको फोटोकपी गर्न सहयोग गरेकी छिन्। पुस्तक प्रकाशनमा ल्याउन अमेरिकादेखि फोन गरेर घचघच्याउने बालसखा मञ्जु हाडाप्रति म ऋणी छु। त्यसै गरी मुद्रणको प्रबन्ध मिलाउने कृष्ण के.सी. तथा आकर्षक आवरण डिजाइनसहित मुद्रणमा निरन्तर खट्ने रवि महर्जन एवं सार्थक प्रिन्टिङ एन्ड अफिस सप्लाइका सबै भाइबहिनी धन्यवादका उदाहरणीय पात्र हुन्।
अन्तमा, १०० वर्ष पुगिसकेकी मेरी आमा गङ्गादेवी राजभण्डारी, जसले बुबा बितेकै वर्ष आफन्तहरूले रोक्दारोक्दै पनि मलाई विश्वास गरेर नृत्य अध्ययन गर्न अनुमति दिनुभयो। मेरो जीवन उहाँको ऋणमा डुबेको छ, जसलाई म चुकाउन चाहन्नँ।
२०८२, माघ

title: Chasing la dolce vita
content:
When he was a child growing up in Emilia-Romagna, my great-grandfather Marco once found an eagle fledgling that had fallen from its nest. He kept it warm in the folds of his shirt and ran home, only to discover as he undressed that the bird had eaten strips of his flesh, its beak tinged red with blood. The rescued eagle thrived in my great-grandfather’s care, its wingspan soon a remarkable length. And all the while, Marco himself grew immensely tall. Then, one day, without warning, the eagle flew away.
The moment my father told me this story when I was a boy, it lodged itself deep in my imagination. I pictured young Marco as a giant striding through the forests of north-central Italy, calling to the bird of prey, waiting in vain for it to land on his outstretched hand. Marco merged with the heroes of my illustrated classical civilisation books, earning his place between the busts of Roman emperors and the chapters on Greek mythology.
What I never realised was that this family legend held clues to who I am and to my relationship to Italy.
Lina Stores deli in Soho, London, has been a pillar of Italian life in England for decades. It’s where we’d sometimes meet our paternal grandparents when visiting London from our home in France. My brothers and I would line up in front of the refrigerated counter and ask for our favourite ravioli, doing our utmost to avoid any slip-ups in Italian that would make the staff wince: ‘ricotta e spinaci’, ‘zucca’, ‘funghi porcini’. Back at our grandparents’ flat, Nonna served the ravioli on an elaborately laid table, and my grandfather appeared with freshly grated Parmigiano. He’d sprinkle the cheese evenly over our pasta; never too much, nor too little. How he did this, and with such speed, we didn’t know. If we had spaghetti, Nonna would wrap her right hand around ours and twirl the fork with us so we held just the right amount, the bespattered tablecloth damning proof of our slapdash habits at home.
My grandparents trusted that these rituals of the table (they saw them as basic codes of Italianness, connecting displaced Italians everywhere) would allow us to paper over the differences in our ethnically blended and peripatetic family. In this way, we’d be able to claim Italian identity for ourselves, despite its competition in our lives with Englishness and Frenchness. It would anchor us, or so they believed, and prevent us being bullied and singled out.
Revving their Vespas and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me
Every summer, on car journeys to Italy we’d listen and re-listen to Italian songs and fairytales to drum the language into us. Once we’d crossed the Alps, any stopover became an opportunity for my father to immerse us in further knowledge. He kept a torch in his pocket, and in the stillness of churches he’d let the beam scurry over frescoes until it hovered, halo-like, above a painted face or a feature in the background. ‘Such bellezza,’ he’d whisper, ‘look at the beauty of that.’ In explaining Masaccio’s brushstrokes, or playing Verdi and Puccini arias at car-shaking volume, we sensed my father was offering us, his sons, yardsticks by which to measure life. He needed us to see ourselves as the inheritors of a civilisation unlike any other. Italianness was his gift to us.
In my teens, I spent a month in Florence looking after the child of a couple of scientists, colleagues of my father. My role was to speak to the boy in English; his parents’ job was to improve my Italian. The moment I was alone with the seven-year-old, he locked himself in his room and refused to come out. As a consolation, one evening, I was entrusted to a 16-year-old nephew who took me to join his friends in a packed central piazza. Within minutes, the assembled youngsters were trying to identify my hybrid accent, crowding round with questions, trying out their English: ‘Are you French or British?’ ‘Which football team do you support?’ ‘Have you got a girlfriend?’ Revving their Vespas, blasting music I didn’t recognise, and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me. I escaped into Florence, only vaguely aware of where I was going. Leaning against a wall on the banks of the Arno, the Ponte Vecchio in the distance, I tried to convince myself that the surrounding ‘bellezza’ vaunted by my father was mine, that I fitted into the circus of Italian life I’d seen in Fellini films, but I felt I was a baffling anomaly, an impostor. The chameleon skills I’d always employed to fudge my way through existence had let me down. My hosts were in a state of panic on my return. Where had I been? I wasn’t going to be allowed out again. I’d failed as a childminder. And as an Italian.
A cousin recently emailed me photographs of my great-grandfather Marco, the first to set the family’s migrations in motion. I was surprised to see that he was as tall as the family legend of the eagle would have it, towering over others, but also that he was standing in front of what was the Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, the place he’d apparently helped to run. This was the very spot in London I’d sat on many occasions when, as a student at King’s College, I’d search for quiet garden squares in which to read and revise for exams. I’d always believed I was drawn to the Italian Hospital because of its name. But I remember how, more than once, I’d had to get up and leave, overwhelmed by an inexplicable sadness. In another photograph, Marco was posing with my great-grandmother Delfina, also from Emilia-Romagna, on a patch of grass in Hyde Park. I recognised it immediately as the hidden slope leading down to the Serpentine lake where I often go.
After an online census revealed my great-grandparents’ old address on Highbury Fields, the sorrow I experienced outside the Italian Hospital returns. But this time its source is evident: we used to take our children to the playground by that house, parking right by my great-grandparents’ front door, our shouts and chatting rebounding off the windows. All these coincidences can doubtless be rationally explained, yet they leave me feeling that I live in the wake of tumultuous decisions made long before I was born, that I’m in a web of unseen connections, in friction with the mysteries of an uprooted Italian past.
Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, Marco would declare that he was finally home
In 1940, when Mussolini declared war on Britain and France, all the ‘enemy aliens’ living in Britain had to be imprisoned, or as Winston Churchill put it: ‘Collar the lot!’ Marco, along with thousands of other Italians, and Germans, was rounded up and interned on the Isle of Man. As Rachel Pistol writes in ‘Enemy Aliens’ (2024), many Italian shops and businesses across the country were broken into and smashed by mobs. Marco was lucky not to be placed on the SS Arandora Star, a prisoner-of-war ship heading to Canada. More than 800 of these internees, including 442 Italians, died when the boat was torpedoed off the coast of Ireland. Just under a quarter were from different corners of Emilia-Romagna – some of them friends of Marco. The Italian Hospital scraped through the war and Marco returned to assist them. Researching this essay, I discovered that the building was broken into in 1947 and my great-grandmother, who was with her husband that day, died while confronting the intruders.
On a visit to Emilia-Romagna some years ago, I met old people who recalled widowed Marco’s long stays every summer. Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, he would declare that he was finally home. Then he would leave for London again, returning the summer following, then again setting off, over and over. Just like us, his descendants.
Between the unification of Italy, in 1861, and 1985, around 29 million Italians left the peninsula. Political instability, high birth rates, natural disasters, unprofitable sharecropping (especially in the South), deprivation and overpopulation were major drivers for this exodus. And the more people left en masse, the more they encouraged others to join them. Today, about 80 million people outside Italy claim full or partial Italian ancestry. This diaspora has generated Little Italys across the world: in New York’s Manhattan, in La Boca, Buenos Aires, and in Clerkenwell, London. Once oases of solidarity, home-away-from-home citadels, where you could find anything – from the Italy football kit to keyrings with Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man – they now mostly feel like places of historic, even faded, hyper-Italianness. By 1920, São Paulo alone was home to 70 per cent of the Italians who emigrated to Brazil; as many as 60 per cent of Argentinians have a link to Italy, and Italian is still one of the main mother tongues spoken in Toronto, Canada. In Australia, 4.4 per cent of the population is of Italian heritage. In America, around 17 million people identify as Italian.
Descendants of Italian migrants generally express an intense pride in their heritage, and many continue to live by its sociocultural tenets in spite of decades, or more, of absence. It is as if time away from Italy, and geographical distance, only amplify a yearning for it. Stanley Tucci, to cite but one well-known example (the same could probably be said of Lady Gaga or Francis Ford Coppola) begins his TV food series Searching for Italy (2021-22) by stating in his broad American accent: ‘I’m Italian on both sides.’
Every summer, as per my own family’s tradition, members of this diaspora return to Italy. They enjoy the peninsula in the heat-filled months: sea, mountains, food, art and music, and its dolce vita. Where Italians living in Italy might imbue their identity with more intrinsically regional elements, the diaspora, in its dissemination around the globe, carries with it a more all-encompassing interpretation of the country. Their version of Italy, like the one I grew up with, is capable of brushing over fractures and complications, and the darker sides of the nation, articulated as it is by ideals that extoll the peninsula as a connected whole.
For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy
By upholding and publicising the symbols of Italy – fashion, art, food, football – the diaspora has helped turn them into a recognisable shorthand for the country abroad. Visiting London’s Italian restaurants with my family, I’m struck by how many still have straw-clad Chianti bottles on the tables, and a packet of grissini tucked next to the plates, not to mention waiters who make a show of noisily grinding pepper onto our food. The performative nature of this overseas Italianness, its theatricality, is reinforced by walls decorated with photos of the owners posing with Italian American celebrities like Al Pacino, Robert De Niro or Sylvester Stallone. It is as if we’ve all been given roles, customers and waiters alike, in a Pirandello play that challenges distinctions between illusion and reality.
My kids love YouTube and TikTok videos in which a nonna or nonno, from a well-ordered kitchen in Italy, reveals how to make the creamiest cacio e pepe or the tastiest tomato sauce. These elderly cooks appear to embody an authentic art to being Italian that cuts through the mimicry and stagecraft. The children laugh loudest when these elderly home chefs from Italy screw up their faces in disgust when asked to taste American shop-bought pizza or frozen lasagne. ‘Do you know what merda means in English?’ one asks.
For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy. In an ideal world, it is seasoned with herbs once grown by the Romans, made with San Marzano tomatoes nourished by volcanic soil, and olive oil from Puglia’s ancient groves. This level of culinary precision largely explains why Italians are baffled, outraged even, by foreigners committing offences with their cuisine – snapping dry spaghetti in two before cooking it, grating parmesan onto seafood risotto, or mixing garlic and onion as a base for the same sauce. It might seem precious to outsiders, but a belief in excellence and the purity of traditions underpins Italianness. Indeed, something akin to the formula for tomato sauce can be applied to all areas of Italian production, from coffee machines and scooters to architecture. For my father and grandparents, Italian ingenuity stemmed from the peninsula’s endemic flair. A Lamborghini or a Gio Ponti chair was simply the latest layer of sediment in an accretion of refinement that had already given rise to Brunelleschi’s Dome and Scarlatti’s sonatas.
Despite endorsing the country as the paragon of human advancement, my father routinely turned down job offers at Italian universities and research centres, choosing instead to work in France. The resulting tension, played out in frequently announced but endlessly postponed homecomings, threw us into ever more convoluted cycles of l’eterno ritorno that had already tormented my family for two generations with their toing and froing between the peninsula and Britain. Now, with a family of my own, and living and working in London, I’m aware of how I’m resuscitating the dilemmas my parents and grandparents faced.
Increasingly, I’m hankering after Italy, wanting to pass on its rituals. I’ve made sure my children have Italian first names and a basic knowledge of Italy’s geography and history, and they seem to accept this as a given. I’ve fed them stories about eagles and ancestors, accounts of my childhood holidays in Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany, snippets of my time studying in Padua and Florence. I refer back to weddings and family gatherings we’ve all been to, seeding these memories in them, tincturing them with the aura of official history. I tell them about films they should watch one day, by Antonioni and Visconti, of the writings of Boccaccio and Dante. This visceral attachment to Italy is something I feel compelled to pass on. All the while, in parallel, I know I must value the family environment my wife and I have built in England – which is their home. It is an acknowledgement, too, of the sacrifices my ancestors made.
At times, the trap snaps shut. I sense I’m merely living out the choices of the dead, unable to escape their restlessness. Visits to Italy only temporarily assuage the feelings of unsettledness, while leaving again stirs it up. I’m losing something I’ve never owned, just as I’ve been defined by a homeland I don’t inhabit, a past I cannot alter.
Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned
Perhaps, like my diasporic peers who return every summer, I find it easier to fall back on wistful memories and fantasy. I revert all too conveniently, obsessively, to the house we stayed in every year during my youth. As if in a vision, I hold on to the hoopoes in the Tuscan grassland, their heads bobbing up and down in search of insects; my parents arriving with fresh focaccia from the village; the lizards darting across the stone walls; the steady strumming of the cicadas, and the sun tensing the vineyard wires until they buzzed and sang. Warm, moonlit evenings, too, with long tables under giant oaks, friends of our parents talking and singing Italian songs late into the night, knowing no one would tell us to go to bed. I want my children to experience all this, yet I know that I can’t recreate it.
I’ve hunted for echoes of these idyllic days in Italian literature and art, and added them to the building blocks of my emigrant longing. Reading Italo Calvino’s novel The Baron in the Trees (1957), I picture the specific branches and trunks I climbed in childhood. I smell and feel the remembered coolness of stone floors and shaded high-ceilinged rooms when immersed in Lampedusa’s novel The Leopard (1958). An Andrea Mantegna painting, like The Agony in the Garden (1455-56), sends me right back to horizons dotted with hilltop villages and fortified towers of crumbling stone. I’m conscious of the pull of Italy whenever I watch its films – and the irrational reverence this triggers. Recently, I found Alice Rohrwacher’s film La chimera (2023) almost too poignant to watch as it teemed with the details of Italian life.
I know that, for every idealised image of the country, there’s a darker insinuation that Italians have had to face abroad. Late 19th-century and early 20th-century migrants from the peninsula frequently encountered discrimination – accompanied by a range of slurs, from ‘wop’ and ‘eyetie’ in Britain and the US, to ‘rital’ in France. Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned, particularly when they were from the south of the peninsula. Hate-mongers, such as the Ku Klux Klan, alleged that the dregs of Italy were being sent abroad to cleanse the peninsula of its undesirables. In Protestant and English-speaking countries, Italian immigrants became easy targets because of their Catholicism, or their associations with anarchism and organised crime.
Direct conflict regularly flared up. In 1891, in New Orleans in the US, 11 Italians were acquitted of the murder of the local police chief only to be seized by a mob of thousands and lynched. In France in 1893, locals turned on Italian immigrant workers in Aigues-Mortes, reportedly killing eight men, though the number is thought to be far higher. And in 1934, in Kalgoorlie, Australia, anti-Italian killings took place against a similar backdrop of resentment against foreigners allegedly taking jobs.
Even assimilated Italians had their loyalty to their newly adopted lands questioned. It wasn’t just more recently arrived Italians like my great-grandfather who were interned as ‘enemy aliens’ during the Second World War. Some of the 4,000 men who were rounded up had spent most of their lives in Britain. This suspicion was mirrored, to a lesser degree, in Australia and the US – and this while half a million Italian Americans served in the US army during the Second World War, and 7,000 Anglo-Italians served in the British army.
In today’s world of hardening borders and changing alliances, challenges lie ahead for diaspora Italians within Italy itself. Rules for claiming Italian citizenship through ancestry or ius sanguinis (‘right of blood’) have been tightened for descendants of emigrants. This route to citizenship is now granted only to people who have a parent or a grandparent with exclusive Italian nationality, or a parent who was a citizen for two years before their birth. A 160-year history of citizenship by descent has been undermined. The question, officially at least, of who is Italian or not will be thrown into further disarray. I know from experience how hard it will be to extricate Italy from the bodies, imaginations and feelings of these figli d’italiani, these sons and daughters dispersed and far away – people who often feel they have earned the right to call themselves Italian, or at least proudly Italo-something, not least because of the stigma and rejection they or their ancestors once encountered.
At the heart of this circling around identity lies a thorny and painful question. Why do so many Italians continue to leave, and stay away? Between 2023 and 2024, 270,000 Italians emigrated, a figure considerably higher than in the previous two years. And behind the statistics lurks another grave concern: Italy’s population has been declining and is set to lose about 7 million people of working age by 2050. In 2025, there were only 355,000 births – the lowest number since the unification of Italy. In this context, the question of impossible returns is all the more troubling.
I’d like to think that there exists a worldwide collective remembrance of all things Italian, even from the days before the Risorgimento, or the movement for unification. I want to believe the countless stories of regions, cities and villages, of injustices and glories, are being kept safe by millions of descendants of emigrants who have become fervent storytellers. They are the unsung chroniclers of the peninsula, the guardians of a rich repository of traditions and customs, precisely because they have had to work harder to preserve this heritage than natal Italians. In families everywhere, from Argentina, Brazil, Canada, the US, Uruguay and Australia to France and the UK, traces of Italy remain in photographs, books and art, in buildings and the rituals of food. It is one of the paradoxes of diasporas that it is those who leave who want their country of origin to be fixed in time and preserved a certain way.
My children and I have now visited most of the spots across London where my family lived and worked. Walking further from the former Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, it doesn’t take us long to reach Clerkenwell’s once-vibrant Little Italy. Though many of the delis and ice-cream parlours have been changed by new waves of immigration and redevelopment, the plaque to Giuseppe Mazzini, a champion of Italian unification, on Laystall Street, reminds passersby of the area’s historic importance to Italianness. Mass is still celebrated in Italian at St Peter’s Church, and near the back of the church is a monument to the dead of the SS Arandora Star. We sit and read the list of surnames as they mingle with the priest’s prayers to form one long lament. I picture the churches of Emilia-Romagna, and the cemeteries where my ancestors are buried, and I see the roads that lead from there to London and back, worn down by constant travelling in both directions, a straddling between nations, where ghosts are as substantial as the living.
My brothers have now exited the cycle of deferred returns by establishing families with Italian women who grew up in Italy itself. One of them has moved to Italy. In his family, Italian is, once again, the language spoken. We’ve all had to play catch-up with Italianness, but I have focused too much on the uncertainty this elicits in me. Instead, I should turn to the strength of the diasporic experience. There is power in duality, in multiplicity, and restlessness. And reassurance, too, in knowing that in London, my home, the invisible figure of my great-grandfather walks ahead of me, an eagle from Emilia-Romagna circling the sky above us.

title: The moving lessons of nomadic herders
content:
The moving lessons of nomadic herders
Loading...
The summer of 2026 hasn’t just been a time for pastoral relaxation in the great outdoors; it’s also been a season of, and for, pastoralists. Global events have brought together hundreds of representatives from communities whose lives and livelihoods are built on pastoral or nomadic herding traditions.
On Monday, the sixth World Nomad Games kicked off in Kyrgyzstan, a former Soviet republic in Central Asia. Hundreds of participants are competing in horse races and horseback wrestling, falconry, and archery, among other events.
Meanwhile, over the preceding two weeks, at a conference in Mongolia – where about a third of the population is nomadic – pastoralists from around the world advocated for rights to public grazing lands and freer movement.
The United Nations has designated 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists – a sign of the movement to recognize pastoralists’ roles and rights as contributing citizens and sources of practical expertise and cultural pride. It denotes an evolving humility and respect among governments and scientists who are seeking ways to incorporate the traditional approaches into a modern system long defined by distinct boundaries, increasing urbanization, and regulated resource access.
The Mongolia meeting, Le Monde pointed out last month, marked a shift from viewing nomadic groups and their practices as “a driver of land degradation” to recognizing their “many benefits: maintaining landscapes, preserving biodiversity, preventing fires, adding value to regions and enabling adaptation to climate change.”
The world’s estimated 500 million pastoralists have fine-tuned the skill of living off the meat, dairy, fibers, and hides produced by their herds of sheep, cattle, camels, yaks, reindeer, and llamas. And they’ve done this while regularly on the move – across the Arctic regions of North America and Scandinavia, the steppes of Russia and Central Asia, mountains of South America and South Asia, and the arid reaches of Africa and the Middle East.
As countries have pursued economic growth and industrialization, pastoralism was seen as antiquated and inconvenient– as a system to be “modernized,” sometimes forcibly. Now, the challenges of severe weather and desertification present risks of similar forced responses, including mandatory restrictions on herd sizes and herders’ movements.
But in other quarters, there’s recognition that the potential threats of climate change can be turned into opportunities for community cohesion and repair. In southern India, for example, villagers are allowing – and even paying – herders to use their land in exchange for dung, the natural fertilizer that farmers need to produce higher-value organic crops.
At the conference in Mongolia, nomadic representatives sought ideas as well as funding to help protect their livelihoods. Alongside that, as the environmental news site Mongabay reported, they sought something less tangible – official acknowledgment of what they have to offer through their accumulated knowledge in adapting to changing landscapes.
Such explicit and shared recognition among humankind has inestimable value.

title: Learning to Live With the Aral Sea’s Changed Landscape
content:
In February, participants from a new school in Nukus joined local foresters on the dried bed of the Aral Sea to plant saxaul. The shrubs can take root in salty ground and help hold down dust blowing across Karakalpakstan. Foresters from the Karauzyak State Forestry Department guided the work, drawing on years of experience in the region.
The planting exercise, organized with the United Nations Development Programme, offered an early indication of how the Aral School intends to teach. Its participants work alongside people already responding to the sea’s retreat, learning from the landscape and those who live with its consequences.
Now, the school is preparing for a second intake with a six-month residency in Nukus from January to June 2027. Architect and curator Joseph Grima will lead the program, which will focus on climate and landscape. Applications are open until October 25.
Based in the capital of Uzbekistan’s autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan, the school brings international practitioners together with participants from the region. The Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF), which established it, announced the new intake and Grima’s appointment during an assembly at the Savitsky Museum in Nukus. The museum owes its remarkable collection to Igor Savitsky, who rescued thousands of works rejected by the Soviet authorities, finding them a refuge in remote Nukus.
Gayane Umerova, chair of ACDF, and Grima spoke to The Times of Central Asia about the school’s long-term goals and how local people will help shape its work.
“The Aral School was never conceived as a single cohort or a single event. It’s a long-term commitment by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) in line with the Government’s plan for Karakalpakstan,” she told The Times of Central Asia. “The programme is designed from the ground up to avoid simply taking knowledge without giving anything back. The cohorts live in Nukus for half a year, not for a two-week field trip, precisely so that the landscape and the people in it are teachers, not subjects.”
“Participants would also work directly with local professional bodies and institutions,” Umerova said. “Local experts sit inside the programme’s design, not as guest lecturers brought in to validate conclusions already reached,” she said.
Once the world’s fourth-largest lake, the Aral Sea shrank as Soviet irrigation projects diverted water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to grow cotton and other crops. The retreat devastated fishing communities and exposed a seabed contaminated by agricultural chemicals. Wind carried salt and dust across the surrounding land.
In Moynaq, once a fishing port, fishermen dug channels through the sand to reach the retreating water. Eventually, they abandoned their grounded boats, leaving rusting hulls on what had been the seabed.
The consequences differ across the former sea. In Kazakhstan, the Kokaral Dam has helped the North Aral recover, raising water levels and supporting the return of fishing. The southern basin remains severely depleted.
For the school, that damaged environment is also a place where people continue to farm and build livelihoods. Its first course concentrated on food and water at a household level. The second will examine the land and river systems that sustain them, including the effects of irrigation and the movement of salt through the landscape.
For Gulnaz Abutova, founder of the Clean Water project, those pressures became tangible while picking cotton in Turtkul in 2014. She told The Times of Central Asia in 2025 about the experience. “I even saw people using water from irrigation channels (aryks) for cooking, boiling it and adding it to their food.”
Grima told TCA he had previously thought of design education as a formula that could be applied anywhere, but “Nukus has shifted that perception.”
“It has reframed a question for me: not ‘how do we bring good design here’ but ‘how does the landscape itself teach the discipline something it doesn’t already know.’”
His background includes leading Design Academy Eindhoven and research into architecture that uses fewer finite natural resources. In Nukus, the approach will bring design into contact with environmental research, asking how changes in land use shape everyday life.
Ahead of the assembly, Grima visited the International Innovation Centre for the Aral Sea Basin and the Amu Darya. He also toured the Academy of Sciences of Karakalpakstan and met specialists from the region.
Umerova outlined how the foundation would judge the school’s progress.
“In practical terms: growth in the number of regional participants in each cohort, deeper integration with local professional bodies, and projects that move from the classroom into implementation, whether that’s in agriculture, water systems, or landscape design,” she said.
“We are hosting the Aral School Assembly this month, which is a deliberate three-day knowledge transfer programme; alumni and mentors pass on the questions they leave behind, so local insight builds and develops across the new cohort instead of resetting,” she told TCA.
“We’re building in publication/presentation and exhibition as explicit next steps and deliverables, so the method and the findings travel beyond the school, and the whole programme community and region itself gets to keep and use them,” Grima said. “The 2027 cohort will deliberately sharpen its focus toward participants from the region itself.”
Recruiting people who already live with the consequences would help keep the work rooted there, he noted.
There is already work to build on. In April, ACDF presented twelve objects developed by the first cohort at Milan Design Week. The collection grew from research into the region’s food and water systems and explored the use of accessible, sustainable materials.
The broader water problems require decisions far beyond the school. A World Bank-backed cooperation project is intended to improve the management of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins, with shared data and coordination between countries central to that work. The residency in Nukus operates at a smaller scale, allowing researchers to examine how those pressures affect particular places and households.
“Culture here isn’t just decoration on top of environmental policy. We see it as a way of building relationships between landscape, heritage, and the people who live with the consequences of what happened to this sea,” Umerova said.
The school forms part of a wider series of ACDF initiatives in Karakalpakstan, including the Aral Culture Summit, first held in April 2025.
“We’ll also be watching whether the Aral Culture Summit and the School continue to reinforce and complement each other, research impacting exhibitions, exhibitions feeding the next round of questions,” she said.
Alongside the postgraduate program, ACDF has announced the first Aral Artistic Research Fellowship. The nine-month fellowship has been awarded to Uzbekistan-born artists Zukhra and Fotima Sharipova, whose work examines landscape, material culture, environmental transformation and locally embedded knowledge.
Their research will continue until June 2027, with ACDF providing production and logistical support. The resulting work is expected to be presented at the second Aral Culture Summit in spring 2027.
Zukhra plans to expose raw cotton canvas to the landscape across two seasons, allowing salt and wind to alter its surface. She will also work with local craftspeople to explore Karakalpak ornament and textile traditions. Cotton gives the project a particular resonance in a region whose water systems were reshaped to support its cultivation.
Fotima will make pigments from local minerals and plants. Her research will build visual and sound archives, incorporating recorded voices into an installation. According to the foundation, both artists begin their fieldwork in Karakalpakstan in September.
The school’s application page says there is no tuition fee. Accommodation and research costs are covered, and participants receive a monthly stipend. The call is aimed at postgraduate practitioners, including people working in design and environmental research. The selected cohort is due to be announced on December 1.
“If we succeed, in a few years’ time the Aral Sea will be spoken about internationally not only for what was lost, but for what is being learned and built here,” Umerova said.

title: Circular Bharat: Turning waste into value
content:
By Sanjiv Kumar, President – Strategy, Renvion Solutions Private Limited
Twenty-five years ago, when India notified the Municipal Solid Wastes (MSW) Rules, 2000, waste management was a very different world. It was largely viewed as a municipal responsibility to collect the waste, transport it and find a place to dispose of it. However, what began primarily as an environmental compliance requirement has gradually developed into an ecosystem of infrastructure, technology, investment, entrepreneurship, resource recovery and employment. That change captures India’s journey from Swachh Bharat towards Circular Bharat.
Swachh Bharat changed the scale
The MSW Rules, 2000 created an important national regulatory foundation. But the launch of the Swachh Bharat Mission in 2014 transformed sanitation and cleanliness from primarily municipal subjects into a national movement. The progress is visible. Door-to-door waste collection, negligible in 2014–15, now covers about 98 per cent of urban wards. More than 250,000 collection vehicles support the system, while MSW processing has increased from about 16 per cent in 2014–15 to around 80 per cent in 2025–26.
Behind these sanitation statistics lies another story the creation of an environmental economy. Collection vehicles need drivers, operators, maintenance and digital tracking. Material recovery facilities (MRFs) need sorters, supervisors and logistics. Composting, biomethanation, recycling, refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and waste-to-energy (WtE) facilities need engineers, technicians and plant operators. Every tonne moved away from dumping towards organised collection, processing and recovery potentially creates environmental as well as economic value.
From disposal to resource recovery
The Solid Waste Management (SWM) Rules, 2016 accelerated this transition by strengthening segregation, processing, recycling, MRFs, composting, biomethanation, RDF and energy recovery. The philosophy gradually changed: landfill should no longer be the first destination of waste; it should increasingly become the last resort. Once waste is segregated, its identity changes. Wet waste can produce compost, biogas or compressed biogas. Dry waste can yield paper, plastics, metals and other secondary raw materials. Combustible fractions can substitute conventional fuels. Construction waste can return to the economy as recycled building material. Waste becomes feedstock. Disposal becomes recovery. Cost can become value. That is circular economy in practice.
Compliance can create markets
Good environmental regulation can do more than enforce compliance: it can create conditions for markets. When segregation is mandatory, collection and sorting solutions are required. When processing is required, infrastructure must be created. When bulk waste generators (BWGs) are given responsibility, a professional B2B waste-management market emerges. When recovered materials are required by industry, investment in recovery becomes more viable. The SWM Rules, 2026 take this evolution further through four-stream segregation, greater BWG responsibility, digital tracking, stronger restrictions on landfilling, environmental compensation and progressive RDF substitution requirements.
Rise of the wastepreneur
Perhaps the most encouraging change is the profile of people entering waste management. A new entrepreneur is emerging: the “wastepreneur” – someone who sees economic value where society previously saw something to throw away. Today, startups are working on automated sorting, plastics recovery, recycling, digital traceability, biomining, decentralised processing, IoT-enabled collection, secondary materials and circular economy technologies. Government initiatives are encouraging this ecosystem. The first cohort of 30 startups under the Swachhata Startup Challenge reportedly managed more than 63,000 tonnes of waste and generated more than 2,000 employment opportunities.
The employment opportunity is equally significant. Waste management remains labour-intensive, and frontline sanitation workers will always be essential. But they are increasingly being joined by engineers, plant operators, recycling specialists, equipment technicians, environmental scientists, logistics professionals, GIS and data specialists, sustainability professionals and compliance experts.
India also had a circular economy long before we started using the term. Waste pickers, kabadiwalas, aggregators and scrap dealers have recovered materials for decades. They are, in many respects, India’s original circular-economy entrepreneurs. The objective of modernisation should not be to displace them, but to integrate and strengthen them through recognition, personal protective equipment, training, technology, social protection and opportunities to become organised aggregators, service providers and entrepreneurs.
From Clean India to Circular India
Waste should no longer be viewed merely as garbage. India’s wider circular economy has been estimated to have the potential to reach around $2 trillion by 2050 and create approximately 10 million jobs. The opportunity extends well beyond municipal waste.
Swachh Bharat gave India a cleanliness movement. Circular Bharat can turn that movement into a resource revolution. We should no longer measure success only by asking, “How much waste did we collect?” We must also ask: How much did we recover? How much material is returned to productive use? How many enterprises did we enable? And how many green careers did we create?

title: Americans mark 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks
content:
Americans commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, remembering the shock, the dead and the sweeping consequences of the al-Qaeda attacks on symbols of U.S. might and prosperity.
The milestone anniversary brought memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names – and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll. On Sept. 11, 2001, al-Qaeda extremists hijacked four commercial jets and crashed them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.
Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to the trade centre to hear his name and all the others read aloud Friday morning. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago.
“Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered.
Trump attends Pentagon observance
The attacks brought down the World Trade Center’s twin towers – icons of U.S. economic power, and among the tallest buildings on Earth – and blew a hole in the Pentagon, the U.S. military’s fortress-like headquarters near Washington. The fourth plane was headed for the nation’s capital, officials concluded, but the aircraft went down in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew members stormed the cockpit and fought the hijackers.
“Sept. 11 reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” President Donald Trump said Friday at the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony Friday.
“The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win,” added the Republican, who was in his native New York on 9/11.
Former President George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden and current Vice-President JD Vance convened for the observance at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in New York. Other administration officials went to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
At ground zero, a new tribute to those who fell ill
For Angilic Casalduc, attending the New York commemoration “helps to show you’re not alone.” She lost her mother, Vivian Casalduc.
“There’s no timeline for grief, and unfortunately, no one can say how can you can grieve, but coming here once a year makes it feel just a little bit better,” she said.
Traditionally, there are no political speeches at the ground zero commemoration, where victims’ relatives read aloud the long list of names and added personal messages. They thanked first responders and the military, talked about their loved ones’ lives, and mentioned family milestones they’ve missed. Many of those who spoke were too young to have met the relatives they lost.
The ceremony has long been punctuated with moments of silence at key points in the attack timeline and this year organizers added another moment to honour people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers’ fiery collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses. Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
The impact of 9/11 endures
How 9/11 is still claiming its first responders.
Reuters
It’s a reminder of how the attacks’ long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the U.S. and beyond.
The U.S.-led global war on terrorism included invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan – the latter Washington’s longest war – and detentions and harsh interrogation of terror suspects in an international network of secret CIA prisons. The U.S. found and killed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011, but accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed still awaits a trial 23 years after his capture.
The attacks changed U.S. air travel, prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers and banking regulations, and generated ongoing debate over the balance between security and freedom. The Department of Homeland Security, many state anti-terrorism laws and billions of dollars in state and local counterterrorism funding all are post-9/11 creations.
So, too, is the culture of individual vigilance summed up by the slogan “ if you see something, say something.”
Sept. 11 generated a wave of patriotism that propelled some Americans to join the military, fire departments, police forces or other public agencies.
Casey Kloepfer became a New York police officer this June. He was 4 when his father, Officer Ronald Kloepfer, was killed at the trade centre.
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honour him and be the best police officer I can,” the 29-year-old, who wears his father’s badge number, said by phone this week.
New York’s mayor comes under scrutiny
Amid the calls to service and for national unity that many remember, the attacks also fanned mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes directed at Muslims.
In the quarter-century since, Muslim Americans have played a growing role in public life from statehouses to Congress to New York City Hall, where Zohran Mamdani is the city’s first Muslim mayor. Yet he faced some criticism for attending the anniversary ceremony at ground zero, something his predecessors have done for years.
Some complaints came from Republican ex-Gov. George Pataki and 9/11 victims’ relatives, who cited among other things past remarks that some of Mamdani’s political associates have made about the attacks. Former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Republican, also inveighed against Mamdani attending, though the two shook hands Friday as they and other officials awaited the start of the observance.
Mamdani, a Democrat, said earlier this week that he loves the city and country and wants the anniversary to focus on victims’ families, first responders and New Yorkers who helped one another after the attacks, which he called a “horrific act of terror.” The 34-year-old mayor was an elementary school student in New York on 9/11.
Times Square billboards pause advertisements
Remembrances extended far beyond the attack sites, including beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium and a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
Sept. 11 isn’t a federal holiday, but Congress has designated it both Patriot Day and a National Day of Service and Remembrance.
“One appropriate way to remember is by serving,” says Jay Winuk, who lost his brother Glenn Winuk and then co-founded the volunteer organization 9/11 Day with friend David Paine. The group helps people find volunteer opportunities and this year arranged for dozens of Times Square billboards to pause their advertising at 9:11 a.m. Friday.
Instead, they simply displayed the time.

title: Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης
content:
Ένα ντοκιμαντέρ που φωτίζει τα ορόσημα μιας διαδρομής σχεδόν ενός αιώνα, αλλά και την πρωτοπορία, και τη φροντίδα για τον άνθρωπο και την κοινωνία.
Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης


Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης
Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay αποτελεί την πρώτη ολιστική παρέμβαση στη χώρα μας η οποία βάζει τα παιδιά στο επίκεντρο των αποφάσεων που τα αφορούν μέσα από έρευνα, εκπαίδευση επαγγελματιών και ένα εθνικό σχέδιο δράσης για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη
«Είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου και ελπίζουμε πάρα πολλά στην υλοποίησή του», επισήμανε ο υπουργός Δικαιοσύνης Γιώργος Φλωρίδης, κατά την έναρξη της εκδήλωσης «ChildSay – Ενσωματώνοντας τη φωνή των παιδιών στη λήψη δικαστικών αποφάσεων για την επιμέλεια» που διοργανώθηκε από το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης και υλοποιείται στο πλαίσιο του ευρωπαϊκού προγράμματος «Πολίτες, Ισότητα, Δικαιώματα και Αξίες». Ουσιαστικά το καινοτόμο αυτό ευρωπαϊκό πρόγραμμα αποσκοπεί σε μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη.
Ειδικότερα, κάθε χρόνο χιλιάδες παιδιά στην Ελλάδα περνούν μέσα από τις διαδικασίες λήψης αποφάσεων επιμέλειας και γονικής μέριμνας, χωρίς η γνώμη τους να ακούγεται ή να λαμβάνεται υπόψη σοβαρά, κάτι που είναι σε βάρος της ψυχικής υγείας και των δικαιωμάτων των ανήλικων παιδιών.
Έτσι, το πρόγραμμα ChildSay που είναι ένα συγχρηματοδοτούμενο από την Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση έργο, αποτελεί την πρώτη ολιστική παρέμβαση στη χώρα μας η οποία βάζει τα παιδιά στο επίκεντρο των αποφάσεων που τα αφορούν μέσα από έρευνα, εκπαίδευση επαγγελματιών και ένα εθνικό σχέδιο δράσης για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη.
Αφορά παιδιά ηλικίας από 6 έως 10 ετών, γονείς, εισαγγελείς, δικαστές και δικηγόρους, αλλά και επαγγελματίες, όπως είναι αστυνομικοί, συμβολαιογράφοι, δικαστικοί επιμελητές, κοινωνικοί λειτουργοί και ψυχολόγοι.
Στο πρόγραμμα αυτό, συνολικής διάρκειας υλοποίησης 24 μηνών, συμμετέχει το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης ως εταίρος, με στόχο να ενσωματωθεί ουσιαστικά η φωνή και τα δικαιώματα των παιδιών στις αποφάσεις της επιμέλειας σε ευθυγράμμιση με τα διεθνή πρότυπα Δικαιοσύνης φιλικής προς το παιδί. Ακόμη, το ChildSay αξιολογεί την ισχύουσα νομοθεσία, εκπαιδεύει δικαστές, δικηγόρους και ψυχολόγους σε παιδοκεντρικές πρακτικές.
Ο κ. Φλωρίδης στον σύντομο χαιρετισμό του έκανε αναφορά σε μια απόφαση του Ευρωπαϊκού Δικαστηρίου Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου, η οποία δημοσιεύθηκε τον Σεπτέμβριο του 2025 και αφορούσε προσφυγή κατά της Ελλάδος. Όπως εξήγησε, το Ευρωπαϊκό Δικαστήριο Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου σημείωνε ότι χρειάζονται ορισμένες προϋποθέσεις ώστε ένα δικαστήριο να μπορεί να ακούσει τα παιδιά και συνέχισε: «Σε αυτή την απόφαση αναφέρεται επί λέξει: “Οι προαναφερθείσες προϋποθέσεις είναι καλά ορισμένες στο ελληνικό νομικό σύστημα. Σύμφωνα με τη νομολογία του Αρείου Πάγου, όπως παρουσιάζεται από την Κυβέρνηση, ένα δικαστήριο υποχρεούται να ακούσει ένα παιδί μόνο εφόσον θεωρεί ότι το παιδί διαθέτει την απαιτούμενη ωριμότητα. Δεν απαιτείται ειδική αιτιολογία για την απόφαση σχετικά με το αν το παιδί διαθέτει την απαιτούμενη ωριμότητα, η οποία καθορίζεται με ελεύθερη εκτίμηση των αποδεικτικών στοιχείων».
«Δηλαδή, η νομοθεσία η δική μας περιλαμβάνει τις προϋποθέσεις για να ακουστεί ένα παιδί. Τι σημαίνει αυτό; Σημαίνει ότι το ελληνικό νομικό σύστημα είναι θωρακισμένο στα θέματα αυτά. Τι μένει; Να δώσουμε ένα ουσιαστικό περιεχόμενο σε αυτές τις δυνατότητες του ελληνικού νομικού συστήματος, όπως αυτές αποτυπώνονται στους νόμους και έχουν διαπλαστεί και από τη νομολογία των ελληνικών δικαστηρίων. Και εδώ είναι που το πρόγραμμα αυτό μπορεί να προσφέρει πάρα πολλά. Και επειδή έχουμε ήδη πέντε χρόνια από την εφαρμογή κάποιων αλλαγών στο Οικογενειακό Δίκαιο, τις οποίες αξιολογούμε διαρκώς, πρόθεσή μας είναι, να συστήσουμε άμεσα μια επιτροπή που να τις δει ώστε να πως τα ελληνικά δικαστήρια αντιμετώπισαν με βάση τις νομοθετικές αυτές αλλαγές τα θέματα των παιδιών και κυρίως τι προβλήματα έχουν ανακύψει από τη νομοθεσία αυτή. Άρα αυτά τα συμπεράσματα που θα εξαχθούν στην πορεία από τη δουλεία αυτής της ομάδας θα είναι πάρα πολύ χρήσιμα για την αλλαγή που σκοπεύουμε να κάνουμε σε κάποια ζητήματα και κάποιες πλευρές του Οικογενειακού Δικαίου», είπε ο υπουργός Δικαιοσύνης.

Από την πλευρά της η προϊσταμένη της γενικής διεύθυνσης ειδικών νομικών ζητημάτων του υπουργείου Δικαιοσύνης Ευτυχία Κατσιγαράκη, αναλύοντας το πρόγραμμα, μεταξύ των άλλων, ανέφερε: «Αυτό ευρωπαϊκό πρόγραμμα εστιάζει σε ένα ιδιαίτερα ευαίσθητο, πολυπαραγοντικό και κατεπείγον κοινωνικό ζήτημα: την προστασία της ψυχικής υγείας και των δικαιωμάτων του παιδιού κατά τη διαδικασία λήψης αποφάσεων επιμέλειας και γονικής μέριμνας. Στον πυρήνα των οικογενειακών διενέξεων, όταν ένας γάμος ή μια συμβίωση φτάνει στο τέλος της, τα παιδιά συχνά βρίσκονται δίχως δική τους βούληση στο επίκεντρο μιας διαμάχης».
«Ένα διαζύγιο μπορεί πράγματι να διαλύει τη νομική σχέση δύο συζύγων· δεν πρέπει όμως, σε καμία περίπτωση, να διαλύει την αίσθηση ασφάλειας, τη συναισθηματική σταθερότητα και το μέλλον ενός παιδιού. Πίσω από κάθε δικόγραφο, πίσω από κάθε δικαστική απόφαση επιμέλειας ή επικοινωνίας, δεν υπάρχουν μόνο νομικοί ισχυρισμοί, δικονομικοί κανόνες και αντιμαχόμενα επιχειρήματα. Υπάρχουν άνθρωποι, υπάρχουν φοβισμένες ψυχές, υπάρχουν οικογενειακές ιστορίες και, πάνω απ' όλα, υπάρχουν παιδιά. Και η δικαστική απόφαση δεν εξαντλείται μέσα στην αίθουσα του δικαστηρίου. Μεταφέρεται την επόμενη μέρα στο σπίτι, στο σχολείο, στις παρέες, στην καθημερινή ζωή του παιδιού. Γίνεται καθοριστικό κομμάτι της προσωπικής του ταυτότητας και εξέλιξης», συμπλήρωσε.
Σε άλλο σημείο της ομιλίας της η κυρία Κατσιγαράκη, τόνισε: «Το παιδί έχει το αδιαμφισβήτητο δικαίωμα να εκφράζει ελεύθερα τη γνώμη του για θέματα που το αφορούν, και η γνώμη αυτή οφείλει να λαμβάνεται υπόψη ανάλογα με την ηλικία και τη συναισθηματική του ωριμότητα. Πρωτίστως, καλείται να εκφράσει ελεύθερα τη γνώμη, τις ανάγκες, τους φόβους, τις επιθυμίες και τις προσδοκίες του, μέσα σε ένα περιβάλλον ασφάλειας και προστασίας. Η φωνή του παιδιού λαμβάνεται ουσιαστικά υπόψη στη διαδικασία, χωρίς να μετακυλίεται σε αυτό η ευθύνη της απόφασης, η οποία παραμένει ακέραιη εκεί όπου ανήκει: στη Δικαιοσύνη».
Ειδικότερα, κάθε χρόνο χιλιάδες παιδιά στην Ελλάδα περνούν μέσα από τις διαδικασίες λήψης αποφάσεων επιμέλειας και γονικής μέριμνας, χωρίς η γνώμη τους να ακούγεται ή να λαμβάνεται υπόψη σοβαρά, κάτι που είναι σε βάρος της ψυχικής υγείας και των δικαιωμάτων των ανήλικων παιδιών.
Έτσι, το πρόγραμμα ChildSay που είναι ένα συγχρηματοδοτούμενο από την Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση έργο, αποτελεί την πρώτη ολιστική παρέμβαση στη χώρα μας η οποία βάζει τα παιδιά στο επίκεντρο των αποφάσεων που τα αφορούν μέσα από έρευνα, εκπαίδευση επαγγελματιών και ένα εθνικό σχέδιο δράσης για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη.
Αφορά παιδιά ηλικίας από 6 έως 10 ετών, γονείς, εισαγγελείς, δικαστές και δικηγόρους, αλλά και επαγγελματίες, όπως είναι αστυνομικοί, συμβολαιογράφοι, δικαστικοί επιμελητές, κοινωνικοί λειτουργοί και ψυχολόγοι.
Στο πρόγραμμα αυτό, συνολικής διάρκειας υλοποίησης 24 μηνών, συμμετέχει το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης ως εταίρος, με στόχο να ενσωματωθεί ουσιαστικά η φωνή και τα δικαιώματα των παιδιών στις αποφάσεις της επιμέλειας σε ευθυγράμμιση με τα διεθνή πρότυπα Δικαιοσύνης φιλικής προς το παιδί. Ακόμη, το ChildSay αξιολογεί την ισχύουσα νομοθεσία, εκπαιδεύει δικαστές, δικηγόρους και ψυχολόγους σε παιδοκεντρικές πρακτικές.
