title: No POP or Paper Mâché: This Family Celebrates Ganesh Chaturthi With Wheat, Mud & a Growing Idol
content: On the first day, it looks almost too simple to be Ganpati. A large plate. A thin layer of finely sifted mud. And, carefully marked on its surface, the familiar outline of Ganesha — his trunk, ears, rounded belly and little crown. Then come the seeds. One by one, wheat kernels are placed along the outline, with just enough space between them to allow each seed to grow. Water is sprinkled over the mud. The family recites the Gayatri Mantra 12 times. Then they wait, and by the second day, tiny green shoots begin to appear. Over the next few days, they grow taller, slowly filling the outline. By the fifth day, the little kernels have transformed into lush green blades, tracing the unmistakable form of Ganesha. At a certain height and angle, the effect is almost magical: Bappa has appeared, not through clay or plaster, but through something living. For Pratiksha Marathe and her parents in Kalyan, Maharashtra, this is their Vanaspati Ganesh — a tradition that has become one of the most meaningful parts of their Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations. The family uses mud, wheat seeds, sunlight and water to create their Ganpati, without plaster, paint or thermocol. “It feels like therapy to create your own version of Ganesha,” says Pratiksha. This year marks the family’s 31st year of celebrating the festival at home. What began in 1995 with a conventional idol has slowly evolved into a celebration that asks a very different question: what if bringing Ganesha home did not have to mean leaving an idol behind in nature? A festival that began with an idol For years, Ganesh Chaturthi in the Marathe household followed a familiar rhythm. Pratiksha, her parents, relatives, neighbours, and close family friends would welcome Ganpati home. There would be puja, aarti, homemade modaks and laddoos, followed by visarjan on the second day. But Pratiksha remembers another part of the festival just as vividly: the scenes that followed. Seeing “thousands of idols lying after the visarjan on Dadar Chowpatty and many other visarjan places” made her think about what happened after the celebrations ended. “What means the world to us is somewhere not accepted by nature. Maybe it’s time to celebrate festivals differently,” she recalls thinking. For the Marathe family in Kalyan, their Vanaspati Ganesh has become a 31-year-old festival tradition with a different approach to visarjan. The family first moved away from plaster of Paris idols and tried Shadu clay, or natural river clay. But even that raised questions about how completely the material returned to nature. Then came 2020. During the pandemic, when getting an idol was difficult, the family still wanted to preserve their decades-old tradition. That was when they turned to an idea they had encountered through their long association with Manashakti Research Centre in Lonavala. The concept was Vanaspati Ganesh — using growing wheat seedlings to create the form of Ganesha. Soon, it became their own annual ritual. It starts with mud, seeds, and a little patience Three or four days before Ganesh Chaturthi, Pratiksha’s father begins preparing the base. He collects mud from the surrounding area, filters and sifts it, then mixes it with water and spreads roughly an inch-thick layer into a large, 18-inch plate. Once the base is ready, Pratiksha draws a simple outline of Ganesha. Her mother sets aside good-quality wheat seeds, which are carefully placed along the outline with enough space for the shoots to grow. Water is sprinkled over the plate as the family recites the Gayatri Mantra 12 times. For the family, all their prayers, aartis, mantras are intentional which creates a calm, positive atmosphere for the seeds to grow. Pratiksha carefully places wheat kernels along the hand-drawn outline of Ganesha, leaving enough space for the shoots to grow. Then the plate is placed where the plants can receive sunlight and is watered twice a day. No plaster, paint or thermocol. Just mud, seeds, sunlight and care. And then, Bappa begins to grow The transformation is what makes the ritual particularly fascinating for children. On Day 1, the wheat kernels are still clearly visible. “By the next day, tiny sprouts begin pushing through the mud. Soon, they turn green and begin growing like blades of grass,” says Pratiksha. Slowly, the green shoots fill the entire outline. By the fifth day, the wheatgrass can grow to around a foot in length. From a particular height and angle, the outline of Ganesha becomes strikingly clear. Children from the neighbourhood often stop to look. Some even imagine what it would be like to make a gigantic version outdoors — a Ganpati visible from the sky. For Pratiksha, however, its meaning goes beyond the novelty. A celebration where nothing is left behind The family’s two-day celebration still retains everything that makes Ganesh Chaturthi special. Their fibre-based Ganesha idol is used for puja every year and is never immersed. There are aartis in the morning and evening, homemade modaks, laddoos, fruits, prayers, and the chanting of Ganesha’s name. On the second day, instead of immersing an idol, they perform a symbolic visarjan by immersing a supari in water. Instead of immersing an idol, the family performs a symbolic visarjan with a supari, while the wheatgrass is harvested and shared as prasad. The wheatgrass completes its own cycle. It is harvested and eaten as prasad, with some also added to everyday food. The mud is either reused the following year or mixed into their house plants. When friends and neighbours learnt about the tradition, some even began asking the family to keep aside wheatgrass for them as prasad. Even the decorations have changed The family’s sustainability journey does not end with the Ganpati. Pratiksha’s father has traditionally been in charge of the decorations, and she began helping him as she grew older. One material they consciously moved away from was thermocol. “When I was in school, I learnt that thermocol is difficult to recycle and can become a persistent pollutant. Since then, we have increasingly relied on cardboard flowers and paper-based decorations instead,” she says. It is a small change, but one that reflects their larger philosophy: festive does not have to mean wasteful. What Bappa leaves behind For Pratiksha, perhaps the most beautiful part of the Vanaspati Ganesh is what happens at the end. The wheat that arrives as tiny seeds eventually becomes something the family can eat. In that sense, Ganesha does not simply disappear after visarjan. He becomes part of the family in another form — returning to the body through food and, eventually, to the earth. From cardboard flowers to paper decorations, the Marathe family has gradually found ways to make their Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations less wasteful. The idea also connects with what Ganesha represents to the family. Pratiksha describes him as the God of intelligence, the remover of obstacles and someone whose stories offer lessons about gratitude, empathy and problem-solving. In an age of increasing dependence on AI, she believes the festival can also be a reminder to retain our ability to think, assess situations and solve problems. “Can we be more empathetic and grateful towards each other?” she asks. Keeping the celebration, changing the way we celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi is much bigger than an idol. It is the neighbours dropping by, the aarti everyone gathers for, steaming modaks, children watching decorations come together and, in Mumbai, the unmistakable energy that takes over entire neighbourhoods. The Marathe family does not want to take away any of that. They simply believe the celebration can evolve. Families can make clay idols at workshops, opt for artificial ponds for visarjan, choose reusable decorations or even volunteer for beach clean-ups after the festivities. The wheatgrass that forms their Vanaspati Ganesh is eventually harvested and eaten as prasad, completing its journey from seed to food. “Festivals are important,” says Pratiksha. “They give a sense of purpose as a community.” But perhaps the responsibility that comes with that joy is just as important. The question is not whether we should celebrate. It is how we can celebrate in a way that allows both our traditions and the environment to breathe. And perhaps that is what makes this little green Ganpati so powerful. He arrives as a handful of seeds, grows through days of prayer and care, becomes prasad, and finally returns to the earth. Nothing is really lost. The celebration simply changes form. All images courtesy Pratiksha Marathe

title: After two years on the throne, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po is forging her own path
content: Today is the second day of the second anniversary of the coronation of Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po. Known as Koroneihana, the four-day event sees people from around the country, and the world, gather together at Tūrangawaewae Marae to celebrate the coronation of Te Arikinui. Yesterday, hapū and iwi from around Tainui waka gathered to honour their loved ones. Today, iwi from across Aotearoa will do the same. Tomorrow, leaders from around the world, MPs and other politicians will arrive. On Saturday, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po will deliver a much-anticipated speech to the nation. Following her father’s death in August 2024, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po spoke publicly for the first time at last year’s Koroneihana. She used the opportunity to outline her priorities as the successor to her father’s throne. The economic prosperity of Māori was the main theme, signalling what was to follow over the next 12 months. Since her father’s passing, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has continued with the expected roles and responsibilities of the Kīngitanga. The regular annual events of poukai throughout Waikato, manu kōrero and kapa haka competitions, gala dinners, and Koroneihana preparations have consumed much of her time since her ascension to the throne. But Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has also set her own direction for the Kīngitanga movement. A highlight of her reign so far has been the launch of an iwi-backed $100m sovereign wealth fund, announced at the Ōhanga ki te Ao economic summit held in Waikato last November that brought together leaders from Australia, Europe, North America, Asia, and the Pacific. “Every opportunity must deliver real outcomes for our people and solid returns that grow wealth for generations to come,” she said during her speech at the event. The fund forms a key part of a wider strategy for the development of the Māori economy, now estimated to be worth approximately $126bn. Aligned closely with Waikato-Tainui, the Kīngitanga is combining its forces with other major political and strategic leadership bodies, sector-specific collectives and advocacy networks and major iwi post-settlement governance entities to work towards a burgeoning Māori economy and mana motuhake for Māori. Kuini Nga wai hono i te po at the Ōhanga ki te Ao summit held in November 2025. (Image: Kiingitanga). “Ōhanga Ki Te Ao is a chance to achieve our economic aspirations independently of government in our pursuit of self-determination, sustainable futures and thriving peoples,” Nga wai hono i te po said during her maiden speech as monarch. The economic focus builds on the legacy of Kīngi Tūheitia Pōtatau Te Wherowhero VII, the father of Nga wai hono i te po. Tūheitia was a strong advocate for kōtahitanga, national unity, social justice, and indigenous cooperation across the Pacific – a legacy that Nga wai hono i te po has continued during her reign. Among her many regular commitments, Nga wai hono i te po has continued to foster positive relations between the Kīngitanga and leaders around the Pacific, including travelling to Rarotonga, where she met with the Ui Ariki – the traditional leaders of the island – alongside members of the Cook Islands government. In May, she travelled to the United Kingdom where she met Prince William and became the first Māori monarch to meet a British royal at Windsor Castle. She also spoke at the First Nations Major Projects Coalition conference in Canada, highlighting the need to protect the taiao, grow indigenous economies and uphold the right of indigenous nations to lead. A trip to Dubai was also led by Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po to promote the sale of Māori grown kiwifruit into the market. The initiative, supported by a $5m investment fund, aims to assist Māori kiwifruit growers as they look to double their exports to the region over the next decade. Beyond economics and international visits, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has emphasised the need for preservation of the natural environment. At the royal regatta dinner at Tūrangawaewae Marae in March, she issued an urgent call to action to restore balance between humanity and ecosystems, noting that “the natural world is constantly speaking through rivers, land, winds, and oceans – and it is time to listen”. Kiingi Tuheitia smiles at the Kiingitanga 165th anniversary event at Tamaki Paenga Hira/Auckland Museum in December 2023. (Photo: Kiingitanga Facebook) Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po is scheduled to deliver her Koroneihana speech on Saturday afternoon. With an election looming, and two particularly strong candidates standing in the Hauraki-Waikato electorate – Labour’s Kingi Kiriona and Te Pāti Māori’s Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, both with strong links to the Kīngitanga – many will be watching closely to see whether the Māori monarch endorses a candidate or party. Her speech is otherwise likely to echo last year’s one, calling for greater economic independence and a strengthening of Māori independence through a thriving Māori language and environment – all of which, she says, will support Māori wellbeing. As Nga wai hono i te po continues to create her legacy, the role of the Kīngitanga in today’s society will continue to evolve. Established in 1858 to unite Māori tribes, halt land sales to European settlers, and protect indigenous autonomy, the challenges the Kīngitanga and te ao Māori now face have shifted, but kotahitanga remains pivotal in the journey towards mana motuhake.

title: How Gloria Steinem helped change the way women’s health is researched
content:
5 min readUpdated: Sep 4, 2026 01:49 PM IST

For much of the 20th century, medical research was conducted largely through a male lens. Women were often excluded from clinical studies, reproductive health was treated as a private matter, and illnesses disproportionately affecting women received comparatively little scientific attention.
Gloria Steinem did not create the women’s health movement, nor did she single-handedly transform medical research. But as one of feminism’s most influential public voices, she helped make women’s health a political issue and helped create the pressure for medicine and research institutions to change.
Reproductive rights: Health as a matter of autonomy
Steinem’s campaign for reproductive rights placed control over women’s bodies at the heart of the feminist movement. She argued that access to contraception and abortion was not simply a social or moral question but fundamental to women’s equality.
That argument helped shift reproductive health from the private sphere into public policy. The growing political movement around reproductive autonomy also encouraged greater attention to contraception, pregnancy, fertility and the health consequences of reproductive decisions. For Steinem, the underlying principle was straightforward: women could not have genuine equality without control over their own bodies.
Menstruation: Breaking the silence
Steinem brought another neglected subject into public conversation: menstruation. Her celebrated 1978 essay, “If Men Could Menstruate,” used satire to expose the stigma surrounding periods and the cultural tendency to regard women’s biology as embarrassing or inconvenient.
The essay was more than a feminist joke. By making menstruation discussable, Steinem challenged the silence surrounding menstrual symptoms and disorders. That mattered because conditions associated with menstruation had often been normalised rather than investigated.
Her broader message was that women’s everyday physical experiences deserved to be taken seriously—and, ultimately, scientifically understood.
Story continues below this ad
Women’s pain: From dismissal to investigation
The women’s health movement gave political force to a common complaint: women were not always believed when they described pain.
It helped shift the lens to conditions such as endometriosis, a chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, often causing severe menstrual and pelvic pain, inflammation, and sometimes infertility. Endometriosis can cause severe pelvic pain, infertility and other complications, yet diagnosis has historically been delayed and the disease remains incompletely understood. In fact, earlier this year, Steinem spearheaded conversations around it.
By challenging the dismissal of women’s bodily experiences, she helped establish the principle that women’s pain should be investigated rather than simply endured. That cultural shift helped create an environment in which neglected conditions could become legitimate research priorities.
Challenging the male model of medicine
Perhaps Steinem’s most important contribution was challenging the assumption that medical knowledge derived from men could simply be applied to women.
Story continues below this ad
By the 1970s and 1980s, women’s health advocates were exposing the consequences of women’s underrepresentation in research. The issue was not merely fairness: biological differences could affect symptoms, disease progression, drug responses and treatment outcomes.
In 1986, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the US agency for biomedical and public-health research, introduced a policy encouraging the inclusion of women in clinical research. In 1990, it established the Office of Research on Women’s Health, giving women’s health a permanent institutional presence within the nation’s leading biomedical research agency.
The Women’s Health Initiative
The new emphasis on women’s health produced large-scale research. In 1991, the NIH launched the Women’s Health Initiative, ultimately enrolling more than 150,000 postmenopausal women.
The programme investigated major causes of illness and death among women, including cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporosis, while also examining the effects of hormone therapy and dietary interventions. Its scale was significant not simply because of the findings it produced, but because it demonstrated that women’s health questions warranted major, long-term scientific investment.
Story continues below this ad
Changing the rules of clinical research
The movement’s influence eventually became embedded in federal policy. The 1993 NIH Revitalization Act required women and minorities to be included in NIH-supported clinical research and required researchers to examine whether treatments affected different populations differently. This represented a fundamental change. Women’s participation in research was no longer merely encouraged as a matter of representation; it became part of the structure of federally funded clinical science.
Steinem’s most important contribution to women’s health research was, therefore, indirect but profound. She helped turn women’s experiences — from reproductive choices to menstruation and bodily pain— into subjects of public debate and demands for institutional accountability. Her enduring message was ultimately a scientific one as much as a political one: Women’s experiences are evidence, women’s health questions deserve investigation, and women’s bodies cannot be understood adequately by treating men as the default patient.

title: 32º Grito dos Excluídos e Excluídas une moradia, terra e vida das mulheres nas ruas de Porto Alegre
content:
Porto Alegre recebeu, nesta segunda-feira (7), a 32ª edição do Grito dos Excluídos e Excluídas, mobilização que ocupa as ruas do país desde 1995 como contraponto popular aos desfiles cívico-militares do Dia da Independência. Neste ano, o lema nacional da caminhada é “Na defesa da Terra, da Paz e da Moradia, erguemos a voz: Mulheres Vivas e Soberania!”, tema que orientou falas, cânticos e apresentações ao longo de toda a manhã.
A concentração começou em frente ao Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia do Rio Grande do Sul (IFRS), na rua Coronel Vicente, no Centro Histórico, marcando a defesa da educação pública e gratuita como um dos eixos da atividade. De lá, os manifestantes seguiram em caminhada até a rua Barros Cassal, no bairro Floresta, em frente ao Cibai Migrações e ao Assentamento 20 de Novembro, onde ocorreu o ato político e cultural que encerrou a programação.
Moradia como eixo da mobilização
A pauta habitacional atravessou praticamente todas as falas do ato. O encerramento em frente ao Assentamento 20 de Novembro não foi escolha aleatória: o empreendimento é fruto de 20 anos de organização de famílias sem-teto e está com a obra em fase final de conclusão.
Ceniriani Vargas da Silva, conhecida como Ni, integrante do Movimento Nacional de Luta pela Moradia (MNLM), destacou o significado de realizar o encerramento naquele endereço. “Esse grito para nós foi bem importante porque também traz a pauta da habitação como algo central”, afirmou. Segundo ela, a mobilização também reuniu as lutas pela terra, pela paz e pela soberania e o enfrentamento à violência contra as mulheres, tema que, avaliou, precisa estar presente em todos os espaços.
Segundo Ni, a inauguração do assentamento está marcada para 22 de novembro, com festa que deve incluir atrações musicais e interdição da rua para a celebração. “Vai ser uma festa linda, histórica para marcar essa grande conquista do movimento popular organizado”, disse. Para ela, o empreendimento também demonstra a capacidade do cooperativismo e da autogestão de produzir moradias de qualidade.
A questão habitacional também apareceu associada às famílias atingidas por desastres climáticos no Rio Grande do Sul. Leonardo Maggi, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Atingidos por Barragens (MAB), afirmou que grande parte da população atingida segue sem moradia definitiva. Enquanto o governo trabalha com a necessidade de 22 mil casas, o movimento calcula que pelo menos 50 mil unidades precisam ser construídas.
“A nossa estimativa é que mais ou menos metade das famílias ainda estão fora dos cálculos de habitação”, disse Maggi, atribuindo a estimativa a levantamentos do próprio movimento e da Confederação Nacional dos Municípios, além de dados do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE).
Maggi citou o caso de Lajeado, no Vale do Taquari, onde, segundo ele, mais de 600 famílias estariam vivendo em abrigo mantido pela prefeitura, embora o município reconheça oficialmente 176 famílias na lista de habitação. “Existe uma incoerência, uma inconsistência no que está sendo feito. Dinheiro tem, só faltou decisão da parte das prefeituras de aplicar o dinheiro que o governo federal mandou para resolver os problemas dos atingidos”, avaliou.
A secretária executiva da Cáritas do Rio Grande do Sul, Jacira Teresinha Dias Ruiz, relacionou a pauta habitacional à Campanha da Fraternidade deste ano, que tem como tema o direito à moradia digna. Para ela, a conquista do Assentamento 20 de Novembro mostra o papel da organização popular na garantia desse direito. “E ela não acontece sem luta. O movimento de luta pela moradia é uma grande experiência, um grande exemplo de conquistas ao longo dos anos, até chegar a esse resultado dessa cooperativa habitacional”, afirmou.
Feminicídio e violência contra as mulheres
O enfrentamento à violência contra as mulheres foi tratado como um dos pontos centrais da edição deste ano do Grito, em referência direta ao lema nacional. De acordo com um dos informes transmitidos durante a concentração, houve um ato específico em memória das mulheres mortas por feminicídio, com a canção “Maria” e um minuto de silêncio pelas vítimas.
Chirlei Fischer, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Trabalhadores e Trabalhadoras por Direitos (MTD), apresentou dados sobre feminicídios no estado e no país neste ano. Segundo ela, 52 mulheres já foram mortas no Rio Grande do Sul e 834 no Brasil.
“Nós mulheres trabalhadoras do campo e da cidade estamos sofrendo muito com a violência”, declarou. “Precisamos denunciar esse feminicídio que cada vez mais cresce, que cada vez mais nos ronda, e dizer que o direito das mulheres precisa ser alcançado.” Fischer também associou a violência de gênero à falta de acesso a moradia, escola e trabalho remunerado digno.
Na mesma direção, Juliana Bergmann, da coordenação do Levante Popular da Juventude, apontou um crescimento nos casos de feminicídio no estado neste ano. Para ela, levar esse debate ao Grito dos Excluídos reforça uma pauta historicamente vinculada à classe trabalhadora e aos movimentos sociais. “É fundamental para varrer o discurso de ódio da internet, das ruas e das casas das nossas companheiras”, afirmou.
Leonardo Maggi, do MAB, relacionou a pauta a um caso ocorrido dentro do próprio movimento. Há quatro anos, segundo ele, uma coordenadora da organização em Porto Alegre foi assassinada pelo marido. “Trazer essa pauta, que é tão forte para todo o povo gaúcho, é muito importante para nós”, disse.
Soberania e disputa eleitoral
Parte das falas relacionou a data à disputa em torno de projetos de país, em ano de eleições gerais. Tomaz Brunet, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST), afirmou que a soberania brasileira vem sendo pressionada por forças internacionais, inclusive por meio de tarifas e outras medidas econômicas.
“Mais do que nunca, neste dia em que comemoramos a nossa independência, a gente precisa reafirmar a força do povo brasileiro e reafirmar que é ele que deve dar a direção do seu país, e não outro povo”, afirmou Brunet, que também destacou a presença das cozinhas solidárias no ato.
Amarildo Cenci, presidente da Central Única dos Trabalhadores do Rio Grande do Sul (CUT-RS), defendeu a permanência da mobilização mesmo em um contexto de governo federal identificado por ele como mais favorável às pautas populares. Para Cenci, a existência de um governo progressista não elimina a necessidade de pressão social por direitos.
“A gente continua na luta por direitos, por moradia, por paz. A paz significa direitos, educação de qualidade e moradia para as pessoas. Nós precisamos que os ricos sejam tributados e que o trabalhador e a trabalhadora permaneçam e entrem cada vez mais no orçamento”, disse.
Cenci lembrou ainda que a mobilização se manteve em edições anteriores mesmo em contextos políticos mais adversos. “Não me lembro de ter faltado um grito, mesmo em épocas em que a gente fazia com meia dúzia de pessoas, em ambientes mais difíceis, de neoliberalismo”, afirmou.
Território indígena e disputa de memória
O ato também reservou espaço para a fala de representantes de povos indígenas. Laércio Guarani, professor de história na retomada Nhe’engatu, em Viamão, relacionou a mobilização à disputa por território e por direitos historicamente negados às comunidades indígenas.
“Nossos direitos, dos povos indígenas, estão sendo atacados a todo momento. A gente vem de uma retomada, de um espaço onde a gente teve que fazer um movimento de retomar, onde um dia foram nossos também esses espaços”, disse.
Guarani também chamou atenção para a ocupação histórica do território onde hoje está construída a capital gaúcha. “A grande Porto Alegre também é uma grande aldeia indígena, para quem não sabe. A gente está em cima de uma aldeia, de um cemitério indígena, neste momento”, afirmou.
Encerramento com teatro e cozinhas solidárias
A programação em Porto Alegre foi finalizada com apresentação teatral do grupo Panapana e almoço preparado pelas cozinhas solidárias presentes no ato, formato que se repetiu em outras edições da mobilização no estado.
A caminhada em Porto Alegre integrou uma mobilização nacional que teve atividades em 18 estados e no Distrito Federal, além de programações realizadas ao longo da semana anterior em cidades como Lajeado, no Vale do Taquari, onde o ato coincidiu com os três anos da enchente de 2023, e Santa Cruz do Sul, integrada ao desfile cívico local.
O Grito dos Excluídos e das Excluídas surgiu a partir de debates da Semana Social Brasileira, promovida pela Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil (CNBB) em 1993 e 1994, e teve a primeira edição nacional em 7 de setembro de 1995.

title: The racist email that made this doctor take on the establishment
content:
Trailblazing eye surgeon Kris Rallah-Baker took on the establishment and won
The moment an eye patch is removed after cataract surgery and a patient can see clearly again: that's the moment of fulfilment for eye surgeon Kris Rallah-Baker.
It's even more rewarding for Australia's first Indigenous ophthalmologist to experience that "patch off" moment in remote Indigenous areas because Kris knows he's not just helping the patient but an entire community.
"A lot of the people you are working on are elders and holders of cultural knowledge," Kris tells Australian Story. "When those people aren't able to get out on country, they're not able to transmit intergenerational knowledge that's been around for thousands and thousands of years.
"So, there's a broader picture and a deeper importance … you're allowing that intergenerational knowledge to be passed on."
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images of people who have died.
Kris knows how losing connection to country can affect a family — much of his own history has been lost. Some of his mob were part of the Stolen Generations, taken away by white authorities and put in missions where their stories and language were forbidden.
One of those was his maternal great-grandmother, Lena Nora. She was the daughter of an Aboriginal woman, Mary Nora, who was a domestic servant on a north Queensland station. Lena's father was the Scandinavian station master.
For reasons unknown, Mary left, or was sent from, the station with Lena and a son, ending up in a "Black camp" in Bowen.
It's believed the camp was raided by authorities. The family was separated, with Lena taken to Barambah mission (now Cherbourg) almost 1,000km away before being sent further south to Myora mission, on Minjerribah, or North Stradbroke Island.
The trauma instilled in Lena a fear and distrust of white authorities.
So when Lena fell ill later in life, she refused to go to hospital.
"She was fearful of white institutions because they'd taken her away and they imprisoned her and they enslaved her," Kris says. "She stayed at home and became more and more unwell and then passed of pneumonia."
Lena's story and the need to try to bridge the cultural gap in healthcare delivery is one of the reasons Kris decided to study medicine and, ultimately, ophthalmology.
It wasn't an easy road. Kris says those in positions of power put barriers in his way because of his Aboriginality. After qualifying, he was subjected to racism by a fellow doctor, this time for not being Black enough.
But an uncle once told a young Kris that getting where you want to be in life is rarely achieved in a straight line.
It's been a zigzag journey, Kris says, to becoming Australia's first Indigenous ophthalmologist, with a private practice in Noosa and pop-up outreach clinics in remote Indigenous communities.
Now he's working to make the path less ragged for others.
Loading...'A life that means something'
On Kris's farm in the Noosa hinterland, there are cattle, sheep and a goat but also his carefully bred flock of rare heritage chickens. Inside is a collection of Georgian antique furniture, his piano, and some of his own paintings and handmade furniture.
He is, he says, "a complex character", with an eclectic range of hobbies.
"For me, a life that means something is a life that gives back to others, but also a life where I've gained as much as I possibly can have gained out of my own life," he says.
"Have I engaged in the depth of life?"
Being successful is part of that rich tapestry. "I have my private practice in Noosa, and I'm unashamed about that because my family has been held behind for generations now, and there's no reason why I can't be successful in this Western system," he says.
One of Kris's first experiences of racism was when he began school in Brisbane after moving with his family from Canberra. At kindergarten in Canberra, he'd been identified as a gifted child — in Brisbane, he was put in an English-as-a-second-language class, purely because of his skin colour.
His mother Raelene ended that as soon as she found out. "It was just this racist assumption about an Aboriginal child," she says. "It was just unacceptable."
Raelene, one of Queensland's first Indigenous health workers, is from the Warrungu mob of the Cardwell/Tully area of north Queensland, and Yuggera from around Brisbane. She also has Irish and Indian heritage. Kris's father, David, has Scottish and Jewish heritage and discovered later in life that he is also Wiradjuri, from NSW's Mudgee area.
"My life has been a life of contrasts," Kris says.
From year 5, Kris went to a private boys' school and excelled at humanities. For a while, he was keen on studying law as a stepping stone to entering politics, an ambition he still holds.
But then Raelene invited an Aboriginal doctor home to chat with a 16-year-old Kris about medicine. By the end of the meeting he set his sights on being a doctor.
He studied medicine at the University of Newcastle but after spending "a horrible year" as a junior house officer at a major Brisbane hospital, his zigzag route began.
"I concluded that I was not happy working in this huge institution," he says. "There was a lot of bullying and harassment across the board … and I thought, 'Nope, my life is worth more than this.'"
He took a lower paying job as a senior Indigenous health worker and "I found myself and I found my happiness".
It was through this work that he met ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist Chris Perry, who recognised Kris's potential.
Says Dr Perry: "His ability to connect with the elders and Queensland Health bureaucracy was very, very good. He's very good with people and he works very hard."
Then Dr Perry asked Kris if he would be interested in a career as an ENT specialist. He wasn't. He told Dr Perry he was interested in ophthalmology.
Dr Perry wasn't offended — he got straight on the phone to eye surgeon colleagues, asking if they could meet with this young Aboriginal doctor.
One of them was Glen Gole who had worked with the late Fred Hollows, the legendary ophthalmologist who dedicated himself to restoring the sight of Indigenous people and those in developing countries.
Professor Gole saw in Kris a keen young doctor who was "worthy of support".
"That changed my entire career trajectory," Kris says. "It was the zigzag."
'Not full-blood, are you?'
Ophthalmology is a competitive specialty, with a rigorous and lengthy training and exam regime.
"I felt that a small number of consultants did not want me to finish because I'm Aboriginal", Kris says.
He says his experience of racism rattled his confidence, causing him to fail the exit exams. But by 2018 Kris graduated, and on receiving the news he "just burst into tears".
But Kris, by now the president of the Australian Indigenous Doctors' Association, wanted to ensure others following in his groundbreaking footsteps were not subjected to discrimination.
He wrote an article about the "direct and unashamed racism" he'd experienced.
It caused a stir but, in the wash-up, The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO) issued an apology for not replying sensitively to Kris's public criticisms and began a transformation of its processes.
"They have reformed the college internally to the point now where they actually are one of the most culturally safe spaces of any of the medical colleges," Kris says.
But racism persists.
Kris was in his Noosa rooms in July 2022, a fully fledged ophthalmologist with stints of outreach work in Alice Springs and Darwin, when an email arrived from an ACT general practitioner.
It read, in part: "You are not full-blood, are you? Half? Quarter? One eight? Like a watered down bottle of Grange. Not the real thing."
It sent Kris reeling.
"After everything I'd been through … I'm finally a consultant and I'm still getting this same crap, the same garbage," he says.
"You think, 'When will this stop?' But you just have to realise that the world is not a fair place and it doesn't matter how many letters you have after your name or how many titles you have, it's not gonna stop."
That didn't mean Kris would stay silent. He took the matter to the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, which investigated and referred it to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal.
The landmark case resulted in the sender of the email being deregistered for a year.
Kris had the option of keeping his complaint anonymous. He rejected that, ready to take criticism — which didn't come — because speaking out was the right thing to do.
"I do it because I care about the Australian health system," he says. "I do it because I want better for other people."
Building trust and restoring sight
At a recent clinic in Cape York's Weipa to perform cataract surgeries, Kris was accompanied by Indigenous medical student Aiden Wu, who knows the zigzag route Kris had to take to realise his dream.
"We're quite fortunate that he's done a lot of the hard yards already," Aiden says.
"If Kris wasn't so genuine and able to … connect me with the right people, I wouldn't be on this trip and I probably wouldn't even be interested in ophthalmology."
It's a busy clinic, with patients bussed in from around the cape for surgery. One of them, Albert Bond from New Mapoon, calls Aiden over. He recognises him. They are family.
The interaction quickly makes Albert more comfortable as they chat about relatives from the Torres Strait.
"If there's someone familiar or someone that you can relate to," Aiden says, "it makes everything a lot easier, a lot more calm."
That's the beauty of having Indigenous medical specialists in these remote areas, Kris says. Of course, non-Indigenous ophthalmologists can win the trust of patients and do good work, he says.
It's just that being Indigenous helps build that trust sooner.
"There's an understanding of a shared history," Kris says. "There's an understanding that they know that they're going to be understood and they're going to be safe.
"It's about trust, because we come from a long history of abuse."
Kris's history is forever tied to his great-grandmother Lena, whose fear of white authorities stopped her from seeking medical help, leading to her death.
But the future, he says, is looking good. It excites him that there are six Indigenous trainees in the RANZCO program at the moment, with the second Indigenous ophthalmologist due to graduate next year. Soon afterwards, the first Torres Strait Islander eye surgeon will graduate, who will also be the first female Indigenous ophthalmologist.
"We're seeing cultural safety being built into training," says Kris, who is proud of his leadership in the process. "We're seeing the rates of preventable blindness, although still high, come down year on year … I think we have a very, very bright future."
Watch Australian Story, Eyes on the Prize, on Monday at 8pm (AEST) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

title: Uncovering a Holocaust survival story
content:
Uncovering a Holocaust survival story
As a young girl taking out a box containing toy soldiers from her dad's dresser drawer, Elizabeth Connolly was just curious, not trying to unearth a little-known piece of history. "I would go in and I would play with them, and I would set them all up on the floor," she said.
But tucked in that drawer next to those toy soldiers was an envelope of photos, which Connolly found intriguing: "I always remember thinking, 'Hmm, they don't look like any of our relatives. I wonder who they are.'"
They appeared quite removed from her reality in Upstate New York. "There was one that just always drew me: It was a mom holding a little girl's hand, coming up the hill, and there was another woman standing behind that was very, very thin," she said.
She'd asked her dad about them: "He would just say they were people that he came upon in a train, and that was it," Connolly said.
Her dad, Carrol Walsh, a U.S. Army sergeant in World War II, kept the photos given to him by a friend, a fellow tank commander. "I think a lot of the soldiers during that time, they came home and they held a lot of those stories in," Connolly said.
That's partly why her son's teacher, Matt Rozell, started a class project to collect the oral histories of veterans. While Rozell was interviewing Connelly's dad in 2001, she interjected to ask him about the train.
"No, I didn't tell him about the train," Walsh answered.
Rozell recalls he was just about to shut down his camera when Walsh continued: "And he said, 'A beautiful April day. We were zooming like crazy through the middle of Germany. We came across this train, and it was full of Holocaust victims.' He said he looked inside the train cars. He saw the people in a very distressed state."
Twenty-five-hundred Jewish prisoners from Bergen-Belsen were crammed inside, on their way to another concentration camp. On April 13, 1945, in the final weeks of the war, advancing American soldiers came upon the stopped train near Magdeburg, Germany, and provided care for the survivors.
Rozell did not realize at the time that he was uncovering a relatively unknown piece of history: "I was a young history teacher," he said. "I was not schooled enough, believe it or not, in the Holocaust."
Rozell posted that interview online, and eventually heard from dozens of survivors and liberators, inspiring him to write a book, "A Train Near Magdeburg."
The former Hudson Falls, New York, teacher also organized reunions to bring together American soldiers with those they helped liberate, including Peter Lantos, who became a renowned neuroscientist and author.
In his London home, Lantos told us how he was just five years old when he was put on that train with his mom. "Her thinking was, anywhere can be better than Belsen," Lantos said. "There were dead bodies lying around unburied, first by dozens, then by hundreds."
His father died of starvation there. In all, he lost 21 family members in the Holocaust.
Lantos remembers the day they were liberated: "There was kind of a noise, and suddenly it became quiet. And then people started to shout, 'Americans! Americans!'"
He does not really like talking about what happened, but, he said, "It's a moral obligation to do it. Because we are the last survivors. I'm 86. In few years' time, no one can tell you, 'Yes, it is true because I was there.'"
James Bulgin, the head of public history at the Imperial War Museum, London, said, "The people on board that train are, in every meaningful respect, on the brink of death at the point in time that the Americans intercept them."
Peter Lantos and Matt Rozell recently joined Bulgin in the Holocaust galleries he curated, which feature the story of the train.
Bulgin said, "You might say, 'Oh, they're being saved from Belsen. They're being sent somewhere else.' But the reality is of course, as soon as they get along the way and then the Nazis realize they're not going to be able to get them to where they're gonna get to, then the plan emerges to kill them."
The episode reveals the chaos at the end of the war, Bulgin says, and the quirks of fate that lead to remembering this story of liberation and survival.
"Matt Rozell, when he was doing his interviews, didn't know that he was going to stumble across the history of the train," Bulgin said. "It tells us so much about the way history actually happens."
That's something award-winning filmmaker Mike Edwards knows well. While working on his upcoming documentary, "A Train Near Magdeberg," his team unearthed a series of photos from that day which he brought to show Bulgin. In one picture, a man wears a photograph of himself showing what he looked like pre-Holocaust.
"I've literally never seen anything like that before," Bulgin said. "It's compelling, because you know about these things and you've seen some of it, but to see new things, every new kind of physical visual trace, gives a new insight."
Mike Edwards has no direct connection to the train, but he has spent more than a decade on this passion project, which he's screened for some students. Asked what about the story has struck him, Edwards replied, "I think it's a story of humanity."
One question posed to Edwards stays with him: "'What do you hope people take away from this story?' I said, 'You know, each one of you, in your own lives, is going to have a "train near Magdeburg moment." You're going to have a choice of whether to care about somebody or not, to treat them as a human being or not. May you remember this story.'"
Now retired from teaching, Matt Rozell says the train story teaches a valuable lesson: "They didn't have to stop. They didn't have to help these people. But they did."
He says there's also a lesson here for all of us in the value of education: "Here's a story that very few Americans know anything about, that they should. You know, we all say, 'Never forget. Never forget.' And it's a great mantra. It's very important. But what if we never learned it to begin with?"

title: 9/11: I want my dad to be remembered as the hero he was
content:
9/11: I want my dad to be remembered as the hero he was
- Published
Ever since he was a young boy and his father relocated to the USA, Godwin Forde had dreamt of living there too.
In September 2001, he was finally old enough to fly out on his own and visit his dad, Godwin Forde senior, and make plans to finish school in the States.
He never got the chance.
His father was one of 67 British people who died in the deadly al-Qaeda attack on the World Trade Centre on September 11, 2001.
Godwin's sister Charlene, then 19 years old, had just moved to live in New York with her dad a week before.
Instead of the happy family reunion they'd always imagined, Godwin's first trip to the US was spent searching New York in vain for the father he'd waited years to reconnect with.
On the day of the attacks, Godwin recalled that he had just returned from school and was planning to go out with his friends, when his foster mum asked him to stay in and wait for a phone call from his sister.
"I took a seat, the news was on, and you could see all the images," he recalled.
Godwin, who is from north-west London, felt uneasy because his dad and sister were living in New York, but as he wasn't aware his father was working in one of the twin towers, he had no reason to be unduly concerned.
Godwin senior worked in security, and had previously worked at Fox News and on the David Letterman show.
He was a fairly well-known figure, often spotted in the background of TV programmes, once reportedly even making a cameo appearance on the FX TV Show Breakfast Time.
But unknown to Godwin junior, he'd recently been promoted to head up a security team on one of the upper floors of the South Tower at the World Trade Centre.
When his sister Charlene rang from New York, she was worried.
"She was explaining that, she hadn't heard from Dad yet. No-one had seen him, and no-one else had heard from him.
"At that point, I just wanted to get to her, to make sure she was OK," explained Forde.
"It was a waiting game."
Godwin flew over to New York two weeks later, and the teenagers searched for their father together, putting up posters, ringing helplines, heading to the pier where there were camps of people anxiously waiting for news of relatives.
They were mostly alone, with some help from the Red Cross.
It wasn't until the end of October that year that they got confirmation that their father hadn't survived.
"We finally got the death certificate. We had to plan a memorial. We couldn't even plan a funeral. We had no body, no belongings."
The siblings eventually heard two stories about what might have happened to their dad.
One of them came from a colleague who was with him at the time when the attacks happened, and she had made it out.
Godwin had the chance to speak to her.
"They used to call him Mr G, she told me. He told her to go and find her way out, but he said he needed to stay to clear everyone and anyone else he could find."
There was also another version of the story.
"One story I heard was that he'd made it out, heard more people were inside so he ran back in, and that's when the building collapsed. But then the other story was that he didn't actually come out at all, and he stayed in, ferrying whoever he could to the exits.
"Either way, both stories are heroic however you look at it."
Since Godwin Forde's death, nothing for his son has been the same.
"I didn't manage to move to the States. That plan got completely derailed. Other goals I had at the time also changed."
What happens for him on September 11th each year, when images of the attacks fill our screens?
"I normally leave the country for a month if possible, and kind of disappear off the grid," he says.
"This year I'm here, and I'm kind of just going through the motions, really."
It's hard to explain to anyone what he has suffered and what he is still suffering, because who else can really understand?
"There is only a select few people who know. It's not something I discuss," he explains.
"Something like this you can never get used to. Having someone taken away like that, you never really get over it."
'Lucky to be half of what he was'
For Godwin there are still mixed emotions about what happened.
There is undoubtedly a sense of deep pride and love for his father.
There is the grief and sadness.
But there are conflicting emotions too.
"There are times when you do get upset and angry at him based on the fact that we are here, and he could have come home.
"But at the same time I do understand that he did his duty and I feel like I would have probably done the same thing."
Godwin would like his father to be remembered as the "hero that he was".
"Someone that would literally go out of his way for anyone," says Godwin.
"I would be lucky if I could be just half of what he was."
