title: Te Wiki o te Reo Māori: Honouring the pioneers who saved the language
content:
Comment: It has been a trying few years for te reo Māori. We’ve seen the education minister cut te reo Māori words from books teaching five-year-olds to read.
We’ve seen the minister of arts, culture and heritage remove te reo greetings from an official Matariki invitation.
We’ve also seen the Government’s ongoing efforts to limit te reo use in the public sector – efforts the Waitangi Tribunal found breached te Tiriti and caused prejudice to Māori.
These attacks on te reo Māori have gone hand-in-hand with the perpetuation of false narratives framing Māori as ‘entitled’ and thus as undeserving. Or at a minimum, deserving of much less than the pittance our hands were forced to accept.
So, Te Wiki o te Reo Māori – the one week a year when we celebrate our reo – has been a long time coming for many. But this year, let us not worry too much about those who wish to attack te reo. Let’s instead remember and celebrate the mahi of those who have helped the language flourish despite the obstacles put in front of them.
Your ability to say ‘Kia ora’ is everlasting, thanks to Naida Glavish, the woman who refused to stop using the greeting when she worked as a telephone operator at the New Zealand Post Office.
Te Wiki o te Reo Māori is also not just the week to speak te reo, but a week, thanks to the efforts of Te Hōhaieti o te reo Māori (Māori Language Society), Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo (Wellington Board of Māori Language) and its founding member, Huirangi Waikerepuru CNZM (Taranaki, Ngāpuhi), who led the te reo Māori claim (WAI011) in the Waitangi Tribunal in the 1980s.
Let us also cast our minds back to when our language had little to nothing or te wā o te kore, and remember a few of those who were instrumental in fostering te reo and their amazing and worthwhile work. They include:
- Ngoingoi Pewhairangi QSM (Te Whānau a Ruataupare) and Dame Kāterina Te Heikōkō Mataira DNZM (Ngāti Porou), co-developers of Te Ātaarangi, the language revitalisation movement established in the late 1970s and still thriving today.
- Lady Tilly Reedy (Ngāti Porou) and Sir Tāmati Reedy KNZM (Ngāti Porou), who curated ‘Te Whāriki’, the revolutionary early childhood curriculum now celebrating 30 years. Lady Tilly was also co-responsible for the naming of Te Kohanga Reo.
- Professor Whatarangi Winiata (Ngāti Raukawa), the pioneer of Whakatupuranga Rua Mano (the progenitor of all future iwi language strategies) and Te Wānanga o Raukawa.
- Dame Iritana Tāwhiwhirangi DNZM MBE (Ngāti Porou, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāpuhi), who led and promoted the Kōhanga Reo Movement.
- Te Wharehuia Milroy QNZM QSO (Tūhoe, Ngāti Kōura), who co-established Te Panekiretanga o te Reo (Institute of Excellence in the Māori Language).
- Henare Kingi MNZM (Ngāpuhi), Māori radio broadcast veteran, respected mentor, and te reo Māori advocate who inspired others, such as Rauru Broughton (Ngāti Ruanui).
These are just some of those who took action, but did so with a strong and clear vision because they wanted better for us as a people and better for our language. They are a powerful minority who saw a gap or an opportunity for our language, and therefore our people, and went full speed ahead. These rangatira, their mana, their integrity, and the kaupapa they helped carry are vast, and their legacy alone as individuals is one that will far outlast, outlive, and outshine that of any government.
We need to continue to build on the foundation they laid down for us. We can do so by being active in using our reo, our voices, and the tools we have to give – just like they did.
So this week, take whatever respite you need and use the week to invigorate yourself. Because the celebration of our language is not signified purely by walking during the annual Te Wiki o te Reo Māori march, but in the everyday moments we choose te reo Māori.
Wear your kākahu, sing your waiata, listen to Māori radio, read your reo Māori pukapuka, and share a joke or many with your hoa.
This week, let’s celebrate our language in the best way we can – by using it, because it really is that simple, and use it in a manner that suits you because everyone’s reo Māori is their own.
Let us celebrate the guardians raising better speakers than themselves, and the teachers of now and of times gone.
Lastly, let’s celebrate everyone simply trying to do their best. Here’s to them, and here’s to you for choosing te reo in the little and significant moments, no matter how big or how small. Remember also that we stand on the shoulders of giants, because our language is one of high chiefs; therefore, so too are we who use it and embrace it.
Better rauORA living, everyone, and kia kaha te reo Māori!

title: Cambodia is closing scam centers but needs help tracking the money
content:
Closing an online scam center stops criminal activity, but it does not dismantle the network behind it.
The people directing the operation may be in another country, while the money can move across borders through bank accounts or digital payment systems. If we want to eliminate online scams rather than simply force them to move elsewhere, we have to follow the money. That is the next phase of Cambodia’s campaign.
Combating online scams is a national priority for Cambodia. Our goal is not just to close sites but to pursue the criminal masterminds and financial networks behind them.
Our campaign is delivering tangible results. Over the last 12 months, Cambodian authorities investigated 832 suspected locations and carried out crackdowns at 663. Eighty-six scam compounds have been dismantled and brought under control pending legal seizure.
Authorities have forwarded 446 cases to court involving 3,927 accused from 29 nationalities, including ringleaders and accomplices. Regulators have also taken action against 27 casinos linked to online scams, revoking 18 licenses and suspending nine.
Recent arrests of high-profile businesspeople and senior officials show that the campaign is reaching beyond low-level offenders. Cambodia’s Anti-Corruption Unit has also acted in four cases involving 15 senior officials and law-enforcement officers suspected of involvement. No one is above the law.
The next step is to make these gains permanent by ensuring that closed operations remain closed and criminal networks cannot simply reappear elsewhere. We are already seeing those networks change tactics, moving away from large compounds toward smaller, decentralized operations. That makes it even more important to pursue the people and financial networks behind them rather than focusing only on physical sites.
In April, Cambodia strengthened its legal framework with the Law on Combating Online Scams. The law gives authorities stronger tools to pursue those who organize or support these crimes and to trace and seize criminal proceeds.
Financial institutions and other regulated businesses must report suspicious transactions to the Cambodia Financial Intelligence Unit, which shares relevant intelligence with investigators. This helps authorities trace criminal proceeds and identify the people behind scam operations.
Cambodian authorities have already frozen more than $300 million in bank accounts linked to online scams, with additional assets undergoing freezing procedures and assessment. But once the money crosses a border, international cooperation becomes essential.
A victim of an online scam may be in London or Los Angeles while the people running the scam are thousands of miles away. Criminal proceeds can pass through several jurisdictions before reaching those who ultimately control the operation. No police force can follow that chain alone.
In July, the United Kingdom assumed the presidency of the Financial Action Task Force, which sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing. Under the UK’s leadership, FATF has made combating fraud a priority, including the financial flows linked to scam compounds. It is focused on strengthening financial intelligence and international information sharing.
Cambodia supports that approach. We continue to work with international law-enforcement partners and through the Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering. In July, FBI Director Kash Patel visited Cambodia to discuss scam operations targeting Americans and to strengthen cooperation between US and Cambodian law enforcement.
Cooperation against transnational crime should cut across geopolitical divisions. The same networks target people in the United States and China, among many other countries.
International cooperation will be a focus of the International Conference on Combating Online Scams (ICCOS 2026), which Cambodia is hosting in Phnom Penh on September 23 and 24. Participants include representatives from China, the UK, and the United States, including the FBI, alongside governments from across Asia and international organizations such as Interpol.
The theme is “Acting Together towards Breaking the Chain and Eradication of Online Scams.” The challenge is to turn international cooperation into operational cooperation. Financial intelligence must move quickly across borders to identify criminal proceeds before they are moved beyond investigators’ reach. Countries also need to be able to freeze and recover criminal proceeds more effectively.
There is also a human cost to consider. Many people found inside scam operations have themselves been trafficked or coerced, while victims around the world have lost their savings to these crimes. Protecting those who have been exploited also requires cross-border cooperation. Following the money helps us pursue those who profit from both trafficking and fraud.
Cambodia will continue to disrupt scam operations and prosecute those responsible. We will work to ensure that closed operations cannot simply reopen elsewhere. But these are transnational criminal networks, and lasting success requires international action.
Cambodia is doing its part. In Phnom Penh later this September, we will work with our international partners to dismantle the financial networks behind these scams and cut off the profits that keep this global criminal industry alive.
Chhay Sinarith is a Senior Minister in the Cambodian Government and the Vice-Chairman of the Commission for Combating Online Scams. He is leading Cambodia’s nationwide campaign to dismantle online scam networks and implement the country’s new Law on Combating Online Scams.

title: Meet 4 people who got the HIV prevention jab
content:
By Mia Malan and Ida Jooste
Almost 55,000 people in South Africa have already had a shot that protects them against HIV for six months at a time, the health department says. Lenacapavir, or LEN, has been available through the health department since June. The injection gives near-perfect protection against HIV and, because it lasts for six months, people only need to return to a clinic twice a year.
For now, LEN is available at 360 government clinics — about one in 10 — across six provinces. The Free State, Limpopo and the Northern Cape don’t yet have it. That should start to change when cheaper generic versions become available in 2027.
The health department plans to use some of its own budget, along with a grant from the Children’s Investment Fund Foundation through the Global Fund, to buy more LEN and expand the number of clinics that offer it. And South Africa needs to scale up fast. Modelling shows that between one-million and two-million people would need to use LEN each year between now and 2043 for the injection to make a big enough dent in new HIV infections to help end Aids as a public health threat.
For now, the health department is focusing particularly on people who have a higher chance of getting HIV: teenage girls and young women aged 15–24, sex workers, transgender women, gay and bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, and pregnant and breastfeeding women. People who use government clinics and want HIV prevention medicine can choose between a daily prevention pill and the six-monthly injection. Both are free.
Getting LEN involves a little more than just one jab. At the first appointment, a health worker gives two injections, either in the stomach or buttocks. The person also takes two LEN tablets that day and another two the next day. If they return for their next injections on time — 24 to 28 weeks after the previous injection — they don’t need to take the tablets again.
But what is it actually like to use LEN — and why are people choosing it over a daily pill?
We spoke to four people from groups the roll-out is particularly trying to reach: a sex worker, a student, a pregnant woman and a transgender woman. Here, in their own words, they explain why they chose LEN, what getting the injections felt like and whether they’ll be back for their next shots.
Precious Mafanga
I’m 39, a mother of four, a wife and a sex worker.
I live at Ikhwezi Hostel in Langa. I’m also a peer educator with Tholwana e Molemo, where I help other sex workers with their health and other needs.
In our work, time is money. We rent rooms for R500 a day, so sometimes we’re chasing minutes. On a good day, it’s one client after another. As soon as he leaves, it’s “next!” You can easily make more than R1,500.
But on a bad day, you might not even make enough to pay the rent. Then there’s pressure to agree when a client offers you more money for sex without a condom. You pay the rent and start all over again the next day.
I got my LEN injections at Delft Community Health Centre near Cape Town in June and spent a few hours at the clinic.
While I was waiting, my phone kept ringing. Clients were calling and I wanted to leave to see them. But I stayed and got my injections.
Before LEN, I took the daily HIV prevention pill for four or five years. It wasn’t easy. You have to remember to take it every day.
With LEN, I don’t have that worry. The medicine stays in my body for six months, so I only have to go to the clinic twice a year.
As a peer educator, I help link other sex workers to clinics where they can get HIV prevention medicine without being judged. When US funding cuts disrupted outreach services, many of our sisters stopped taking their daily prevention pills. Some later tested positive for HIV.
That’s why LEN is so important for us.
But we still hand out condoms because LEN doesn’t prevent pregnancy or other sexually transmitted infections.
I’ve sent my eldest child’s partner to get LEN. And now that I know younger people can get it too, I’m sending my 17-year-old.
I wish people understood our work as sex workers. We’re not selling our bodies. We’re selling a service. We’re exchanging sex for money.
Because if I sold my body to a client, I wouldn’t have a body anymore.
Siviwe Gaika
I’m 24 and live in New Brighton, a township in Gqeberha. I’m studying towards a law degree at Nelson Mandela University. It’s my second degree; I already have one in social sciences from Rhodes University. I also run the social media accounts for Advocates for the Prevention of HIV and Aids.
Before LEN, I wasn’t using HIV prevention medicine because the only option I knew about was a daily pill. My life is busy: if I’m not in lectures, I’m studying or working. Taking a pill every day would have been one more thing on an already long to-do list.
So when I heard about LEN, I thought, ‘If I only have to go to the clinic and deal with the nurses twice a year, I can do that."
I got my shot at Kwazakhele Community Health Centre in Gqeberha, about 20 minutes from where I live. But it took three visits.
The first time I went, in June, I was told there wasn’t a nurse trained to give LEN. The second time, staff said the clinic didn’t have a certificate to prescribe it.
I went back in early July and finally got my shot. I had to wait about four hours, partly because I didn’t have a clinic file and they had to open one for me. There wasn’t a separate queue for LEN either, so I had to wait in the general queue.
The nurse who gave me the injection was patient. She explained how LEN works, that I could choose between the daily pill and LEN, and what side effects I might have.
She also got me to set a reminder on my phone to take the two LEN pills I needed the next day.
I deliberately took the pills in public because I wanted someone to ask me what I was taking. I was in the library when my alarm went off. One person came over and asked about the pills, so my plan worked.
I also recorded myself taking them and posted the video on TikTok. I told people what I was taking and how long it had taken me to get LEN — because four hours is a long time to wait.
I told them about the two bumps I got under my skin where I was injected too. I couldn’t wear jeans for about two weeks and took a break from the gym. But the bumps gradually got smaller, and they don’t bother me anymore.
That’s been my journey.
Lindiwe Mqatazana
I’m 25 and a waste picker, working on contract for the City of Cape Town.
In July, I suspected I was pregnant, so I went to Vuyani Clinic in Gugulethu for a test. When it came back positive, I decided there and then that I wanted to start LEN.
There’s an unborn child now, so I have to stay safe for him or her.
The nurse explained that LEN is safe for me and my baby. After I tested negative for HIV, she told me I could choose between the six-monthly LEN injection and the daily HIV prevention pill. I chose LEN.
I had used the daily pill before, but it made me feel nauseous. I also travel home to the Eastern Cape often. When you’re on the road, it’s easy to forget your tablets.
Getting LEN was easy. I went to the clinic early in the morning, so they could see me straight away. From walking in to walking out it took about an hour-and-a-half.
The nurses used ice to numb the injection sites for about 10 minutes. My friends are scared of LEN because they think it has to be injected into your stomach. But because I’m pregnant, the nurses injected it into my buttocks. You can choose.
I can feel a small bump under the skin on my left buttock, but I haven’t had headaches or other side effects.
As young women, we often don’t use condoms. We date. But everything has changed for me now that I’m pregnant.
I think I’ll tell people at work about LEN too, because some of them are in danger.
Dimpho Tsotetsi
I’m Dimpho Divine Tsotetsi. I’m a trans woman and work as a peer educator. I used to work at a donor-funded transgender clinic, but it closed after US President Donald Trump cut funding for such facilities in 2025.
I got my LEN shot on July 1 at Chiawelo Community Health Centre in Soweto. I arrived at 9.15am and got the injections at 10.45am.
First, I had to join the general queue to get tested for HIV. Once I tested negative, I could move to a special LEN queue.
The nurse gave me two LEN tablets. About 30 minutes later, I got two injections, one on each side of my tummy. I have a small bump under my skin at each injection site. [LEN forms a depot under the skin, which slowly releases the medicine over six months.]
The bumps bothered me at first. I normally wear a waist trainer, but it was uncomfortable for about a month. Now I wear it only sometimes and choose looser, flowy clothes. I can still feel the bumps when I wear tight clothes.
Before LEN, I took the daily HIV prevention pill for nine years. I struggled to take it consistently. You get pill fatigue. You also have to remember to take your pills with you when you go out or travel.
So I’m definitely going back for my second LEN shot after six months. The bumps caused some discomfort, but that’s nothing compared with the burden of taking a pill every day.
There’s another advantage for trans people. In our community, some people associate taking HIV prevention medicine with being promiscuous. A partner can find your pills. They can’t find an injection you got at a clinic.
LEN makes my life simpler.
This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism. Sign up for the newsletter.

title: A Belgian professor and 20 years of pediatric liver transplants in Vietnam
content:
Raymond Reding, MD, PhD, is a Belgian specialist in pediatric liver transplantation at Saint-Luc University Clinics in Brussels, where he has been involved in the development of one of Europe's established pediatric liver transplant programs.
His connection with Vietnam dates back to the late 1990s, when a university cooperation program began training doctors from Children's Hospital 2 in pediatric gastrointestinal and liver transplant care.
A connection that changed everything
Reding's connection with Vietnam began in 1995, when he read an article about the successful separation of the Vietnamese-German conjoined twins.
Impressed by the surgery, he contacted Professor Tran Dong A, who had led the operation, and proposed collaborating on pediatric gastrointestinal and liver care, including liver transplantation.
Reding initially came to Vietnam with a more modest goal: to share his knowledge and experience in treating pediatric gastrointestinal diseases.
But his visits soon took a different direction.
Hospital leaders wanted to go beyond knowledge-sharing and build a pediatric organ transplant program, a completely new and highly challenging field in Vietnam at the time.
Reding was asked to help turn that ambition into reality, beginning a collaboration that would eventually make pediatric liver transplantation a lasting capability at Children's Hospital 2.
Reding recalled Tran Dong A, then head of surgery at Children's Hospital 2, telling him that the hospital truly wanted to perform organ transplants, but that realizing the goal would require extensive preparation.
The two sides therefore started with the fundamentals, working toward the first pediatric liver transplant in southern Vietnam.
On December 5, 2005, that operation was successfully performed at Children's Hospital 2, opening a new chapter for pediatric liver transplantation in the region.
The first transplant would not happen overnight.
Reding and the hospital team spent five years preparing for the operation, working on everything from specialized equipment and infrastructure to comprehensive protocols for running an entire transplant program.
But Reding said the most critical factor was the people.
The team focused on training doctors and medical staff who were not only technically skilled, but also able to understand one another's every move, coordinate seamlessly and remain ready to face unprecedented challenges.
Building a self-sustaining program
Since the first transplant in 2005, Children's Hospital 2's program has continued to grow.
A total of 74 liver transplants have now been performed at the hospital. During Reding's most recent visit, he and the hospital team carried out four living-donor liver transplants in just one week.
The journey has also been marked by difficult and tense moments.
Reding still remembers a surgical complication that occurred on the very first day of the hospital's first liver transplant, when pediatric patient Xuan Quy had to undergo an immediate second operation. Working together, the team managed to save the transplanted liver.
The program's ability to stand on its own was tested even further during the COVID-19 pandemic.
With international flights grounded and travel severely restricted, Reding could no longer be there to work alongside the doctors at Children's Hospital 2.
For about two years, however, the team continued performing liver transplants and maintained and developed the program without his direct support.
When Reding returned after the pandemic, he was impressed by how much the team had advanced, progress that motivated him to keep returning to Vietnam and working alongside them.
Today, Reding sees clear progress in both the number of transplants the hospital can perform and, more importantly, the quality of its care.
"The number of transplants the hospital can perform has increased, but what is much more important, in my view, is the quality," Reding said.
He said the team's medical expertise has improved significantly and now meets international standards, putting Children's Hospital 2 among the leading pediatric transplant centers in Vietnam and Southeast Asia.
More importantly, the team has become strong enough to operate independently and continue developing the program.
For Reding, the progress also points to a larger ambition for pediatric transplantation in Vietnam.
He estimates that the country could have around 100 pediatric transplant cases a year and hopes Children's Hospital 2 can eventually perform most of them, including for children from northern Vietnam.
He believes Vietnam has the potential to develop transplant centers that serve as regional referral centers, not only for Vietnamese patients but also for children from neighboring countries.
In his view, Children's Hospital 2 has the potential to become a trusted regional center for pediatric transplantation as its expertise and capacity continue to grow.
The doctor who gave children a second chance at life
For the doctors and families who have worked with Reding, he is more than a doctor. He is a lifeline for children with severe liver disease, giving them a second chance at life when they are on the brink of death.
Professor Tran Dong A, who first brought Reding into collaboration with Children's Hospital 2, said their relationship has grown far beyond medicine. "Professor Raymond Reding and I have become very close friends," Tran Dong A said.
For Dr. Pham Ngoc Thach, deputy director of Children's Hospital 2, Reding's greatest contribution has been helping the hospital build a strong transplant program that allows more children with severe liver disease to receive treatment in Vietnam.
"The greatest contribution of Professor Raymond Reding is helping turn a highly complex technique into a strong medical capability for the hospital," Thach said.
Dr. Tran Thanh Tri, head of the hospital's liver, biliary and pancreatic surgery and liver transplant department, was among the Vietnamese doctors sent to Belgium for liver transplant training in 2002.
He said Reding's influence extends beyond technical knowledge. "I have learned so much from Professor Reding. He is not only my mentor, but also the person who shaped the way I practice my profession," Tri said.
But for the families whose children have received a new liver, Reding's contribution is measured in something much more personal: the chance to keep their children alive and watch them grow up.
N.T.B. was diagnosed with F4 cirrhosis and received a liver transplant from his mother at just 22 months old, with Reding and the Children's Hospital 2 team performing the procedure. Now five, he is healthy and in his second year of school.
His mother, Vu Anh Nguyen, still remembers meeting Reding before the operation. "Our family was extremely happy and felt very fortunate when Professor Raymond Reding agreed to perform the transplant with the Children's Hospital 2 team," Nguyen said.
"We met him the day before the surgery and were deeply impressed by how gentle, cheerful and approachable he was."
"He is not only a foreign surgeon, but also the person who gave our child a chance at life and gave us back our family life. Our family will always remember and be grateful to Professor Reding," Nguyen said.
For the families of children once on the brink of death, Reding's legacy is not measured in surgical techniques or the number of procedures performed. It is measured in children who survived, families who stayed together and ordinary childhoods that became possible.

title: Artesanos de Monsefú preparan homenaje al papa León XIV con estola única tejida a mano
content:
Una pieza artesanal que une la tradición mochica, la identidad lambayecana y los símbolos de la fe católica será obsequiada al papa León XIV como homenaje de los artesanos de Monsefú , con motivo de cumpleaños N* 71 y su próximo retorno a tierras chiclayanas.


El maestro artesano monsefuano representante del Taller Arte Surimana, Jesús Ayasta Caicedo, elaboró una estola de 2.50 metros de largo por 15 centímetros de ancho, confeccionada íntegramente a mano mediante el tradicional telar de cintura y posteriormente bordada con motivos representativos de la cultura mochica.
En diálogo con la Agencia Andina, Ayasta Caicedo informó que la elaboración demandó aproximadamente 25 días de trabajo, desde el tejido y diseño hasta el bordado y forrado, convirtiendo la pieza en una creación única que busca expresar el afecto de los artesanos lambayecanos hacia el Santo Padre.
Indicó que
la estola será entregada a la Diócesis de Chiclayo, con la esperanza de que pueda llegar al papa León XIV y, eventualmente, ser utilizada durante alguna de las actividades previstas para su visita a Lambayeque.
La iniciativa también refleja el potencial de Monsefú como destino de turismo cultural.
Igualmente, artesanas de este distrito han preparado bordados, textiles, accesorios, artículos religiosos y otros productos inspirados en la tradición del distrito y en la visita papal, que serán obsequiados al Sumo Pontífice  por su cumpleaños -en su retorno a la Ciudad de la Amistad.
Según las artesana, Yolanda Delgado de Mimbela, informó que estos productos ya vienen despertando interés entre visitantes nacionales y extranjeros, mientras los talleres continúan innovando sin dejar de lado las técnicas y expresiones culturales propias de Monsefú.
La llegada del Papa, prevista para el 13 y 14 de noviembre, representa así una oportunidad para que el talento de los artesanos lambayecanos trascienda las fronteras y muestre al Perú y al mundo la riqueza cultural de esta región del norte peruano.
Publicado: 14/9/2026

title: South Korea’s ‘sea women’ seek justice after marine habitat devastated by harbor work
content:
- A community of hanyeo, South Korea’s free-diving women fishers, accuse a harbor project in their village of devastating the local marine habitat they’ve depended on for decades for their livelihoods.
- The women are demanding compensation from construction giant Ssangyong, taking their fight to Seoul after the loss of their traditional fishing grounds.
- They are considering a lawsuit against either the company or the government, but face a costly, years-long legal battle requiring scientific evidence linking the construction activity to the habitat’s destruction.
- With many of the haenyeo now in their 70s and 80s, time is not on their side — and some say the settlement on offer would barely cover the cost of their fight.
GUMAN-RI, South Korea — This fishing village, on the eastern coast of the Korean Peninsula, is filled with scars. Every summer, typhoons rumble in from the Pacific Ocean to snap trees and flip fishing boats. Huge ships, including a 4,000-ton cargo vessel in 2005, have sunk or run aground on the rocky coast, sullying marine food sources. In the 1950-1953 Korean War, dozens of villagers were massacred.
Time and time again, however, the resilient residents of Guman-ri have figured out a way to soldier on. But their latest setback has stupefied them.
In 2021, South Korean construction giant Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. began work to expand and repair the breakwaters at the local harbor. Since then, the surrounding marine habitat has slowly withered away. By early 2025, the lush seabed had become a graveyard for dead marine plants and animals.
Gone are the glimmering abalones, chunky sea snails, and translucent green seaweed that once populated the waters around the cape, despite its designation as a protected marine area. In their place is white, dusty cement debris, which the villagers have blamed on the construction of the breakwaters.
The habitat’s demise is itself an environmental tragedy. But it has brought an emotional and financial death knell to the village’s nearly two dozen haenyeo, the “sea women,” who dive to harvest a variety of shellfish and marine plants without oxygen tanks.
Kim Choon-hee, a 78-year-old haenyeo, points to the cement debris covering the gravel of the village beaches. “None of that was there,” she says. “It is now everywhere.”
David versus Goliath
Kim is besties with fellow haenyeo Im Gil-seok and Lee Yeon-oak. The three women, all born in 1947, have swum and dived for more than five decades in the waters off the tight-knit village.
On land, it’s clear that age has caught up with them. Lee can’t sit for more than 10 minutes because of a bad back. Im has been taking pills for years after a stroke. Kim has a stooped posture because of a slightly bent back.
But in the water, it’s as if they’re in their 20s. The septuagenarians gracefully glide through the water to depths of up to 10 meters (33 feet) and can hold their breath for 90 seconds, all without an oxygen tank.
“It almost feels like I’m flying,” Kim says with a chuckle, describing her underwater swim.
Their 12-hour days include swimming for hours in the chilly seas, tugging their 20-kilogram (44-pound) catches to shore, and squatting for several more hours to cut and clean their catch before they sell it at the local market.
For much of the past 50 or so years, the long days would have earned the haenyeo enough to put food on the table and even send their kids to school.
That changed, however, when Ssangyong began construction work at the harbor, which sits between Guman-ri and the neighboring fishing village of Daebo-ri.
At first, the haenyeo weren’t worried when construction cranes began lifting 5-ton rocks like Lego pieces, throwing gravel and sand everywhere. After all, the underwater marine forest was unaffected.
By 2023, however, the effects of the construction started to show, they say. Abalones, once bigger than their hands, shrank in size, they tell Mongabay. Carcasses of sea cucumbers littered the seafloor. Shrubs of surfgrass disappeared. Within two years, the marine life had completely vanished.
“There is nothing now,” Im says.
The loss of the fishing grounds has affected 53 haenyeo in the two villages: 23 in Guman-ri and 30 in Daebo-ri.
Unbeknownst to them, it was the local office of the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries that proposed the construction work in 2017. The office, located in Pohang, the biggest city in North Gyeongsang province, touted the need to expand breakwaters to better protect the villagers’ fishing boats from typhoons.
The proposal was endorsed by seven elderly fishers who represented the two villages. When the haenyeo found out what had happened in 2025, they confronted the men for not consulting them before accepting the government’s plan. However, the fishers told them that they didn’t know what could happen to the coastal habitat or the livelihoods of the haenyeo.
The men apologized. But by then, it was too late. The local ecosystem, which Kim describes as “a gold mine of seafood,” had collapsed.
In June this year, all the haenyeo from Guman-ri and Daebo-ri, in their 60s to 80s, went to Seoul to stage a protest. They hired two buses to drive them five hours to the headquarters of Ssangyong E&C.
For two days, on June 29 and 30, they staged a sit-in under the scorching sun outside the high-rise building that houses the construction firm.
Clad in black rubber diving suits and carrying tewak, floating devices that double up as baskets to carry their catch, the women wore red headbands that read, “Compensation for the damage.”
As they yelled chants, they waved banners that also read, “We’ve lost our livelihoods. Compensate our neighborhoods!”
The haenyeo demanded Ssangyong, which earned a net profit of 154.2 billion won ($112 million) last year, compensate them after allegedly destroying their livelihoods and the sea they depend on.
Unable to afford hotel rooms, they slept on the streets. “It was a tearful experience because it was demeaning,” Lee recalls.
Their protest, however, attracted attention from national media and lawmaker Lee Sang-hwi, who represents their district.
After the sit-in, Ssangyong offered an out-of-court settlement. The divers decline to disclose the proposed settlement sum, but Jeong Mi-ja, 77, the unofficial leader of the haenyeo, says it amounted to little. “After we pay for the costs of [going to] Seoul, it’s finished,” she says.
Ssangyong did not reply to Mongabay’s request for comment by the time this story was published.
Between a rock and a hard place
The haenyeo are leaning toward signing the settlement, although they say they realize the money offered by Ssangyong is far from enough.
The alternative is going through a costly years-long lawsuit, with no guarantee of winning.
They will also have to hire outside experts to collect enough scientific data to establish a causal relationship between the construction work at the harbor and the destruction of Guman-ri’s coastal habitat.
The haenyeo say they’re also aware that the alternative to a settlement, a lawsuit, could last a decade or even more. And by the time it ends, regardless of the outcome, some of them would be over 90. They might even be dead, Im tells Mongabay.
Choi Jae-hong, a lawyer in Seoul who specializes in environmental cases, says the haenyeo are fighting an uphill battle.
They will have to prove that the debris from the construction either “destroyed the food sources of the marine life in the area and starved them to death, or that [the debris] clogged the breathing organs and suffocated the marine life,” he tells Mongabay by phone.
“That’s really hard to prove,” Choi continues. “And expensive.”
The fact that the waters off Guman-ri aren’t private property further undermines their case, he adds.
Research, however, has shown how coastal construction can adversely affect nearby marine habitats.
“The diffusion of suspended sediment resulting from construction clouds the water, undermines marine animals’ ability to breathe and feed, and destroys spawning grounds and habitats,” Yoon Han-sam, a professor of marine and harbor engineering at Pukyong National University in Busan, writes in a paper published in the Journal of the Korean Society for Marine Environment and Energy. “This is the most common cause of damage to fishing grounds.”
For now, some of the haenyeo hire buses two to three times a week to travel three hours north to coastal towns like Yeongdeok to earn a living.
Instead of the usual dawn wake-up time, their day now starts at 2 a.m. It takes them two hours to get ready, including getting suited up, and another three hours to reach their new diving grounds.
The 16-hour day ends at 6 p.m. Even the indefatigable haenyeo say the work is unsustainable.
A bleak future
The women are also contemplating a lawsuit against the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, which they accuse of proceeding with the construction project without their consent.
The Pohang Regional Office of Oceans and Fisheries has denied accusations of wrongdoing. An official tells Mongabay that the office notified Guman-ri’s representatives about the construction multiple times between 2017 and 2020.
It was the responsibility of those representatives, and not the government, to then inform the haenyeo, the official says.
Choi, the lawyer, says the haenyeo are likely to face a steeper uphill battle to sue the authorities because under South Korean law, the government doesn’t need to directly apprise them about the construction plan. “If they want to go [to] court, it might be actually better to file a lawsuit against Ssangyong.”
The haenyeo don’t necessarily expect to win any hypothetical lawsuit against the government. But if they do, some of the reparation money could be used to clean up the harbor, says Seo In-mahn, Jeong’s nephew.
“The marine habitat in front of Guman-ri and Daebo-ri isn’t the sole possession of the haenyeo grandmothers,” says Seo, 67.
“It is the community’s,” he says. “If you think about it, the habitat is also that of the entire country, and the world.
“So shouldn’t the entire world care about what’s happening here?”
Banner image: Guman-ri resident and haenyeo Kim Choon-hee walks along the village coastline on Aug. 15, 2026, looking at debris suspected of coming from the nearby construction. Image by Andrew Jeong for Mongabay.
Citation:

title: The A’uwẽ-Xavante people's denunciation of megaprojects in Brazil
content:
This article, written by Djalma Ramalho (Aranã Caboclo), was originally published on the Cultural Survival website on August 17, 2026. It is republished here in an edited version with permission. Learn more about their campaign here.
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Under a heavy sky, on the shores of Lake Léman in Geneva, Switzerland, red words cut across the landscape. In front of the Jet d’Eau of Bains des Pâquis, Geneva’s emblematic fountain, two messages appeared: “Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming” and “Stop the megaprojects fragmenting Ró, the A’uwẽ-Xavante territory.”
The intervention marked the international launch of a campaign led by A’uwẽ-Xavante leaders, communities, and organizations, during the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) in July 2026. They are an Indigenous group from Brazil’s Centre-West region, with a population of around 25,300. According to the 2022 Census, Brazil has 1,694,836 people who identified as Indigenous, from 391 ethnicities.
While government representatives debated international policies and standards inside the United Nations, the Indigenous delegation occupied public space to convey a message: There can be no legitimate development when its realization depends on the destruction of the material, spiritual, and political conditions that sustain a people’s existence.
Dreaming is not a metaphor
For the A’uwẽ-Xavante people, dreaming is a concrete dimension of social, spiritual, and political life. In her research on dream performance among the A’uwẽ-Xavante, anthropologist Laura Graham demonstrates that dreams establish relationships among the living, ancestors, and immortal beings. Songs received during sleep are shared with the community and may become collective performances that bring together narrative, music, dance, memory, and cultural continuity.
In one episode documented by Graham, an elder recounts receiving songs from ancestral creators intended for the living, so that by singing them collectively, the A’uwẽ could continue to exist as A’uwẽ. The dreamer, therefore, does not appear as the individual owner of a creation, but rather as a mediator of knowledge that belongs to, and circulates among, the people as a whole, and becomes part of the community’s living heritage.
In recent years, according to the leaders who developed the campaign, dreams have also begun to convey warnings related to growing pressures on their territories. The expansion of railways, highways, hydroelectric projects, monocultures, and other large-scale developments is, therefore, understood not merely as a physical transformation of the landscape, but as a threat to the relationships that make it possible to receive, transmit, and enact this knowledge.
To defend the right to dream, then, is to defend the territorial conditions that make dreaming possible.
Ró: Cerrado, world, territory, and life
The word Ró also has no full equivalent in the conventional translation of “territory.” Geographer Maria Lucia Cereda Gomide explains that Ró can simultaneously mean “Cerrado, world, our land, everything.” It refers to a territorial and cosmological complex that extends from the village space to the Cerrado [biome in Central Brazil], encompassing its waters, animals, plants, and the spirits that inhabit this world. Ró is a living network of relationships. It encompasses hunting, gathering, and fishing grounds; ancient villages; burial grounds; rivers and pathways; medicinal plants; ceremonial sites, and ancestral presences that sustain collective life.
A technical note by the Brazilian Anthropological Association, published in 2025, emphasizes that A’uwẽ-Xavante territoriality depends on practices such as journeys through the Cerrado, the gathering of roots, fruits, and fibers, fishing, hunting, and circuits of reciprocity that connect families, clans, age groups, and different Indigenous lands. Territorial fragmentation, therefore, compromises not only access to natural resources but also the ability to perform ceremonies, transmit knowledge, and maintain the social and cosmological relationships through which the A’uwẽ constitute themselves as a people. It would also cut across relationships that cannot be contained within the administrative boundaries drawn by the state.
So, the message projected in Geneva – “Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming” – is a demand for the protection of the integrity of Ró and for the continuity of their existence itself. A’uwẽ-Xavante leader Hiparidi Top’tiro states in the campaign’s document: “Any project that affects one of our territories is a problem for the entire A’uwẽ-Xavante People.”
Territories, lives, and dreams cut by tracks
The campaign’s central demand is protection of the rights of the A’uwẽ-Xavante people in the face of the construction of the Center-West Integration Railway (FICO), also known as EF-354. Presented by the Brazilian government as a strategic project to reduce logistics costs and expand freight rail transport, it is part of a broader corridor designed primarily to move soybeans, corn, and other commodities produced in the region. By advancing the project without ensuring adequate free, prior, and informed consultation, the Brazilian state has failed to protect the rights of Indigenous peoples.
The FICO Railway is a federal project of approximately 1,641 kilometers (1,020 miles) under the responsibility of Infra S.A. Its first section, covering approximately 363 kilometers (226 miles), between Mara Rosa, in the state of Goiás, and Água Boa, Mato Grosso state, is currently being built by the mining company Vale as compensation for the early renewal of another concession. Studies and administrative processes related to the route have identified Xavante territories within its area of influence, raising serious concerns about territorial, environmental, social, and cultural impacts.
In May 2026, Infra S.A. itself reported that approximately 80 kilometers (50 miles) of the final portion of the section currently under construction depended on the completion of the Basic Environmental Plan – Indigenous Component (PBA-CI) and on negotiations with Xavante communities. This makes clear that the relationship between the railway and Indigenous territories is not merely indirect, but a central issue affecting the project’s implementation.
The technical note issued by the Brazilian Anthropological Association states that the railway affects areas of traditional occupation, claimed lands that aren’t yet demarcated, gathering areas, former villages, burial grounds, waterways, and sacred sites. The document recommends suspending construction and the installation license until adequate consultation has taken place, and altering the route so that the railway does not cross A’uwẽ-Xavante territoriality.
The campaign’s advocacy brief, Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming, launched in Geneva, argues that FICO cannot be assessed merely as an isolated railway line. It is part of a broader architecture of highways, railways, waterways, and export corridors that is likely to intensify commodity flows, non-Indigenous occupation, and economic pressure on already fragmented territories.
Consultation under dispute
In February 2026, the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon (COIAB) denounced irregularities in the consultation process related to FICO. According to the organization, meetings scheduled for some Indigenous lands were held at very short intervals, leaving communities insufficient time to conduct internal discussions in accordance with their own decision-making processes. They also documented reports of pressure on Indigenous leaders, the absence of independent technical assistance, and communication difficulties among communities distributed across territories that have historically been fragmented. The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office (MPF) opened an administrative proceeding to monitor the consultation process.
Both the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples establish that states must consult and cooperate in good faith with Indigenous Peoples before approving projects affecting their lands, territories, or resources, to obtain their Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC).
Consultation does not simply mean informing a community that a project will proceed but also respecting their decision-making timelines, freedom from coercion, and ability to withhold consent from measures that could compromise their future.
To Europe: Coloniality also travels by rail and electric car
The intervention in Geneva carried a particular symbolic weight. The city is home to the United Nations Office and to numerous institutions connected to the international human rights system. Indigenous representatives are often given only a few minutes to present territorial conflicts shaped by decades of violations.
The campaign also challenges the contradictions of the so-called green transition. Railways, logistics corridors, mining operations, and large-scale infrastructure projects are frequently presented as necessary instruments for building a low-carbon economy. Yet when they advance without the effective participation of affected people, they can reproduce long-standing colonial mechanisms: territorial appropriation, the concentration of economic benefits, and the transfer of environmental and social costs onto Indigenous peoples and traditional communities.
The projection in front of the Jet d’Eau confronted this paradox. Europe, historically implicated in the colonization of Indigenous territories, remains connected to these regions through networks of finance, consumption, mining, agribusiness, and export infrastructure. Changing the energy source without transforming these relationships is not enough. A transition that continues to treat Indigenous territories as sacrifice zones may be technologically new, but it remains politically colonial.
For the A’uwẽ-Xavante, a fragmented territory does not simply mean a reduction in physical space. It means the interruption of pathways, songs, ceremonies, memories, and ancestral relationships. No megaproject can claim to represent the future if its existence depends on destroying the dreams of those who have always cared for the land.

title: Governance Rooted in the Land: Maasai Models of Collective Leadership and Community Responsibility
content: Governance Rooted in the Land: Maasai Models of Collective Leadership and Community Responsibility tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:02 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe By Alice Tipap (Maasai) For countless generations, the Maasai have governed their communities without separating leadership from land, culture, spirituality, livestock, and collective responsibility. Our governance system is not built around one powerful individual. It is a living network of Elders, women, spiritual leaders, family heads, and community assemblies, each carrying different responsibilities. Authority is earned through service, wisdom, integrity, experience, and the ability to protect the well being of the whole community. These structures continue to guide communities through drought, land conflicts, social change, and increasing pressure from conservation, tourism, and investment projects. Although State institutions now exercise formal administrative power, Maasai customary governance remains central to community identity and decision-making. Governance as a Collective Responsibility The Maasai understanding of leadership is based on the principle that no person exists alone. An individual belongs to a family, a clan, a neighborhood, an age-set, a territory, and the wider community. Decisions affecting grazing land, water, livestock, ceremonies, peace, and community relations are therefore not expected to be made privately. Traditionally, important matters are discussed through community gatherings where traditional leaders (spiritual, clan, and age-set), Elders, and other respected members contribute their knowledge. Discussion continues until there is broad consensus and a decision that protects the collective interest. The Maasai age-set system is one of the most recognizable foundations of our social and political organization. Men pass through age-related stages with different responsibilities, moving from boyhood to warriorhood and into adulthood. Each age-set develops its own identity, solidarity, duties, and leadership, playing important political and representative roles. The Olaigwanani is an age-set or a clan leader and spokesperson. His responsibility is not to rule as an individual, but to represent, coordinate, advise, and guide. A respected Olaigwanani must listen carefully, communicate clearly, maintain unity, and act in accordance with community values. He is supported by Elders and cannot legitimately make major decisions without consultation. Elders hold authority because they carry historical knowledge, experience, customary law, memory of relationships among clans, territories, and generations. They mediate disputes, advise families, guide ceremonies, negotiate peace, and interpret community responsibilities. Their legitimacy depends on fairness and trust. An Elder who repeatedly acts selfishly or dishonestly may lose moral authority, even if he retains social status. Customary dispute resolution is intended to restore relationships rather than merely punish the offender. When conflict occurs over livestock, marriage, grazing areas, or family responsibilities, Elders bring the parties together to hear both sides and seek an agreement that allows the community to continue living together. Maasai self-governance is inseparable from pastoral land management. Rangelands are not empty spaces waiting for investment. They are collectively used landscapes that contain wet-season and dry-season grazing areas, livestock routes, salt licks, water points, medicinal plants, sacred sites, wildlife habitats, and areas reserved for calves or vulnerable animals. Community members have traditionally used detailed ecological knowledge to decide when different areas should be grazed or rested. Pasture quality is assessed through the presence of particular grasses and plants, soil conditions, water availability, livestock health, and seasonal patterns. This system depends on mobility. During drought, livestock may need to move across large areas to reach water and pasture. Community leaders negotiate access, coordinate use, prevent premature grazing of reserved areas, and address conflicts between neighboring groups. These practices have allowed people, livestock, and wildlife to coexist across variable dryland environments. The modern fragmentation of rangelands by conservation boundaries, farms, tourism concessions, roads, trophy-hunting areas, and private investments has weakened these governance systems. When communities lose access to dry season grazing areas or livestock routes, they also lose the ability to apply their knowledge responsibly. The result is overcrowding, pasture degradation, conflict, livestock deaths, and poverty. Women’s Leadership and Authority The Maasai governance system often focuses only on males. However, Maasai women have always exercised important forms of social, cultural, spiritual, and household authority, even when they are excluded from formal public leadership. Women manage households, food and water distribution, water, housing, and much of the daily knowledge connecting family well being to livestock and the environment. They preserve and transmit songs, oral histories, medicinal knowledge, ceremonies, and values to the children. Women also observe changes in water availability, nutrition, livestock productivity, disease, and household vulnerability. This knowledge is essential to community decision-making. Women may collectively express approval, concern, blessing, or protest through gatherings, songs, ceremonies, and direct engagement with elders. Their moral voice can influence family and community decisions. Patriarchal practices have limited women’s participation in land allocation, village leadership, and formal negotiations with government or investors, but today, Maasai women are demanding fuller recognition by strengthening governance so that it reflects the knowledge and rights of the whole community. Indigenous Women Development Affairs supports women to participate in village councils, land discussions, environmental governance, and advocacy. Maasai women are also beginning to serve on leadership bodies responsible for grazing, conservation, and finance. Self-Governance Under Pressure In Tanzania, customary Maasai governance now operates alongside village governments, district authorities, courts, conservation agencies, and national laws. This creates both opportunities and tensions. Some traditional leaders work closely with elected/appointed leaders, while others are consulted only after decisions have already been made. In many cases, communities receive information about our land use plans, restrictions, conservation/tourism investments, or carbon projects after negotiations have advanced. When outsiders/negotiators identify only a few individuals as community representatives and bypass broader assemblies, they create division. Meaningful self-governance requires Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Communities must receive information in languages they understand, have sufficient time to discuss it through their own institutions, and include women and youth. They must be free to accept, reject, or reshape proposed activities. Consultation cannot be reduced to attendance sheets or meetings called after decisions have been made. Current pressures in Ngorongoro and Loliondo demonstrate why Indigenous governance remains essential. Restrictions on land access, livestock confiscation, reduced services, and displacement threaten not only livelihoods but also the institutions through which Maasai communities govern themselves. Reports have documented serious concerns regarding access to health services, pressure to relocate, and interference with pastoral life in Ngorongoro. Preserving Maasai governance does not mean freezing it in the past. It means strengthening its core principles of collective responsibility, accountability, consensus, respect for Elders, protection of land, intergenerational learning, and service to the community while ensuring equality and responding to new realities. We need stronger collaboration among customary leaders, women’s groups, youth, local government structures, civil society, and legal advocates. We need documentation of customary laws, grazing institutions, oral histories, and ecological knowledge, while protecting sacred and confidential information. Young people should learn not only the names of leadership structures, but also the values that make them legitimate. Digital tools can help record community decisions, map resources, preserve oral knowledge, and communicate threats. However, technology must remain under community control. Knowledge should not be extracted, commercialized, or published without consent. For the Maasai, self-governance is ultimately about maintaining a living relationship with people, territory, livestock, wildlife, ancestors, and future generations. As environmental and political pressures increase, the survival of Maasai governance will depend on recognition of our collective land rights and our authority to determine our own futures. Our governance systems are not obstacles to development. They are proven models of resilience, stewardship, peacebuilding, and belonging. Protecting them is essential not only for Maasai cultural survival, but for the dryland ecosystems that our communities have sustained for generations. A strong Indigenous governance system must be honest about internal inequalities. Culture should protect dignity: it should not be used to silence women, youth, persons with disabilities, or poorer households. Our traditions are living systems capable of reflection and change. Alice Tipap (Maasai) is Climate Change Action Coordinator at Indigenous Women Development Affairs (IWDA). title: Tái hiện đồ chơi Trung thu xưa giữa lòng Hà Nội
content:
Tái hiện đồ chơi Trung thu xưa giữa lòng Hà Nội
Tối 10/9, hàng chục món đồ chơi Trung thu truyền thống được phục dựng và trưng bày tại triển lãm "Lưu trăng".
Triển lãm thuộc chuỗi hoạt động văn hóa Tết Trung thu 2026 do Ban quản lý hồ Hoàn Kiếm và phố cổ Hà Nội phối hợp Câu lạc bộ Đình Làng Việt tổ chức tại Trung tâm Văn hóa Nghệ thuật.
