title: Follow the Flowers, Find Ethiopia
content:
Follow the Flowers, Find Ethiopia
Addis Ababa, September 11, 2026 (FMC) — There is a moment each year when Ethiopia seems to change its rhythm.
The rains begin to loosen their hold. The hills remain intensely green, the air grows brighter, and the countryside takes on the colour of renewal. In towns and villages, preparations gather pace. New clothes appear. Homes are made ready. Songs return to the streets. Families begin their journeys home.
And then the flowers arrive.
The delicate yellow blooms of Adey Abeba have become one of the gentlest signatures of Ethiopia’s New Year. But they are also an invitation—to look beyond a single celebration and discover a country whose seasons are marked not only by weather, but by memory, movement, music, faith, food and the meeting of communities.
For a traveller arriving in Ethiopia at this time of year, the calendar can feel less like a sequence of dates than a route through a living cultural landscape.
The journey begins with Enkutatash, celebrated on Meskerem 1 as Ethiopia enters 2019. It is a day of family gatherings, traditional food, church observances, children’s songs and greetings exchanged between generations. Yet its meaning reaches beyond the festivities. It is one of those occasions when the ordinary social fabric of the country becomes especially visible: families reconnect, neighbours visit, children move from house to house, and communities welcome another year together.
Then the journey continues.
Across Ethiopia, September and the weeks that follow bring a remarkable succession of cultural and religious celebrations. Among them is Gifaataa, the New Year festival of the Wolaita people, celebrated between mid-September and early October. UNESCO inscribed Gifaataa on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2025, recognising a tradition in which people prepare their surroundings, return home to their families and seek reconciliation before the festival begins.
In other communities, the season carries its own ceremonies, music, dances and ways of welcoming renewal. Ethiopia’s cultural landscape is not a single story repeated in different places. It is a collection of stories lived side by side.
That becomes particularly visible as the country approaches Meskel.
In Addis Ababa, the enormous Demera bonfire transforms the heart of the capital into a place of ceremony and gathering. Across the country, the commemoration of the finding of the True Holy Cross brings together people of different ages, backgrounds and communities.
UNESCO inscribed Meskel on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013, noting among its social dimensions the reunion of families, reconciliation and the strengthening of social cohesion.
And when the season moves toward early October, another major cultural moment emerges with Irreecha, the Oromo thanksgiving celebration associated with the close of the rainy season.
It is a time of gratitude, gathering and collective expression, extending the season of celebration beyond the New Year itself.
This is why September in Ethiopia is difficult to describe simply as a holiday season.
It is a cultural passage.
The landscape itself participates. The country is emerging from Kiremt, the main rainy season, leaving the highlands and valleys richly green before the brighter, drier months settle in.
Rivers and waterfalls have been replenished; fields carry the memory of the rains; mountain slopes and rural landscapes appear at their freshest.
For visitors, this creates a rare meeting of landscape and culture.
A journey can move from the ancient streets and distinctive architecture of Harar to the monumental history of Aksum; from the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela to the lakes and highlands around Bahir Dar; from the dramatic landscapes of the Simien Mountains to the Rift Valley and the communities whose traditions give each place its own character.
But the most memorable encounters may not always be found on a monument.
They can happen around a coffee ceremony, at a family table, beside a festival procession, in a marketplace, on a rural road or in a conversation with someone who has a story about the place where they live.
This is where Ethiopia’s heritage becomes more than something to be viewed.
It becomes something to experience.
The country’s cultural wealth also tells a larger story about how Ethiopians have understood community and continuity.
Traditions have carried knowledge across generations—through music and oral history, craftsmanship and architecture, agricultural practices and customary systems, religious observances and communal celebrations.
Some of these traditions have now found recognition on the global stage. UNESCO’s current list includes seven elements associated with Ethiopia, ranging from Meskel and Ethiopian Epiphany to the Gada system, Fichee-Chambalaalla, Gifaataa, Shuwalid and Xeer Ciise.
Yet recognition is not the reason these traditions endure.
They endure because people continue to live them.
That distinction matters.
For Ethiopia, cultural heritage is not simply an inheritance preserved behind glass. It is part of the country’s social sovereignty—the ability of communities to retain their own stories, languages, values and ways of marking life while presenting them confidently to the wider world.
And that confidence gives the country’s hospitality a particular character.
Visitors are not merely being shown Ethiopia; they are being invited into moments that Ethiopians themselves value. The welcome is found in the sharing of food, the ceremony of coffee, the exchange of greetings, the opening of a home and the instinct to gather around occasions that matter.
In that sense, culture becomes a form of diplomacy long before a passport is stamped.
The season also offers a different way of seeing Ethiopia’s history.
A country with some of Africa’s most recognisable ancient monuments is often approached through the lens of the past. But travel through Ethiopia reveals something more dynamic: history is continually being interpreted by people living in the present.
Ancient cities remain inhabited. Religious traditions continue alongside contemporary life. Indigenous knowledge sits beside modern education and technology. Traditional celebrations fill streets that are also part of rapidly changing cities.
The old and the new do not always stand apart.
They share the same landscape.
That may be the most compelling reason to experience Ethiopia now.
The country is not asking the world merely to admire its history. It is revealing how history, culture, nature and contemporary life continue to shape one another.
Follow the flowers, and the road leads to a New Year.
Follow the celebrations, and it leads to communities.
Follow the communities, and it leads to stories.
Follow those stories, and a much larger Ethiopia begins to emerge—one whose identity has been carried across centuries, whose landscapes are entering a brilliant new season, and whose people continue to give their traditions new life.
The flowers will fade.
The celebrations will move on.
But the roads remain open, the mountains remain on the horizon, the coffee will still be poured, and the stories will still be waiting.
This is Ethiopia at the turning of the season: not simply a destination to see, but a country to encounter.

title: Beyond silence: Why sign language is a fundamental right, not a privilege
content:
Ammon News - A sudden midnight medical emergency inside a family home is a terrifying prospect for any parent. For a deaf mother or father, however, the crisis carries an added, invisible barrier: the agonizing race against time to call for help, explain precise symptoms, and understand urgent instructions when conventional communication channels fail.
In such critical moments, the breakdown rarely stems from sign language itself, but from an environment unprepared to listen. True accessibility means that emergency response networks, public institutions, and civic spaces are structured to receive, process, and act upon information from deaf citizens with the same speed and accuracy afforded to anyone else.
Marking the International Day of Sign Languages on September 23, this report explores how institutional innovation is transforming emergency access in the Kingdom, alongside the broader societal push to treat sign language not as a courtesy, but as an inherent right.
Recognizing that standard voice calls exclude the deaf community, the Public Security Directorate (PSD) operates a specialized, round-the-clock emergency dispatch service linked directly to the main 911 operations room.
The system functions through the dedicated "114 Deaf JO" mobile application, which routes video calls to operations officers fluent in sign language. When a call is placed, trained personnel assess the emergency–logging the caller's precise coordinates, the nature of the crisis, and whether active injuries or hazards exist – while dispatching the appropriate field units.
Crucially, the protocol bridges the critical window before paramedics arrive. Operations officers can guide callers through emergency first aid via live video sign language, maintaining continuous oversight through the OnCall management system until responders reach the scene. While requests span humanitarian aid and traffic accidents, the platform has also become a vital lifeline for reporting cybercrimes and securing specialized police intervention.
While technological interventions mark a major leap forward, international advocates argue that systemic integration must go much deeper. In a statement observing this year's global theme – "The Human Rights of Deaf People" – the international advocacy network "Communication Without Borders" stressed that legal recognition of sign language is merely a starting point.
Full civic inclusion requires unobstructed access to national sign languages across education, employment, and public services. Advocates emphasize that sign languages are complete, sophisticated linguistic systems rather than auxiliary gestures. Guaranteeing early childhood exposure to sign language and inclusive education is essential to cognitive development, while adhering to the core principle of disability advocacy: "nothing about us without us." For Rawan Abu Khuffash, the first hearing-impaired graduate of the Faculty of Sharia, accessible communication is synonymous with personal dignity and autonomy.
"When public and private institutions fail to provide accessible communication channels, they strip deaf citizens of their independence," Abu Khuffash said. Navigating legal, medical, or administrative transactions without an interpreter often forces individuals to rely on intermediaries, compromising personal privacy and increasing the risk of miscommunication.
As institutions prepare to mark the international day, Abu Khuffash urged a cultural and professional shift across Jordan's labor market – one that invests in staff training, digital accommodations, and barrier-free environments.
Ultimately, the national dialogue surrounding the deaf community converges on a singular truth: accessibility and communication are not optional amenities or charitable concessions. They are foundational pillars of a truly inclusive society where every citizen can navigate life on equal terms.
Petra

title: How Iraq’s iconic masgouf fish found a home in Dubai
content: Dubai: Unlike most grilled fish dishes, Iraqi masgouf is not cooked directly over a flame. Instead, the fish is opened, cleaned and seasoned before being placed beside glowing embers, where it cooks slowly under the careful supervision of the chef.The process is as important as the dish itself. Time, patience and constant attention to the fire are central to a tradition that has been passed down through generations of Iraqi families and has travelled far beyond the banks of the Tigris and Euphrates.In Dubai, masgouf has found a new audience among Emiratis and residents from a wide range of nationalities, evolving from a dish associated primarily with the Iraqi community into one of the emirate's recognised culinary experiences.Decades of traditionChef Azad MohammedFor Chef Azad Mohammed's family, the story of masgouf dates back to 1973 in Iraqi Kurdistan, where the family first began preparing the dish.In 1999, they brought that experience to the UAE through Erbil Iraqi Kebab restaurant, carrying with them skills and techniques accumulated over decades. The profession remained within the family, with knowledge passed down from one generation to the next, making the preparation of masgouf both a craft and a family tradition.Traditionally, masgouf is associated with river fish and open-fire cooking, making it an integral part of Iraqi food culture. Yet its significance extends beyond its ingredients. Preparation requires space, time and careful management of the fire, creating a visual spectacle for diners waiting for their meal.The fish is opened and placed near the embers, allowing heat to reach it gradually. The chef continuously monitors the fire, adjusting temperature, distance and cooking time to achieve the desired result.Azad said handling the fire, selecting the right fish and preparing it correctly are inseparable from the quality of masgouf, adding that years of experience have helped his family preserve the traditional method they learned in Iraq.A craft learned through experienceMuch of the knowledge involved in preparing masgouf remains unwritten.Like many traditional dishes, masgouf carries more than flavour. Picture: Dennis MallariChefs learn to read the heat of the fire, judge when the fish should be moved closer or further away and monitor subtle changes during the grilling process. Over time, these skills become practical knowledge transmitted through generations.According to Azad, mastering these details requires years of experience.He noted that not every type of fish is suitable for preparing masgouf in the traditional Iraqi style, as different varieties vary in texture and their ability to withstand the slow grilling method.Among the fish commonly used are sea bream and sea bass, with understanding their characteristics forming an essential part of the chef's expertise.More than a mealLike many traditional dishes, masgouf carries more than flavour.The aroma of the wood fire, the anticipation surrounding the cooking process and the gathering of family and friends around the fish become part of the experience and memory associated with the dish.When masgouf travels to a new city, it carries not only a recipe but also the customs and stories connected to it. The dining table becomes a space where a piece of its place of origin is recreated.Restaurant owners say the dish's popularity in Dubai extends well beyond Iraqi diners and increasingly includes Emiratis and residents from different cultural backgrounds.Its growing presence reflects the broader exchange of culinary traditions within Dubai's multicultural society, where food often serves as an introduction to another culture.Numbers behind the traditionAccording to Azad, between 100 and 150 fish are prepared daily, with each fish averaging around four kilograms in weight.This amounts to between 400 and 600 kilograms of fish being prepared every day.The figures highlight the scale of the operation and the labour-intensive nature of the craft. Each fish must be cleaned, prepared and carefully grilled, with the process relying on experience and constant supervision of the fire.In an era when many kitchens prioritise speed, masgouf remains deliberately slow. The fish needs time, the fire demands attention and customers must wait.For many diners, however, that waiting is part of the experience.One restaurant customer summed up the connection simply by saying: "I never miss Friday."For many families, the dish has become part of a weekly ritual centred on gathering together.A journey that continuesIn Dubai, where cuisines and cultures from around the world meet, masgouf has found a new audience without abandoning the elements that define it: fish, fire, time and expertise.Between the glowing embers and the dining table, the dish continues its journey as more than just a meal. It remains a craft that carries the memory of a place, a cooking tradition passed down through generations and a culinary experience that has crossed borders while retaining its Iraqi identity.

title: Burnham: My dad would want me to push on and make change
content:
Burnham: My dad would want me to push on and make change
Burnham’s father died earlier this week after suffering from Alzheimer’s
- Bookmark
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his father Roy would want him to be "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make" as he returned to work on Wednesday.
The Prime Minister stated his relatives have been "helped through this difficult time by people’s warmth and compassion", highlighting messages from across political divides.
Downing Street confirmed the passing of his father Roy, who lived with Alzheimer’s, earlier this week, leading Mr Burnham to pause public engagements.
Asked about his wellbeing on returning to work, Mr Burnham said: "We’re doing OK, thank you.
"It is hard, and it will be hard for a little while. But better to get back to the job," he remarked.
Speaking at McLaren’s Technology Centre in Woking, Mr Burnham noted: "I also want to thank the leaders of the other parties, all of whom sent a message.
"It shows there is decency in British politics still, and that’s that’s what we need to see.
"So it’s a thank you from us all, the whole family. But my dad would want me to be back out there … bringing some of the changes that he always pushed me to make."
Mr Burnham has previously discussed his father's condition, which prevented Roy from knowing his son was now Prime Minister.
That personal experience remains a key motivation behind the Prime Minister’s push for social care reform.
In a major speech this July, Mr Burnham pledged action to assist "my dad and the millions like him" affected by system inequities.
On X this Wednesday, he posted: "We are grateful to everyone who has shared a kind message about my dad, particularly the leaders of the other parties.
"My family and I have been helped through this difficult time by people’s warmth and compassion. It means a great deal to us and we wanted to say thank you."
Sympathies were expressed to the Prime Minister by opposition leaders, including Kemi Badenoch of the Conservatives, Sir Ed Davey of the Liberal Democrats, Reform UK’s Nigel Farage, and Zack Polanski of the Green Party.
Dementia UK’s chief nursing officer, Paul Edwards, noted that by discussing his story, the Prime Minister "helped shine an important light on the profound impact that dementia can have on the whole family, as well as the urgent need to improve dementia care and support".
Roy Burnham, who died in his mid-80s, worked as a telephone engineer for the Post Office and later BT.
He raised Mr Burnham alongside his mother Eileen and two brothers in Culcheth, Cheshire.
In his 2024 memoir Head North, co-written with Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram, Mr Burnham reflected on his 1970s and 1980s upbringing.
He recalled: "Neither my dad, Roy, nor my mum, Eileen, went to university.
"But both could have done if they had grown up in a different time and in a different place.
"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go. But that did not make them pushy parents in any way.
"Their approach was one of quiet encouragement and confidence-building. Our family home in Culcheth was always full of music, life, laughter, love and support."
